senses.definition: To make ashamed; to embarrass; to destroy the self-possession of, as by exciting suddenly a consciousness of guilt, mistake, or inferiority; to disconcert; to discomfit.

core.definition: To make someone suddenly feel embarrassed or self-conscious, often by exposing a mistake or a sense of inferiority.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the vowel is short, like the a in 'cat'. End with the sh sound. Avoid saying 'uh-BAYSH' with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it describes a sudden loss of composure, which is uncomfortable but not cruel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'embarrass' or 'make someone feel awkward' in everyday talk. Abash appears mostly in writing, news, or fiction, as in 'He was abashed by the praise.' The adjective 'abashed' is far more common than the verb, so you will often hear 'she looked abashed'.

distinctions.note: Embarrass is everyday and general; abash is more literary and suggests a sudden loss of confidence or composure.
Abash makes someone feel self-conscious; abase lowers their rank or dignity.

examples.everyday: She looked a little abashed when everyone clapped for her mistake.
examples.professional: Our CFO looked abashed when the audit found spreadsheet errors she had missed.
examples.analytical: Socrates often abashes his interlocutors by showing that their confident definitions contradict each other.

nuance.analogy: Like a student called on with the wrong answer, going quiet and red-faced in front of the class.
nuance.etymology: From Old French esbair 'to astonish', from es- (ex-) and a root related to 'gape'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long a as in 'abase'; abash has a short vowel.
Using abash as a noun; the common form is the adjective 'abashed'.

abash.etymology: Attested from 1303, as Middle English *abaisen*, *abaishen*, *abashen* (“lose one's composure, be upset”), from the later 14th-century also transitive "to make ashamed, to perplex or embarrass"; from Anglo-Norman *abaiss*, from Middle French *abair*,…

senses.definition: To go with or attend as a companion or associate; to keep company with; to go along with.
senses.example: Geoffrey accompanied the group on their pilgrimage.

senses.definition: To supplement with; add to.
To cohabit (with). (Can we add an example for this sense?)
To be found at the same time.
senses.example: Thunder almost always accompanies lightning during a rain storm.

senses.definition: To perform an accompanying part or parts in a composition.
To perform an accompanying part next to (another instrument or musician).
senses.example: The strings were accompanied by two woodwinds.

core.definition: To go along with someone, or to play a musical part alongside a singer or soloist.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the KUM syllable. The first vowel is a weak uh, not 'ay,' and the final -ny is pronounced 'nee.' The middle syllable is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It sounds more formal than go with or come with.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say go with or come with in casual speech and use accompany mainly in formal or written English, as in 'She was accompanied by her lawyer.' In music, accompany means to play piano or guitar behind a singer. The passive be accompanied by is common in invitations and announcements.

distinctions.note: Go with is casual and everyday; accompany is more formal and often appears in writing or announcements.
Escort implies guiding or protecting someone, often a person of rank; accompany simply means being with someone.

examples.everyday: I'll go with you to the dentist so you're not going alone.
examples.professional: Please accompany the proposal with the updated cost model and the test results.
examples.analytical: A theory of freedom must accompany an account of responsibility, or it collapses into mere preference.

nuance.analogy: Like a bass line that follows the melody without taking the spotlight.
nuance.etymology: From Old French acompagnier, from a- 'to' and compagnon, companion, from Latin companio.
common_mistakes: Adding with after accompany when a person is the object: say accompany him, not accompany with him. With is correct when something accompanies something else, as in accompany the report with a summary.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ay' (uh-KAM-puh-nee) instead of uh-KUM-puh-nee.

senses.definition: An English unit of land area (symbol: a. or ac.) originally denoting a day's plowing for a yoke of oxen, now standardized as 4,840 square yards or 4,046.86 square meters.
Any of various similar units of area in other systems.
A wide expanse.
senses.example: I like my new house—there’s acres of space!

senses.definition: A large quantity.
(historical) An area of 10,240 square yards or 4 quarters.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A unit of land area equal to 4,840 square yards, about 0.4 hectare, used in the United States for measuring land.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AY, and make the second syllable a reduced, r-colored vowel, not a full ker or kree. Americans say it like the word acre, with a clear r at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a standard measurement in everyday real estate and farming talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use acres for farms, parks, large lots and real estate listings, as in a three-acre lot. Abbreviate it as ac. in writing. Most house lots are described in square feet, and hectares are used mainly in science or by people from other countries.
word_family: acre-foot (noun, a unit of water volume)

distinctions.note: An acre is one unit of land area, while acreage is the total amount of land, as in the farm's acreage.
A hectare is about 2.47 acres; Americans use acres in everyday land talk and hectares mainly in science or international reports.

examples.everyday: Our neighbors just bought three acres out past the lake, so they're finally getting their own pond.
examples.professional: The developer's proposal covers forty acres, but only twelve are zoned for housing.
examples.analytical: Medieval land measures such as the acre tied land to labor, since it was roughly the area one team of oxen could plow in a day.

nuance.analogy: A square about 209 feet on each side makes one acre, so picture a large city block, not a whole neighborhood.
nuance.etymology: From Old English aecer, field, cognate with Latin ager.
common_mistakes: Saying the second syllable with a full vowel, as in AY-ker, instead of a reduced r-colored vowel.
Using acre for the total amount of land; that amount is acreage.
nuance.biblical_note: The Revised Standard Version uses acre in Isaiah 5:10, where ten acres of vineyard yield one bath, a comment on poor harvest. The Hebrew word tsemed, a yoke of land, is the amount a yoke of oxen could plow in a day. Key passage: Isaiah 5:10.

acre.etymology: From Middle English *acre*, *aker*, from Old English *æcer* (“field where crops are grown”), from **akr*, from Proto-Germanic **akraz* (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₂éǵros* (“field”).

senses.definition: For a particular purpose.
Created on the spur of the moment; impromptu.
Postulated solely to save a theory from being falsified, without making any new predictions.
Independent of previously instated network structure, like routers or access points.
On the spur of the moment.
For a particular purpose.

core.definition: Made or arranged for one specific purpose, not planned in advance; improvised for the situation at hand.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'ad' like 'add' with light stress, then stress HAHK. The H is soft and the vowel is the open American 'ah' of 'hot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can imply a quick fix, but it is often used positively to describe a sensible, purpose-built solution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ad hoc constantly in business and tech, such as an ad hoc committee or an ad hoc meeting. It is slightly formal but very common at work and in news. You can say 'on an ad hoc basis' to mean as needed, not on a fixed schedule.

distinctions.note: Improvised suggests making something up on the spot without preparation; ad hoc implies it was created deliberately for a specific purpose.
Temporary is about how long something lasts; ad hoc is about why it exists and how it was formed.

examples.everyday: We're doing an ad hoc carpool to the game since my car is already full.
examples.professional: I'm setting up an ad hoc group to fix the dashboard bug before Friday's release.
examples.analytical: Postulating an unobservable variable to rescue the model is ad hoc, because it adds no testable predictions.

nuance.analogy: Like a patch sewn onto a torn jacket for today's trip: it works for this purpose.
nuance.etymology: Latin, 'for this': ad, 'to' + hoc, 'this'.
common_mistakes: Using ad hoc as a noun, as in 'an ad hoc'; it is an adjective or adverb, so say 'an ad hoc committee'.
Pronouncing the second word as 'hawk', which makes the vowel too long.

senses.definition: Adhesive, sticking to something.
Having the quality of clinging or sticking fast to something.
Attaching or pressing against a different organ.
Showing adherence to a treatment.
A person who has membership in some group, association, or religion.

core.definition: A person who strongly supports a particular belief, group, leader, or cause and is part of it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, HEER, and use a reduced first vowel, so it does not sound like 'ad-HEER-unt'. The final t is light and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes committed membership, though in political or religious contexts it may sound partisan.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adherent in formal writing about religion, politics, or movements, such as 'adherents of the faith' or 'an adherent of the theory.' In casual talk, people say 'follower,' 'supporter,' or 'member.' Calling someone an adherent in conversation can sound formal or slightly distant.

distinctions.note: Follower is the everyday word and can mean someone who admires a person online, while adherent implies a more formal, committed membership in a belief or movement.
Member describes formal membership in a group, while adherent focuses on belief and commitment to a doctrine or cause.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a big adherent of that diet, so she's always pushing it on everyone.
examples.professional: The product team's most committed adherents are the engineers who helped build the original API.
examples.analytical: Early adherents of the theory treated its predictions as settled facts, which later critics challenged.

nuance.analogy: An adherent is like a member of a choir who keeps singing the same song, even when the rest of the crowd moves on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adhaerens, 'sticking to,' the present participle of adhaerere, 'to stick to.'
common_mistakes: Using 'adherent to' when 'adherent of' is more common for a person who supports a belief.
Using adherent as an adjective in everyday speech, where 'loyal' or 'committed' would be more natural.

adherent.etymology: From Middle English *adherent*, from Old French *adherent*, from Latin *adhaerēns*, present participle of *adhaereō* (“to stick to, cling”).

senses.definition: An act of religious worship.
Admiration or esteem.
The act of adoring; loving devotion or fascination; an intense love sometimes bordering on veneration or infatuation.
senses.example: Because of Gerald's adoration for Katie, he was blind to her flaws.

senses.definition: Worship of Christ in the Eucharistic host in the Catholic Church, often while exposed in a monstrance.
(historical) The selection of a pope by acclamation and before any formal ballot (excluded as a voting method in 1621 by Pope Gregory XV).
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Deep love, admiration, or devotion toward someone or something, or the act of worshipping God.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the RAY syllable, and the first vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat.' Learners often reduce the middle syllable too much, and the American r should be clearly pronounced before the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes warm, strong devotion, though in a casual context it can sound exaggerated if used for ordinary liking.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say 'adoration' about a fan's feelings for a celebrity or a parent's feelings for a child, usually with a touch of drama. In church or religious writing, it means worship directed toward God. Americans rarely use it for a casual preference, so for something mild, say 'love' or 'really like' instead.

distinctions.note: Admiration is respect for qualities someone has; adoration is much stronger and emotional, close to worship.
Love is the general term; adoration implies an intense, almost reverent devotion that focuses on one person or thing.

examples.everyday: Our dog looks at my daughter with total adoration every time she walks in the door.
examples.professional: The product team's adoration for the old design system made it hard to propose a change, even when the data showed users were struggling.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes the adoration due to God alone from the lesser honor that may be given to the saints.

nuance.analogy: Adoration is like a spotlight pointed at one person or thing: all your attention and warmth go to that single focus.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adoratio, from adorare 'to worship, to address with prayer,' from ad- 'to' plus orare 'to pray or speak.'
common_mistakes: Using it for mild liking, which sounds dramatic in American English; 'I have adoration for pizza' is too strong.
Mispronouncing the first vowel as 'ah' instead of short 'a.'
Confusing it with 'adorable,' which is an adjective meaning cute or lovable.

adoration.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *adoration*, from Latin *adōrātiō* (“worship, adoration”), from *adōrō* (“beseech; adore, worship”), from *ad* (“to, towards”) + *ōrō* (“beg”).

core.definition: An ancient town in the lowlands of Judah, and a nearby cave where David hid from King Saul.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, DUL. The final syllable is a reduced 'um', and the first vowel is a weak 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a historical place, though the cave is associated with David's early outlaw years.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter 'Adullam' in Bible reading, church teaching, or an archaeology or history class. In everyday speech it would only come up when discussing David's life. A place name like this does not usually need further explanation in a Bible class, but a teacher might describe it as a cave in Judah.

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher said David hid in a cave at Adullam when he was running from Saul.
examples.professional: In the lesson on David's early years, we'll look at Adullam as the place where his band of followers first gathered.
examples.analytical: The cave of Adullam in 1 Samuel 22 marks David's transition from a fugitive to the leader of a band of outcasts and debtors.

nuance.analogy: Adullam is like a hideout that became a recruiting ground, a place where people in trouble found a leader.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Adullam, a place name of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'AD-ul-um'; the main stress falls on DUL.
Confusing it with Adonijah or Adonikam, which are different names.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Adullam' (עֲדֻלָּם) is a place name in the Judean lowlands. Genesis 38:1 mentions Judah's friend Hirah the Adullamite. 1 Samuel 22:1 describes David escaping to the cave of Adullam, where his family and others joined him. 2 Samuel 23:13 recalls three of David's mighty men going down to him at the cave of Adullam during a time of danger.

senses.definition: Of, or characterized by adultery.
senses.example: adulterous behavior

core.definition: Involving or guilty of adultery, meaning sexual relations between a married person and someone who is not their spouse.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of the root, DUL. The middle syllable is an unstressed, r-colored schwa, so say 'ter' lightly, and the final '-ous' is a reduced 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word always signals moral disapproval, and it is often used in religious, legal or literary contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'adulterous' mostly for relationships, behavior or people described in a formal or moral way, such as 'an adulterous affair' or 'an adulterous husband.' In everyday talk people more often say 'cheating' or 'unfaithful,' which sound less stiff. The word can also be used in Bible study and sermons, where 'adulterous generation' is a familiar phrase.

distinctions.note: 'Unfaithful' is the common, everyday word and can describe emotional or disloyal conduct, while 'adulterous' specifically refers to sexual infidelity within marriage.
'Promiscuous' describes a pattern of having many sexual partners and does not require a marriage vow to be broken, so it does not mean the same as 'adulterous.'

examples.everyday: My neighbor's husband was caught in an adulterous affair, and now the whole street is talking about it.
examples.professional: The HR investigator said the complaint was not about office politics but about an adulterous relationship between two managers who were married to other people.
examples.analytical: Jesus describes the adulterous heart in the Sermon on the Mount, suggesting that sin begins before any outward act is committed.

nuance.analogy: Think of a marriage as a locked door with one key: 'adulterous' describes someone who has tried that lock with a key that belongs to someone else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adulterare, to corrupt or defile, from ad- plus alter, another.
common_mistakes: Using 'adulterous' for any broken promise or emotional betrayal; in American speech it refers specifically to sexual infidelity in marriage.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'uh-dul-TER-us'; the main stress is on the first syllable of the root, DUL.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Old Testament the root is na'aph (נָאַף), used for sexual unfaithfulness in marriage, and the New Testament uses moichalis (μοιχαλίς) for an adulterous person. Matthew 12:39 speaks of an 'evil and adulterous generation,' where the image is spiritual infidelity to God, as in the prophets' language of Israel's unfaithfulness. Mark 8:38 uses the same phrase for a generation that rejects Jesus and his words. James 4:4 addresses 'adulterers and adulteresses' to rebuke believers who love the world more than God.

senses.definition: The rules, policies and processes that guide how AI is developed and used.

core.definition: The rules, policies and processes that guide how AI is developed, deployed and monitored inside an organization or society.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the I in AI and the first syllable of governance, GUV. The middle syllable is reduced to er, and the ending is nuns, not nance.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests responsibility, though it can sound bureaucratic in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in corporate, legal and policy settings, such as compliance meetings or risk reports. It is more formal than AI rules and often appears in phrases like AI governance team. In everyday talk, people usually say AI regulation or rules for AI instead.

distinctions.note: Regulation means laws and official rules imposed by government, while AI governance is broader and includes internal company policies and processes.
AI ethics asks what is morally right, while AI governance turns those values into concrete rules, roles and accountability structures.

examples.everyday: My company just hired someone to handle AI governance, so I guess they're getting serious about it.
examples.professional: Before we roll out the chatbot, legal wants an AI governance review that covers data retention and bias testing.
examples.analytical: Effective AI governance depends less on any single rule than on whether institutions can assign responsibility when automated decisions cause harm.

nuance.analogy: Like traffic laws and signals on a busy highway: they don't design the cars, but they decide how everyone shares the road.
nuance.etymology: From Old French governance, from governer, meaning to steer, from Latin gubernare, meaning to steer a ship.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a long nance sound instead of the reduced nuns.
Confusing governance with government; governance refers to the processes, while government is the body that governs.

conversation.text: AI governance covers the policies, roles, and processes for approving and monitoring AI systems.
Under our AI governance framework, high-impact models need sign-off from legal and risk.
International AI governance discussions focus on safety standards and cross-border cooperation.

senses.definition: The belief or teaching that because only the spiritual "law of faith" (Romans 3:27) is essential for salvation, obedience to any practical or moral law has no role to play, even as a guide to conduct or as a test of the genuineness of faith.
Opposition to the Torah.

core.definition: The belief that Christians, saved by grace through faith, are not bound by moral law and its demands.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOH. The word is long, so keep the 'anti' as /ænti/ and the final -ism as a quick 'iz-um'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is almost always used as an accusation or a label for an error.
nuance.usage_note: A theological term used in church history and doctrinal debates. Few people claim the label for themselves, and it is often used against opponents. Say 'antinomian' for the adjective or the person.

distinctions.note: Legalism over-emphasizes rule-keeping as a way to earn favor; antinomianism rejects the binding force of moral law. They are opposite errors.
Libertinism is a lifestyle of moral license; antinomianism is a theological position about law and grace, though critics link them.
Anarchism rejects political authority; antinomianism rejects moral law within a religious framework.

examples.everyday: Some people worry that preaching grace too loosely leads to antinomianism.
examples.professional: In today's lecture, we'll look at how Luther responded to charges of antinomianism.
examples.analytical: Paul anticipates the charge of antinomianism in Romans 6, insisting that grace does not license sin.

nuance.analogy: Like believing that since your debt is forgiven, you may stop caring about how you spend money.
nuance.etymology: From Greek anti, 'against', + nomos, 'law'; coined in the Reformation era.
common_mistakes: Misplacing the stress; it is anti-NO-mian-ism.
Confusing it with 'antinomy', a contradiction between two principles.
nuance.biblical_note: Paul addresses the charge in Romans 6:1-2, rejecting the idea that we should sin so grace may abound. Romans 3:31 says faith upholds the law, and Galatians 5:13 warns against using freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. The Greek word nomos means 'law'.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy rejects antinomianism, holding that grace and ascetic effort cooperate in the life of salvation and that the commandments are essential to the spiritual life.
Catholicism teaches that faith must work through love and obedience, and condemned antinomian views at Trent, which held that the commandments are not for the justified.

Protestants reject antinomianism while stressing justification by faith alone. Lutherans distinguish law and gospel, Reformed speak of a third use of the law as a guide, and Wesleyans stress holiness; each charges others with leaning toward antinomianism or legalism.

antinomianism.etymology: From *antinomian* + *ism*, coined by Martin Luther, notably used in his Against the Antinomians (1539).

senses.definition: Marked by extreme anger or fury.
Of or relating to apoplexy.
A person suffering from apoplexy.

core.definition: Extremely angry or furious, so that someone seems about to lose control; in medicine, relating to a stroke.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLEK, the third syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on the first. Don't pronounce the middle letter-p as a separate sound; the p is a quick 'p' followed by the 'l.' The -tic ending is 'tik.'

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes intense anger that is often seen as excessive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apoplectic in casual speech as an exaggeration, as in 'Dad was apoplectic when he saw the bill.' It is common in news and humor, and it can sound stiff in formal contexts. The medical sense relating to apoplexy, or stroke, is rare outside medical writing, so the everyday anger sense is the one you need.

distinctions.note: Angry is the neutral everyday word, while apoplectic signals an extreme, almost explosive level of fury.
Furious is strong but common, while apoplectic is more dramatic and suggests the person is nearly out of control.

examples.everyday: My landlord got apoplectic when he saw the late payment, and he texted me six times before lunch.
examples.professional: The client was apoplectic about the missed deadline, so we spent the afternoon calming them down on a call.
examples.analytical: The commentator's apoplectic tone turned a policy debate into a personal attack, which weakened his actual argument.

nuance.analogy: Being apoplectic is like a kettle that has boiled over: the pressure builds past the point where it can stay contained.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin apoplecticus, from Greek apoplēktikos 'disabled by a stroke,' from apoplēssein 'to strike down.'
common_mistakes: Confusing apoplectic with apoplexy, which is the noun for a stroke and not a synonym for anger.
Using apoplectic for mild annoyance; it describes extreme fury, so it can sound exaggerated.

apoplectic.etymology: From French *apoplectique*, from Late Latin *apoplēcticus*, from Ancient Greek *ἀποπληκτικός*, from *ἀπόπληκτος*, from *ἀποπλήσσω*, from *ἀπό* (“of, from”) + *πλήσσω* (“I strike”).

senses.definition: An act or instance of appropriating.
That which is appropriated.
Public funds set aside for a specific purpose.
The use of borrowed elements in the creation of a new work.
The assimilation of concepts into a governing framework.
In church law, the making over of a benefice to an owner who receives the tithes, but is bound to appoint a vicar for the spiritual service of the parish.
The principle that supplies granted by a legislature are only to be expended in the manner specified by that legislature.

core.definition: Taking something, often without permission, for one's own use; or, in government, money formally set aside for a specific purpose.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AY, the fourth syllable. The verb 'appropriate' stresses PROH, so the stress shifts in the noun; keep the middle 'pree' sound, not 'pray'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in budget or legal contexts; negative when it describes taking someone else's property or culture.
nuance.usage_note: In American news, appropriation most often refers to 'cultural appropriation', meaning adopting elements of a minority culture without respect, or to congressional spending bills called appropriations. In casual talk, 'borrowing' is neutral, while 'appropriation' sounds accusatory. Americans use the plural 'appropriations' for government budgets.

distinctions.note: Appropriation is an action of taking or allocating; appropriateness is the quality of being suitable.
Theft is a crime of taking property; appropriation can be legal, as with funds allocated by Congress, or cultural rather than legal.

examples.everyday: People get into arguments about cultural appropriation online all the time.
examples.professional: Finance needs the appropriation request approved before we can buy the new servers.
examples.analytical: Legal scholars debate whether the appropriation of an artist's style constitutes theft or fair use.

nuance.analogy: An appropriation is like a budget envelope: money is set aside for one purpose and cannot be spent somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'appropriare', to make one's own, from Latin 'proprius', one's own.
common_mistakes: Using 'appropriation' for friendly borrowing, which can sound accusatory.
Confusing 'appropriation' with 'appropriateness'; one is an act, the other a quality.

appropriation.etymology: From Middle English *appropriacion*, *appropriacioun*, from Medieval Latin *appropriātiō*.

senses.definition: Full of ardor; expressing passion, spirit, or enthusiasm.
Providing light or heat.

core.definition: Showing intense passion, enthusiasm, or devotion; also, giving off strong heat or light.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second is a weak schwa, so it sounds like AHR-dunt, not ar-DENT. Keep the r strong and do not insert a vowel between the d and the n.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises strong, sincere enthusiasm, but it can sound slightly formal or dramatic when describing everyday hobbies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ardent most often in formal or written contexts, as in an ardent supporter, an ardent fan, or an ardent believer. In casual speech people usually say big fan or really into something, but ardent fan is a natural, slightly elevated way to describe a devoted fan. Avoid it for something trivial unless you want a humorous tone.

distinctions.note: Enthusiastic is the everyday word for eager interest; ardent is stronger and suggests deep, committed devotion.
Fervent is close in meaning and often used for religious or political feelings; ardent is more general and common for fandom or love.
Avid means eager and frequent, often about a hobby or habit; ardent focuses more on emotional intensity.

examples.everyday: My sister is an ardent fan of the Giants, so she watches every game with her friends.
examples.professional: Jamal is an ardent advocate for better testing before we ship new models.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard was an ardent critic of a faith that had become merely respectable.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that burns hot and steady when everything around it has cooled.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ardens, burning, the present participle of ardere, to burn.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in ar-DENT, which sounds like a different word to Americans.
Using ardent for a mild liking, where into it or a big fan sounds more natural.

ardent.etymology: First attested circa 14th century as Middle English *ardaunt*, borrowed from Anglo-Norman *ardent* and Old French *ardant*, from Latin *ardentem*, accusative of *ardēns*, present participle of *ardeō* (“to burn”).

senses.definition: Expresses surprise or disbelief.

core.definition: An expression of surprise, disbelief, or annoyance, used to ask whether someone is joking or serious about something unbelievable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KID, and 'are you' runs together into one quick sound, 'ar-yoo.' Learners often stress 'are' or 'you' instead, which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative depending on tone: said with a laugh it is playful, said flatly or sharply it sounds annoyed or sarcastic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this constantly with friends, family, and coworkers, often with a rising or emphatic tone. It can sound rude if you say it to a boss or a customer about a serious decision. Natural replies include 'No, I'm serious' or 'Nope, I'm not kidding.' Avoid it in formal emails.

distinctions.note: 'No way' expresses disbelief or refusal; 'are you kidding' questions whether the speaker means what they just said.
'Seriously?' is a more neutral request for confirmation, while 'are you kidding' often carries irritation.

collocations: are you kidding me right now

examples.everyday: You got a free upgrade on the flight? Are you kidding?
examples.professional: They moved the launch deadline to Friday again? Are you kidding me?
examples.analytical: Are you kidding? A sample of twelve users cannot justify a claim about the whole market.

nuance.analogy: Like a verbal double-take: your face says 'wait, what?' before your mouth finishes the sentence.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'kid,' meaning to tease or joke; the phrase is a modern American idiom.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a real question asking for confirmation of a joke; it is a reaction to something surprising
Stressing 'are' or 'you' instead of KID, which makes the phrase sound robotic

conversation.text: Are you kidding? You met the president?
Are you kidding me? They canceled the flight again?
"Do you want to come?" "Are you kidding? I'd love to!"

senses.definition: Checking on someone who seems upset.

core.definition: A question checking whether someone is all right, especially when they seem upset, hurt, stressed, or unusually quiet.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on KAY, with a lighter stress on oh. The r in 'are' is strong in American speech, and 'you' often reduces to 'yuh' in fast talk.

nuance.connotation: Positive and caring; it shows concern. It can feel intrusive if someone is clearly fine and you ask in a dramatic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this warmly to friends, coworkers, and even strangers who look upset, such as someone who dropped groceries. Natural replies include 'I'm okay, thanks,' 'Yeah, I'm fine,' or 'Not really.' Avoid asking it when nothing seems wrong, because it can sound patronizing. 'Are you doing okay?' is a softer variant.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning and common throughout the US; 'all right' can sound slightly more old-fashioned.
'Fine' asks about general wellbeing; after someone looks upset, it can sound dismissive.

collocations: Are you okay after the fall?

examples.everyday: You dropped your coffee all over the sidewalk. Are you okay?
examples.professional: You went quiet during the design review. Are you okay before we continue?
examples.analytical: In pastoral conversation, 'Are you okay?' opens a space for honesty without demanding a confession.

nuance.analogy: Like checking the weather on a friend's face: a quick look to see whether a storm is coming.
nuance.etymology: 'Okay' is a nineteenth-century American word of uncertain origin; the question combines 'are you' with that adjective.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally; 'okay' is oh-KAY, with the stress on the second syllable
Pronouncing it as 'okey' or spelling it aloud as 'O.K.' in casual speech

conversation.text: You've been quiet all night. Are you okay?
"Are you okay?" "Yeah, I just have a headache."
I heard you fell off your bike. Are you okay?

senses.definition: Being ambitious.
Desiring success.
Expressing a hope or intention but not creating a legally binding obligation.
A person with aspirations.

core.definition: Showing or having strong hopes to achieve a higher status, success, or lifestyle, often one you do not yet have.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the RAY syllable, and the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun' with a weak final syllable. Learners often stress the -tion ending or pronounce the 'a' in 'as' as 'ay'; keep it short, as in 'ass'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually praises ambition, but it can imply that someone is pretending to a status they have not reached.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'aspirational' often in marketing, real estate, fashion, and everyday talk about lifestyle, as in 'an aspirational brand' or 'aspirational housing.' Saying 'He's aspirational' about a person is less common and may sound slightly odd; say 'He's ambitious' or 'He has big goals' instead. In casual talk, 'aspirational' often means 'something people want but cannot quite afford.'

distinctions.note: 'Ambitious' describes a person's drive; 'aspirational' describes a goal, product, or image that people look up to or hope to reach.
'Aspiring' means trying to become a particular thing now, as in 'an aspiring actor'; 'aspirational' focuses on the desire or the ideal state being promoted.

examples.everyday: That store is pretty aspirational for me, but I love window shopping there.
examples.professional: Our Q4 target is aspirational, so let's agree on a realistic floor and a stretch goal.
examples.analytical: Many aspirational narratives in consumer culture sell not a product but a version of the self that viewers are invited to pursue.

nuance.analogy: Like a ladder leaning against a wall you have not climbed yet: it points upward, but you are not at the top.
nuance.etymology: From 'aspiration,' from Latin 'aspirare,' to breathe upon or aim toward.
common_mistakes: Saying 'He is aspirational' for a person when 'ambitious' is more natural.
Confusing it with 'inspirational,' which means something that motivates or uplifts people.

senses.definition: In motion; characterized by motion.
Out of bed; up and about.

core.definition: Out of bed and moving around, or stirred up with activity, excitement or emotion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on STUR, the only stressed syllable, with a strong American r. Do not say it as 'uh-STEER', because the vowel is the r-colored sound of 'bird'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests liveliness, awakening or excitement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see astir mostly in novels, poetry and descriptive writing, as in 'The town was astir with rumors.' People rarely say 'I was astir' in speech; they say 'I was up' or 'I was already up.' It sounds dramatic in conversation but works well in storytelling or writing.

distinctions.note: Awake means not sleeping. Astir means moving around actively, often just after waking or with excitement.
Stirred can mean emotionally moved or mixed. Astir describes a place or crowd that is in general motion or activity.

examples.everyday: The kids were already astir by six, and the house was loud.
examples.professional: By the time the call started, the whole team was astir about the new release.
examples.analytical: Political passions were astir across the country after the ruling.

nuance.analogy: Like leaves when the first wind blows: everything begins to move.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English, from a- (on, in) plus stir, from Old English styrian 'to move'.
common_mistakes: Using astir before a noun, as in 'an astir crowd'. It is mostly used after a linking verb, as in 'was astir'.
Pronouncing it 'uh-steer' with a long ee vowel.

senses.definition: Of a throwback or exhibiting primitivism.
Relating to earlier, more primitive behavior that returns after an absence.
Of the recurrence of a trait reappearing after an absence of one or more generations due to a chance recombination of genes.

core.definition: Relating to a primitive, ancestral trait or behavior that suddenly reappears after a long absence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves to VIS, the syllable before -tik, unlike atavism where the stress is on the first syllable. Don't say AT-uh-vis-tik.

nuance.connotation: Negative or critical. It suggests that something primitive or uncivilized has returned, and it is usually used to criticize.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use atavistic mostly in writing, essays, reviews and political commentary. It sounds serious and somewhat harsh, so use it when you mean that something backward has come back. In casual conversation, 'old-fashioned' or 'primitive' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Primitive describes something early in development or simple; atavistic adds the idea that the thing has returned after being gone.
Archaic describes something old that is no longer used; atavistic suggests a return of an old instinct or trait.

examples.everyday: That crowd yelling at the referee had a kind of atavistic energy that made me uncomfortable.
examples.professional: The old approval process had an atavistic quality, with managers signing paper forms for every small change.
examples.analytical: Political rhetoric that appeals to tribal loyalty can reveal atavistic impulses beneath a modern surface.

nuance.analogy: Like a dormant volcano that suddenly rumbles: the ancient force was always there, and it has come back.
nuance.etymology: From atavism, from Latin atavus 'ancestor'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in AT-uh-vis-tik.
Using it as a neutral word for 'old'; it implies a harsh, primitive return.

senses.definition: A way for a model to weigh how relevant each part of the input is when producing each part of the output.

core.definition: A technique that lets a model weigh how relevant each part of its input is when producing each part of its output.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MEK, the first syllable of mechanism, and the final -ism is a reduced schwa plus m. Attention itself is lightly stressed, so do not say uh-ten-SHUN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in research and engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in data science and AI use attention mechanism in papers, documentation, and presentations about transformers and sequence models. In team conversation people often shorten it to 'attention.' When explaining to executives, a common framing is 'the model's way of focusing on what matters.' The word refers to a mathematical operation, not a physical device.

distinctions.note: The mechanism is the general operation, while an attention head is one parallel component of a multi-head mechanism.
Memory stores information, while an attention mechanism decides which stored or input information to focus on at each step.
A convolution uses a fixed local window of weights, while an attention mechanism computes learned weights over all input positions.

examples.everyday: The translation app uses an attention mechanism, so it can focus on the right words in a long sentence.
examples.professional: We added an attention mechanism to the forecasting model, and its error dropped during holiday weeks.
examples.analytical: The authors argue that the attention mechanism yields interpretable weights, although those weights do not necessarily explain the model's decisions.

nuance.analogy: It works like a spotlight the model moves across its input, brightening the parts most relevant to the output it is producing now.
nuance.etymology: Attention comes from Latin attendere 'to give heed'; mechanism comes from Greek mēkhanē 'device, contrivance'.
common_mistakes: Thinking an attention mechanism is hardware or a physical part; it is a mathematical operation inside a model.
Stressing the wrong syllable in mechanism, saying mech-uh-NIZ-um.

conversation.text: The attention mechanism lets each token gather information from other tokens, weighting each one by its relevance.
We replace the standard attention mechanism with a linear-time approximation and report the quality trade-off.
The attention mechanism is how the model decides which earlier words matter most for predicting the next one.

core.definition: A prophet or diviner hired by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel, who ends up blessing Israel and becomes a symbol of greed and false prophecy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BAY, and reduce the final syllable to a quick 'um' sound, not 'ahm'. Many non-native speakers add an extra syllable and say 'bay-LAH-em'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most Christian and Jewish uses, because he is seen as a mercenary prophet who is greedy and manipulative, although the story also shows God's power over him.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Balaam mostly in Bible study, sermons and religious writing. The phrase 'Balaam's donkey' or 'a talking donkey' is a common story reference. In casual talk, saying someone is 'a Balaam' is rare and would sound pointed, so use it in a religious or literary context.

distinctions.note: Balak is the king of Moab who hires Balaam, while Balaam is the prophet hired to curse Israel.
A true prophet speaks God's word, while Balaam is a hired diviner whose blessing of Israel is forced by God, so the term carries a sense of mercenary religion.

examples.everyday: My friend told me the story of Balaam's donkey, which talks to him when he cannot see the angel in the road.
examples.professional: When I teach Numbers 22 to the youth group, I start with Balaam's donkey because it captures the surprise of the story.
examples.analytical: Balaam's oracles in Numbers 23 and 24 override Balak's intent, so the narrative presents him as a diviner whose words are controlled by God.

nuance.analogy: Balaam is like a hired consultant who is paid to say what the client wants and ends up saying the opposite because someone more powerful is directing his words.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Bil'am, a name whose meaning is uncertain; it is possibly connected to words meaning 'devour' or 'lord of the people'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bay-LAH-em' instead of BAY-lum, adding an extra syllable.
Assuming Balaam is an Israelite prophet; he comes from Pethor in Mesopotamia and is outside Israel.
Confusing the donkey story with Balak's own actions; Balak hires Balaam but is angry when Balaam blesses Israel.
nuance.biblical_note: Balaam, son of Beor, is a non-Israelite diviner from Pethor in Mesopotamia whom Balak, king of Moab, hires to curse Israel. In Numbers 22, God allows Balaam to go but then sends an angel to block his path, and the donkey speaks to him. In Numbers 23 and 24, Balaam blesses Israel four times instead of cursing them. The New Testament treats him as a warning figure: 2 Peter 2:15 speaks of following the way of Balaam for wages, Jude 11 refers to the error of Balaam, and Revelation 2:14 mentions the teaching of Balaam. Numbers 31:8 and 31:16 report that Balaam later dies with the Midianites.

senses.definition: An educated guess or estimation within acceptable bounds.
senses.example: No more stalling. Give me a ballpark figure of our projected losses.

core.definition: An approximate number or amount, which is a rough estimate that is close enough for planning but not exact.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FIG in figure, and ballpark has secondary stress. Figure is pronounced FIG-yer in American speech, not FIG-yoor.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is a polite way to ask for an estimate without demanding precision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say ballpark figure in meetings, budget discussions and casual planning, such as asking about costs for a house project. A natural reply is Around fifty thousand, give or take, or I'd say somewhere in the low hundreds. It is informal, so in a formal report you would use estimate instead.

distinctions.note: Rough estimate is more neutral and works in formal writing, while ballpark figure is more casual and spoken.
Guesstimate is more humorous and suggests a guess with little supporting evidence.
Exact figure means a precise number, which is the opposite of a ballpark figure.

collocations: a ballpark figure on the costs

examples.everyday: Do you have a ballpark figure for what the car repair will cost?
examples.professional: Give me a ballpark figure for the cloud costs, and I'll take it to finance before Friday.
examples.analytical: Without the full dataset, the best we can offer is a ballpark figure, and the uncertainty should be stated explicitly.

nuance.analogy: A ballpark figure is like a map drawn from a distance: it shows the right region, but not every street.
nuance.etymology: From the baseball ballpark, used figuratively for a rough area; figure here means a number.
common_mistakes: Using of instead of for after ballpark figure, which is less natural in standard American speech.
Using ballpark figure in a formal report where estimate would be more appropriate.
Stressing park instead of figure, which makes the phrase sound less natural.

ballpark-figure.etymology: Operating on the themes discussed at *in the ballpark*.

conversation.text: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the kitchen remodel?
I don't need exact numbers yet, just a ballpark figure for the budget.
A ballpark figure is fine for now; we'll refine it next week.
Give me a ballpark figure, and we'll fine-tune it later.
As a ballpark figure, I'd say the project will cost about two hundred thousand.
I can't give you a ballpark figure until I see the requirements.

senses.definition: Producing balm.
Soothing or fragrant.
Of weather, mild and pleasant.
Foolish; slightly crazy or mad; eccentric.

core.definition: Pleasantly warm, mild and soft, usually describing weather or the air on a calm summer evening.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final y is pronounced as a clear ee sound. Keep the L silent, as in balm.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests pleasant, soft, comfortable weather, usually in warm places or seasons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use balmy mostly for weather, especially for warm evenings in Southern California, Florida or Texas in spring or early fall. The word sounds pleasant and slightly descriptive, so it is common in travel talk and weather reports. In British slang balmy can mean crazy, but Americans almost never use it that way.

distinctions.note: Mild is the general word for not harsh, while balmy suggests pleasant warmth with a soft breeze.
Humid means sticky and uncomfortable, while balmy describes weather that feels pleasant.
Warm is neutral and can be too hot, while balmy specifically implies comfortable, gentle warmth.

examples.everyday: It's a balmy evening, so let's eat on the patio instead of inside.
examples.professional: We got lucky with the balmy weather for the outdoor team offsite, which made the whole day easier.
examples.analytical: The poet's balmy summer imagery sets up a sharp contrast with the cold, grinding violence of the war poem that follows.

nuance.analogy: Balmy weather feels like a warm bath after a long day, gentle enough that you forget you are wearing clothes.
nuance.etymology: From balm, the aromatic resin, with the sense of fragrant and soothing weather developing from that idea.
common_mistakes: Confusing balmy with barmy, a British word for crazy or foolish.
Using balmy for hot, humid weather, when it means pleasantly warm.
Pronouncing the L, as in BAHL-mee; the L is silent.

senses.definition: To wail over; to feel or express deep sorrow for.

core.definition: To express strong grief or sorrow over something, often by loudly lamenting it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WAYL, which sounds like 'wail'. The first syllable is a weak bih, not bee, so avoid saying 'bee-WAIL'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and mournful; it signals deep sorrow or distress.
nuance.usage_note: Bewail is mostly literary or formal, and you might hear it at a funeral or in a poem. Americans in everyday conversation would say lament, mourn, or complain about. Using bewail for a small annoyance sounds dramatic.

distinctions.note: Lament is more common and works in both formal and casual speech; bewail suggests louder, more open grief.
Mourn focuses on grief over a loss, especially a death; bewail can cover any deep sorrow, including a social wrong.

examples.everyday: She sat on the porch and bewailed the fact that her flight got canceled.
examples.professional: Managers often bewail the lack of time for planning, but they rarely change the meeting schedule.
examples.analytical: The prophet bewails a nation that has forgotten its covenant, weeping over the loss of justice.

nuance.etymology: From be- (thoroughly) + wail, from Middle English waylen, probably from Old Norse væla.
common_mistakes: Using bewail for small complaints like a late bus; it is too strong and literary.
Confusing bewail with bewilder, which means to confuse.

senses.definition: The diversity (number and variety of species) of plant and animal life within a region.

core.definition: The variety of plant and animal life in a particular region, habitat, or on Earth as a whole, including the number of species.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VUR, a strongly r-colored vowel, so pronounce a clear American r there. Keep the other syllables short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it suggests a healthy and varied ecosystem; losing it is treated as a serious problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in news, schools, environmental policy, and conversations about parks, conservation, and climate. In casual talk people may say 'wildlife' or 'species', but biodiversity is the standard umbrella term. It is usually uncountable, so say 'loss of biodiversity' rather than 'biodiversities'.

distinctions.note: Species diversity counts only the number and evenness of species, while biodiversity also includes genetic and ecosystem variety.
Biomass is the total mass of living organisms in an area, not how many different kinds there are.

examples.everyday: The state park has so much biodiversity that we spot a new bird or wildflower every time we hike.
examples.professional: Our environmental impact report tracks biodiversity at each project site, using species counts and habitat surveys.
examples.analytical: Measuring biodiversity requires more than counting species, because a grassland dominated by one grass can be less resilient than one with fewer dominant species but more varied communities.

nuance.analogy: Like a diversified investment portfolio: spreading holdings across many kinds of assets makes the whole more resilient to a single shock.
nuance.etymology: Bio- from Greek bios 'life' combined with diversity, from Latin diversitas 'difference'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on VUR in bye-oh-duh-VUR-suh-tee.
Using 'biodiversities' as a plural; the word is usually uncountable, so say 'many species' or 'types of biodiversity'.
Confusing it with 'biosphere' (the living part of Earth) or 'ecosystem'.

senses.definition: A phone number you have blocked, or a caller whose number is hidden.

core.definition: A call from a phone number that is hidden or blocked, so your phone shows no caller ID.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NUM, with a weaker stress on blocked. Blocked ends in a /t/ sound after the k, so it is one syllable, not blocked-ed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but often suspicious, since many blocked calls are telemarketers or scams.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a call shows as 'blocked number' or 'private number' on the screen. Many people just say 'no caller ID' or 'unknown caller' on smartphones. A common reply is 'I'll let it go to voicemail' if you do not recognize the call.

distinctions.note: Unknown number means the number is not saved in your contacts; blocked number means the caller deliberately hid their ID.
Spam call describes any unwanted call; blocked number only describes how the caller ID appears.

collocations: a call from a blocked number

examples.everyday: I'm not picking up, it's a blocked number and it's probably a scam.
examples.professional: The client called from a blocked number, so I couldn't confirm who it was before I answered.
examples.analytical: Dispatchers treat calls from blocked numbers differently because they cannot verify the caller's identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a letter with no return address.
nuance.etymology: Combines block (to prevent or stop) with number.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the number is blocked' to mean you cannot reach a person; it usually means the caller hid their ID.
Stressing NUM weakly and blocked strongly; the main stress is on the second word.

conversation.text: A blocked number keeps calling me late at night.
Doctors' offices sometimes call from a blocked number.
I never pick up when it's a blocked number.

senses.definition: A person who talks too much or too loudly, especially in a boastful or self-important manner.
A jerk, a disagreeable person.

core.definition: A person who talks too much or boasts loudly and arrogantly about themselves, usually without much substance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BLOH. The second syllable is hard with an r, so pronounce the r clearly. The vowel in hard is the 'ahr' of cot-caught in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes someone annoying and self-important. It is mildly insulting and is used when joking or complaining.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blowhard for a loud, boastful person, often a coworker or a man at a bar who won't stop talking. It is informal and can be a sharp insult, so use it carefully. Saying 'he's a blowhard' is common in conversation, and a natural response is 'Yeah, nobody can get a word in.'

distinctions.note: Braggart focuses on boasting about achievements. Blowhard emphasizes long, loud talk, often about opinions, and is more humorous.
Loudmouth stresses being loud and indiscreet. Blowhard stresses self-important talk and pomposity.

examples.everyday: Don't invite Mark to the barbecue, he's such a blowhard about his fishing trips.
examples.professional: We need someone to lead the review who listens, not a blowhard who dominates every meeting.
examples.analytical: The essay critiques the public theologian as a blowhard whose rhetoric displaces the humility the tradition demands.

nuance.analogy: Like a loud horn that sounds more than it signals anything useful.
nuance.etymology: From blow (to boast or puff up) and hard, with the sense of a person who blows hard, meaning talks loudly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word as two separate words blow hard with equal stress.
Using blowhard for a skilled speaker; it always suggests arrogance.
Spelling it as blow-hard in formal writing; the standard spelling is blowhard.

blowhard.etymology: Essentially deverbal in nature, albeit not from a unitary phrasal verb; from *blow* *hard*.

senses.definition: Pompous, officious talk.
A gust of wind.
Fitful noise and violence.
To speak or protest loudly.
senses.example: When confronted by opposition his reaction was to bluster, which often cowed the meek.

senses.definition: To act or speak in an unduly threatening manner.
To blow in strong or sudden gusts (refers to winds).

core.definition: To talk loudly and angrily in a threatening way, often to hide uncertainty or to seem more powerful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the final syllable to an American r-colored schwa. The middle s is a clear s, not a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests noisy, empty threats or pompous behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bluster in news writing, commentary, and conversation about loud people who make big claims without substance. It is less common in casual speech than yell or rant, so it can sound a little literary. A natural response when someone blusters is "Let's just focus on the facts."

distinctions.note: Threaten suggests a real warning of harm; bluster is noisy and often empty, with little intent to act.
Shout is a neutral description of volume; bluster adds the sense of pompous or empty posturing.
Rant implies a long, emotional outburst; bluster focuses on loud, self-important threats.

examples.everyday: My uncle likes to bluster about the referee, but he never actually does anything about it.
examples.professional: The manager blustered about deadlines in the meeting, but he did not offer a plan to meet them.
examples.analytical: Much of the political rhetoric in this debate is bluster, designed to signal strength rather than to propose policy.

nuance.analogy: Bluster is like a loud car alarm: it makes a lot of noise to signal a threat, but it often does not stop anything.
nuance.etymology: Middle English blusteren, probably from Middle Dutch or Low German; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle s as z, as in "BLUZ-ter".
Using bluster for a gentle or private complaint; it implies loud, pompous behavior.

bluster.etymology: From Middle English *blusteren* (“to wander about aimlessly”); however, apparently picking up the modern sense from *blüstren* “to blow violently”; compare later Low German *blustern*, *blistern*.

senses.definition: Showy in speech and given to using flowery or elaborate terms; grandiloquent; pompous.
High‐sounding but with little meaning.
Loud, aggressive, highly exaggerated, or explosive in manner or delivery; over‐the‐top.

core.definition: Overly grand, showy, or exaggerated in speech, writing, or style, often sounding impressive but empty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'bas', with the short 'a' of 'cat'. The ending '-ic' is pronounced /ɪk/, so it's bom-BAS-tik, not 'bom-BAS-teek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes showy language or a loud, exaggerated style that seems to hide weak content.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bombastic' to criticize speeches, reviews, TV personalities, or films that are over the top. It is more common in writing and media commentary than in casual talk, where people might say 'over the top' or 'pompous'. It can be used for a style of music or performance that feels huge and exaggerated.

distinctions.note: 'Pompous' focuses on a person's self-importance, while 'bombastic' focuses on exaggerated language or style.
'Eloquent' is positive and suggests graceful, effective speech, while 'bombastic' suggests excess and emptiness.

examples.everyday: The movie trailer was so bombastic that it made the story look way bigger than it really is.
examples.professional: The vendor's bombastic pitch promised everything, but none of the metrics were actually shown.
examples.analytical: Her essay rejects the bombastic style of nineteenth-century sermons in favor of plain, careful argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a brass band that plays too loudly for a small room, bombastic language overwhelms the listener with more noise than meaning.
nuance.etymology: From 'bombast', with the adjective ending '-ic'.
common_mistakes: Using 'bombastic' as a positive word for impressive speaking; it usually means excessive or empty.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: A small stall for the display and sale of goods.
A boxlike room or enclosure just big enough to accommodate one standing person, such as a phone booth or polling booth.
An enclosed seating area consisting of a table next to a wall set between two high-backed benches, as in a diner or café.
An enclosure for keeping animals.
A recording studio.
(dated) A temporary shelter, often in the form of a tent, shed, or canopied structure.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: An enclosed seating area in a restaurant, with a table between two high-backed benches along a wall.

pronunciation.tip: The ending is a voiceless th, as in 'think,' with the tongue between the teeth. Don't end the word with a t sound or a 'b' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Booths feel cozy and casual in diners and cafés.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say booth for the bench-and-table seating in diners, and ask 'Can we get a booth?' when they want privacy or room for a family. In a casual restaurant, it is a relaxed and common request. The word also means a stall at a fair or market, or a phone or voting booth, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A booth has high benches with sides and a seat along a wall; a table is open on all sides, so booth suggests privacy and comfort.
A stall is a stand at a market or fair for selling goods, while a restaurant booth is a seating area.

examples.everyday: Can we grab a booth by the window? I don't want to sit at the counter.
examples.professional: We booked the back booth for the team dinner so we could talk without the noise.
examples.analytical: The booth's high backs create a private, enclosed space, which changes how the diners relate to one another.

nuance.analogy: Think of a booth as a small room inside the restaurant, with its own walls and seats.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse búð, meaning a shelter or stall.
common_mistakes: Calling any restaurant table with chairs a booth; it needs benches and a wall-side seat.
Confusing the vowel with the one in 'both' or 'bath'; booth uses the oo sound of 'boot'.

booth.etymology: Middle English *bothe*, from **bóð*, from Proto-Germanic **bōþō*, **būþiz*, **buþǭ*, from Proto-Indo-European **bʰuH-*.

conversation.text: Could we get a booth instead of a table, please?
The kids love sitting in the big corner booth.
All the booths are taken, but we have a table by the window.

senses.definition: Without boots.
Profitless; pointless; unavailing.

core.definition: Pointless or unsuccessful, achieving nothing despite effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress goes on BOOT. The -less ending is weak and reduced, closer to 'luhs' than to 'less'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests effort that failed to achieve its goal.
nuance.usage_note: Bootless is rare in everyday American speech and sounds old-fashioned or literary. In modern professional writing, Americans prefer fruitless, pointless or unsuccessful. You will meet it in older texts, poetry and formal writing, so you can recognize it, but you rarely need to say it yourself.

distinctions.note: Fruitless is common and neutral in modern English; bootless is more literary and suggests effort that yielded nothing.
Pointless often describes an action with no reason behind it; bootless emphasizes an effort that failed to produce a result.

examples.everyday: We spent an hour on the phone with customer service, and it was completely bootless.
examples.professional: Our bootless attempts to fix the server outage cost the team two days of work.
examples.analytical: Argument over questions that no evidence can settle is often bootless, since reason has no way to reach a conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like running on a treadmill: lots of motion, no progress.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bōt, meaning remedy or advantage; bootless means without advantage.
common_mistakes: Thinking bootless relates to footwear; it means fruitless, not without boots.
Using bootless in casual speech where pointless or useless sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A worker in brass; a brassworker.
An upright standing or hanging metal bowl used for holding burning coal for a source of light or heat.

core.definition: A metal bowl or stand that holds burning charcoal or coals to give heat or light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'zh' sound is like the 's' in 'measure', and the final syllable is a reduced American 'er' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an object, often with a historical or decorative feel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use brazier in daily life. It appears in historical writing, antiques descriptions, and literature. In everyday American speech people say fire pit, charcoal grill, or heater. The word also refers to a brass worker in older English.

distinctions.note: A grill is for cooking food, while a brazier mainly holds fire for heat or light.
A fire pit is usually built into the ground or a patio, while a brazier is a portable metal stand or bowl.

examples.everyday: We set up a brazier on the porch to keep the guests warm.
examples.professional: The historic site uses a replica brazier to demonstrate lighting in the medieval hall.
examples.analytical: The ancient brazier in the courtyard serves as a symbol of warmth and ritual gathering in the narrative.

nuance.analogy: A brazier is like a portable campfire held in a metal bowl on legs.
nuance.etymology: From Old French brasier, from braise, 'live coals', ultimately from Germanic.
common_mistakes: Saying 'brassier', which sounds like a bra and is incorrect.
Using brazier to mean a grill for cooking food, which is not its usual meaning.

brazier.etymology: From Middle English *brasiere*, from *brasen* (“to cover with brass”), from Old English *brasian*, *bræsian* (“to cover with brass”).

senses.definition: The act of burying; interment; placing remains into the earth.
senses.example: His whole family was present at his burial.

core.definition: The act of burying a dead body, usually in a grave or tomb, often with a funeral or religious ceremony.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so the word has two syllables, not three, with the final -al as a soft 'ul.' The r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and solemn. It is a respectful word used in funeral and cemetery contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say burial when talking about putting a body in the ground, and funeral for the ceremony around it. Many Americans now choose cremation, so people may say 'burial or cremation' when making plans. In a conversation about someone's death, a natural reply is 'I'm so sorry,' and people might ask about the burial service or the cemetery.

distinctions.note: A funeral is the ceremony for the dead, while burial is the act of placing the body in the ground. A funeral may happen before a burial or a cremation.
Interment is a more formal word for burial, used in legal or official documents and cemetery records.

examples.everyday: The burial is going to be at the cemetery on Oak Street on Saturday morning.
examples.professional: Our company will cover the burial costs for employees who die while working under our health plan.
examples.analytical: Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah as a burial place shows how important a family grave was to the patriarchs' hope of inheriting the land.

nuance.analogy: A burial is like putting a seed in the soil: the body is placed in the earth, and the act marks a transition from life to rest.
nuance.etymology: From bury (Old English byrgan, 'to bury') plus the suffix -al, forming a noun for the act.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as BYOO-ree-al, following the spelling of bury as a long u vowel.
Confusing burial with funeral; saying 'the burial was beautiful' when you mean the service.
nuance.biblical_note: Burial in Scripture is an act of honor and family responsibility. The Hebrew verb is qabar, meaning 'to bury.' Genesis 23 describes Abraham buying the cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah. Genesis 25:9 tells that Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham there. Matthew 27:57-60 describes Joseph of Arimathea placing Jesus' body in his own new tomb.

senses.definition: A young cow or bull of any bovid, such as domestic cattle or buffalo.
Leather made of the skin of domestic calves; especially, a fine, light-colored leather used in bookbinding.
The young of various animals, especially elephant, giraffe, reindeer, seal, or whale.
A mass of ice broken from a larger glacier, ice shelf, or iceberg.
A small island, near a larger island.
A cabless railroad engine.
The muscle in the back of the leg below the knee.
The back of the leg below the knee.
(dated) An awkward or silly boy or young man; any silly person; a dolt.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A young cow, bull, or other large animal, or in the Bible a young ox used in worship or feasting.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short "a" as in "cat," and pronounce the final f clearly. The plural is calves, pronounced with a /v/ sound, so students often need to practice the change from f to v.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious or literary contexts it can suggest sacrifice, feasting, or idolatry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calf in farm talk, veterinary contexts, and recipes like veal. In everyday speech, a calf is simply a baby cow. Calf is also used for a part of the leg below the knee, which is common in fitness and clothing contexts. In Bible study, the golden calf is a well-known symbol of idolatry.

distinctions.note: A cow is an adult female, while a calf is a young animal of either sex.
Veal is the meat from a young calf; calf is the animal itself.
Calf can mean the back of the lower leg in everyday English, but leg is broader and more general.

examples.everyday: The farmer's neighbor said the new calf was already standing up an hour after being born.
examples.professional: The livestock report shows a higher calf survival rate this year after the new feed program.
examples.analytical: The golden calf in Exodus 32 shows how quickly a community can turn gifts of God into an object of worship.

nuance.analogy: A calf is like a seedling in farming: young, growing, and needing care before it becomes a full animal.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cealf, young of cattle, from a Germanic root related to German Kalb.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the plural calves with an f sound instead of a v sound.
Using calf for an adult cow; calf refers only to a young animal.
nuance.biblical_note: The calf appears in Scripture as a sacrificial and festival animal, and it is central to the story of the golden calf. Exodus 32:4 says Aaron made a molten calf, and 1 Kings 12:28 describes Jeroboam making golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Luke 15:23 mentions the fatted calf killed for a celebration when a lost son returns.

calf.etymology: From Middle English *calf*, from *cælf*, *calf* (West Saxon *ċealf*), from **kalb*, from Proto-Germanic **kalbaz*, further etymology unknown.

senses.definition: Call again in a moment.

core.definition: A friendly phrase meaning 'I will call you again very soon,' used when you cannot talk right now.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on BACK. The word 'you' is unstressed and sounds like 'yuh' or 'yoo' in fast speech, and 'call you' links together as 'ca-lyou'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is polite and reassuring, and it tells the other person you intend to continue the conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when they cannot talk immediately, such as when they are driving, in a meeting or at work. It is informal but polite, and it is common in business and personal settings alike. A natural reply is 'Okay, talk to you soon' or 'Sounds good, thanks.' Do not use it when you have a fixed appointment, because then you would say 'I'll call you back at three.'

distinctions.note: Call you right back means very soon, often within minutes, while later suggests a longer delay.
Call you right back refers specifically to a phone call, while get back to you can refer to an email or any other reply.

collocations: I have to call you right back
Let me call you right back
I'll call right back once I'm off the highway

examples.everyday: I'm in the car right now, but I'll call you right back once I park.
examples.professional: I'm in another meeting, but I'll call you right back as soon as this ends.
examples.analytical: Her reply, I'll call you right back, signals a brief pause rather than a refusal to continue the discussion.

nuance.analogy: Like a fast return ticket on a train: you come back quickly, not in some distant future.
nuance.etymology: 'Call' is an Old English word, 'right' means immediately or directly, and 'back' means in return.
common_mistakes: Saying 'call you back right now' and stressing NOW, which implies urgency rather than a short delay.
Dropping 'right' and making the phrase sound vague.

conversation.text: Can I call you right back? Someone's at the door.
Sorry, I'm getting on an elevator. I'll call you right back.
Let me check the calendar and call you right back.

core.definition: A member of the Carmelite religious order, a Roman Catholic order of monks, nuns, and friars founded in the Holy Land and associated with the prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to 'muh', and the final syllable rhymes with 'light'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious contexts. It suggests prayer, contemplative life, and devotion to Mary and Elijah.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Carmelite mainly in Catholic settings, such as a Carmelite monastery or a Carmelite sister. Outside church life the word is uncommon, and people may simply say 'Carmelite nun' or 'Carmelite friar' to be clear. The order is Catholic, not Protestant.

distinctions.note: Carmel is the place; Carmelite is the person or group associated with the place.
Benedictines follow the Rule of Saint Benedict and are a different religious order with a different history.
Franciscans follow Saint Francis of Assisi, while Carmelites trace their origin to Elijah and Mount Carmel.

examples.everyday: My aunt is a Carmelite nun in Ohio, and she prays for our family every morning.
examples.professional: The Carmelite house runs a retreat center and a publishing ministry for parish leaders.
examples.analytical: Teresa of Avila's reform of the Carmelite order drew on Elijah as a model of contemplative prayer and solitude.

nuance.analogy: A Carmelite is like a long-distance runner who trains in the mountains: the discipline and the vision of the place shape everything they do.
nuance.etymology: Named for Mount Carmel, the place in Israel traditionally linked to the Carmelite order's origin.
common_mistakes: Using Carmelite for any member of a Protestant group, since it is a Catholic order.
Stressing the last syllable (kar-muh-LITE).
Confusing Carmelite with Carmel, the mountain itself.
nuance.biblical_note: Carmelites trace their origins to the hermits who lived on Mount Carmel, inspired by the prophet Elijah. The Bible does not use the word Carmelite, but 1 Kings 18:19-39 describes Elijah's contest on Carmel, and 1 Kings 18:42 shows him praying on its top. 2 Kings 2:25 places Elisha's journey from Carmel, which links the prophetic tradition to the order's spirituality.

senses.definition: A group of businesses or nations that collude to limit competition within an industry or market.
senses.example: oil cartel

senses.definition: (historical) A combination of political groups (notably parties) for common action.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A written letter of defiance or challenge.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) An official agreement concerning the exchange of prisoners.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A ship used to negotiate with an enemy in time of war, and to exchange prisoners.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A group of businesses that secretly agree to fix prices or limit competition in an industry. Also an illegal criminal organization that controls drug trafficking.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TEL, and the first vowel is the open ah of cot. Many learners put stress on the first syllable, which sounds wrong to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests illegal collusion, unfair pricing, or dangerous criminal groups.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cartel in news, business, and political discussion. It usually implies illegal or unethical behavior, so calling a group a cartel is a serious accusation. In everyday speech, people might say 'the oil cartel' or 'drug cartel.' For a legal arrangement between companies, the word trust or alliance is sometimes used instead.

distinctions.note: A monopoly is controlled by a single company. A cartel is a group of separate companies working together.
A syndicate can be a neutral business group or a criminal organization. Cartel usually implies collusion to limit competition or drug trafficking.

examples.everyday: I read that the big egg producers were accused of acting like a cartel.
examples.professional: Legal said the supplier group could be investigated as a cartel if they coordinated prices.
examples.analytical: A cartel is unstable because each member has an incentive to cheat and sell slightly below the agreed price.

nuance.analogy: A cartel is like a group of rival cab companies that secretly agree to charge the same high fare.
nuance.etymology: From Italian cartello, meaning placard or written challenge, through French cartel.
common_mistakes: Using cartel for any small business group; the word implies collusion or criminal activity.
