pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'par', and 'ex' is 'eks'. In American legal speech, people often say 'PAR-tee' or 'PAR-tay', so you will hear variations; the given form is acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but in legal contexts it can imply unfairness, since only one side is heard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ex parte' mainly in courtrooms, legal writing, and news about judges' decisions. Most people would never use it in everyday talk. In legal settings, you might hear 'an ex parte hearing' or 'an ex parte order'. The American alternative for a casual description is 'one-sided' or 'without the other side present'.

distinctions.note: 'One-sided' is a general word for unfair or unbalanced; 'ex parte' is a precise legal term for a proceeding where only one party appears.
'Inter partes' means a proceeding with both parties present; 'ex parte' means only one is present.

examples.everyday: My lawyer friend said the judge can sometimes issue an order ex parte, without the other side there.
examples.professional: The compliance team flagged an ex parte communication between the vendor and the regulator.
examples.analytical: An ex parte decision undermines procedural fairness because it cannot test the claims against counterevidence.

nuance.analogy: An ex parte hearing is like judging a soccer match after hearing only one team's account of the game.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ex 'from' and pars 'part, side'.
common_mistakes: Using 'ex parte' in everyday speech as a synonym for 'one-sided' without legal context.
Putting the stress on 'ex' (EKS par-tay) instead of on 'par'.

senses.definition: In an exponential manner.
Rapidly, greatly.

core.definition: In a very rapid way that grows or changes by an increasing rate, often used to mean hugely or dramatically.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on NEN, and the final -ly is pronounced as a light lee sound. Many learners stress the wrong syllable or add an extra syllable after the -sh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical writing; in everyday speech it is positive when used for growth and neutral to negative when describing problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exponentially in business, news and science, and in casual talk to emphasize a big change, as in 'She's improved exponentially since last year.' It is slightly formal for chatty speech, so many people prefer a phrase like 'by a lot.' A natural reply is a simple agreement or a question about what caused the change.

distinctions.note: Rapidly describes speed, while exponentially describes growth that accelerates in proportion to its size.
Greatly is general and neutral; exponentially implies a compounding increase and sounds more technical.

examples.everyday: My cooking has improved exponentially since I started taking that class at the community college.
examples.professional: Our customer support tickets have grown exponentially this quarter, so we need to add staff or automate triage.
examples.analytical: Under the assumed model, the population size changes exponentially with time, so the doubling period determines the entire trajectory.

nuance.analogy: It is like interest compounding in a savings account: each new amount earns interest on the growing total.
nuance.etymology: Formed from exponential with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using exponentially to mean just very or really in every context, which can sound exaggerated.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as separate words instead of quick reduced sounds.

senses.definition: A quality of design that takes possible future advances into consideration and attempts to accommodate them.
The capability of being extended.

core.definition: The ability of a software system to be extended with new features or components without major redesign.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the BIL syllable, the fourth syllable. The ex- at the start is /ɪk/ in careful American speech, and the endings -ity and -ibility are reduced to uh and tee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is valued as good design that makes future change easier.
nuance.usage_note: American software engineers use extensibility when discussing architecture, APIs, plugins, and frameworks. It is a technical term in code reviews, design documents, and architecture meetings. In casual talk, people might say 'easy to add features to.' Do not use it to mean the ability to handle more users; that is scalability.

distinctions.note: Scalability is the ability to handle more load or users; extensibility is the ability to add new features or components.
Modularity is about dividing a system into separate parts; extensibility is about how easily new parts can be added to it.

examples.everyday: My phone's app store is so useful because the platform was built with real extensibility.
examples.professional: We should review the API for extensibility before the next release, so new partners can add features without breaking anything.
examples.analytical: Extensibility is a virtue of design, but a system can be so open that its core concepts become hard to reason about.

nuance.analogy: Extensibility is like a power strip with spare outlets: you can plug in new devices later without rewiring the house.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extendere, 'to stretch out,' with the English suffixes -ible and -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing extensibility with scalability when talking about handling more users.
Confusing extensible, the adjective, with extension, the noun for an added part.

senses.definition: With lavish expenditure or behavior; in an extravagant manner.

core.definition: In a very lavish, excessive, or over-the-top way, often about spending or praise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on STRAV. The final '-ly' is a light 'lee' sound, not 'lee-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral to negative, but warm when praising: 'extravagantly generous' is affectionate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it with spending or praise: 'She dressed extravagantly' or 'He thanked us extravagantly.' It sounds more natural in writing or description than in short replies. In everyday talk, 'way too much' or 'lavishly' often works better.

distinctions.note: Lavishly describes generous abundance without criticism; extravagantly often hints at excess or waste.
Excessively means too much, usually negatively; extravagantly can be admiring or critical.

examples.everyday: Thanks for dinner, but you didn't have to order so extravagantly for just the two of us.
examples.professional: We shouldn't spend extravagantly on the offsite when the budget is this tight.
examples.analytical: The novel describes the aristocrat's household so extravagantly that the reader sees its moral emptiness.

nuance.analogy: Like a cake covered in more frosting than it can hold: the excess becomes the main thing you notice.
nuance.etymology: From extravagant plus the adverb suffix -ly; extravagant comes from Latin extra 'outside' and vagari 'to wander'.
common_mistakes: Writing extravagently; the correct spelling is extravagantly.
Using it for a simple, moderate expense when the meaning is excess.

senses.definition: A golf shot that curves intentionally to the player's right (if they are right-handed) or to the left (if left-handed).
A haircut where the hair is short or shaved on the sides of the head and longer on top. See also high-top fade and low fade.
A fight.
The act of disappearing from a place so as not to be found; covert departure.
A gradual decrease in the brightness of a shot or the volume of sound or music (as a means of cutting to a new scene or starting a new song).
To hit the ball with the shot called a fade.
To grow weak; to lose strength; to decay; to perish gradually; to wither, as a plant.
To lose freshness, color, or brightness; to become faint in hue or tint; hence, to be wanting in color.
To sink away; to disappear gradually; to grow dim; to vanish.
senses.example: The milkman's whistling faded into the distance.

senses.definition: To cause to fade.
To bet against (someone).

core.definition: To gradually lose color, brightness, strength, or intensity, or to become less visible over time.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a diphthong that glides from 'ay' to 'ee'. Keep the final 'd' voiced and clear, not silent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive, as with fading jeans, or negative, as with fading memories or fading strength.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fade' constantly in everyday talk, such as 'The color faded in the wash' or 'The music faded out'. It also appears in sports and haircut vocabulary, and in golf for a shot curving to the right. It is natural and informal, and it fits both spoken and written English.

distinctions.note: 'Fade out' emphasizes a sound or image disappearing gradually, often in films or audio, while 'fade' alone is more general.
'Wither' describes plants or living things drying up and dying, while 'fade' describes color or intensity weakening.

examples.everyday: Don't put those red towels in with the white ones, or the color will fade.
examples.professional: The signal begins to fade whenever we move the access point, so we should test coverage again.
examples.analytical: In the text, the psalmist's sense of God's presence seems to fade, only to return in the closing lament.

nuance.analogy: Fade is like a sunset: the light is still there, but it gradually grows weaker until it is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'faden', from Old French 'fader', meaning 'to become weak or withered'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fade' transitively for a person, as in 'He faded the shirt'; the transitive sense is rare and not natural.
Confusing 'fade' with 'fate', which sounds similar but has a different vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb 'marainō' (to wither or wilt) describes what happens to plants and to wealth in Scripture. In James 1:11 the rich man is said to fade away in the midst of his pursuits, comparing human prosperity to a flower that withers in the heat. In 1 Peter 1:4 the inheritance kept in heaven is described as unfading, the opposite of this withering.

fade.etymology: From Middle English *fade*, *vad*, *vade* (“faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch *vade* (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French *fade* (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin.

senses.definition: To be fooled by; to walk into (a trap) or respond to (a scam or trick).
senses.example: I can't believe how many people still fall for the coin glued to the sidewalk.

senses.definition: To fall in love with.
senses.example: He really fell for the attractive waitress at his favorite restaurant.

core.definition: To be tricked by a lie or scam, or to fall in love with someone.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'fall', and 'for' is weak, so it sounds like 'fer' in fast speech. The r is strong in American English. Linking sounds like 'FAW-luh-FER'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative when used for being tricked, and positive or playful when used for romance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fall for' in two common ways: to be fooled by a trick, scam, or joke, and to start falling in love with someone. It is casual and everyday. A natural reply to a scam story is 'Oh no, how did you fall for that?' and for romance, 'Wow, you really fell for him!'

distinctions.note: 'Be fooled by' is a more general way to say you were deceived. 'Fall for' is more colloquial and often describes falling for a clever trick.
'Fall in love with' is the full phrase for romance and is more neutral. 'Fall for' is casual and can also mean being tricked.

examples.everyday: My mom almost fell for that phone scam about a fake lottery prize.
examples.professional: Our staff must not fall for phishing emails that look like they come from the payroll system.
examples.analytical: Many readers fall for the author's rhetorical flourish and fail to test the claim behind it.

nuance.analogy: Falling for a trick is like stepping onto a rug that hides a hole: you do not see it until you are already in it.
nuance.etymology: 'Fall' from Old English 'feallan', with 'for' in the sense of being deceived by or drawn toward.
common_mistakes: Using 'fall for' with 'to' instead of directly, as in 'fall for to a trick'.
Confusing 'fall for' with 'fall in' when speaking of love; 'fall for someone' is the natural phrase.

conversation.text: I can't believe I fell for that phone scam.
Don't fall for it, that email isn't really from your bank.
He fell for her the first time they met.

senses.definition: A situation in which two opposing options are presented as the only possibilities, when others are available.

core.definition: A fallacy that presents only two options as possible when other options actually exist.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, LEH, in 'dilemma'. The first 'i' is a short, reduced vowel, and the final 'a' is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it names a manipulative or careless reasoning pattern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'false dilemma' in logic, debate, politics, and media analysis. It is often used when someone says 'either you're with us or against us.' In casual talk, people might say 'those aren't the only two choices,' which is more natural.

distinctions.note: A real dilemma has two hard options that truly exist, while a false dilemma wrongly omits other possibilities.
False dilemma limits the choices, while false equivalence treats two different things as the same.

examples.everyday: My brother said we either have to sell the house or go broke, but that's a false dilemma; we could rent part of it.
examples.professional: The proposal presents a false dilemma between shipping fast and shipping safely, when we could do both with better testing.
examples.analytical: The speaker frames the debate as a false dilemma, ignoring intermediate positions that would address both concerns.

nuance.analogy: Like a fork in a road that looks like only two paths, when a map would show several more.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dilemma, 'double proposition,' from di-, 'two,' and lemma, 'premise.'
common_mistakes: Using 'dilemma' alone to mean a false choice; the word 'false' is needed in the logical sense.
Pronouncing the middle 'i' as a long 'eye' sound.

senses.definition: Dirty with feces or other impurities.

core.definition: Dirty, foul, or full of waste matter, impurities, or sediment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle is a reduced 'yuh', and the last syllable is 'lunt', with a light, unstressed vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative, describing something disgusting or polluted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use feculent in conversation; it appears in literature, historical writing, and occasionally in medical or environmental descriptions. Everyday speakers would say dirty, filthy, murky, or polluted. Using it casually can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Filthy is an everyday word for very dirty; feculent is more literary and specifically suggests sediment or waste.
Turbid describes cloudy liquid; feculent adds a sense of foulness or waste matter.

examples.everyday: The creek was so feculent after the storm that nobody wanted to let the dog swim in it.
examples.professional: The inspector reported feculent runoff entering the storm drain from the construction site.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses feculent imagery to suggest the moral decay of the city's industrial districts.

nuance.analogy: A feculent pond is like a fish tank nobody has cleaned in years, murky with waste settling at the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Latin faeculentus, from faex (dregs, sediment).
common_mistakes: Confusing feculent with fecund, which means fertile.
Pronouncing it with the stress on the second syllable.

feculent.etymology: From Middle French *feculent*, from Latin *faeculentus*, from *faex*.

senses.definition: Very hot; burning, scorching; also, glowing with heat.
Of cold: intense, severe.
Of a person, or their actions, interests, or nature: exhibiting persistent belief or conviction, and enthusiasm or zeal; ardent, earnest, passionate.
(historical) Of a drug: having an abundance of heat as one of the four qualities believed to be characteristic of all things; hot rather than cold, dry, or moist.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Showing intense, sincere passion or belief; very enthusiastic or zealous about something you care about.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. Americans say the r clearly, and the middle syllable is weak, so it sounds like 'FUR-vunt', not 'FER-ven-t'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests sincere passion, devotion and strong conviction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fervent' in formal speech, writing, and discussions of belief, causes, or deep feelings. In casual talk, people say 'passionate,' 'really into it,' or 'super committed.' It can sound stiff in a casual setting, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Passionate is more common and can describe romantic or personal feelings, while fervent often describes belief or serious conviction.
Ardent is close in meaning but more literary and emphasizes warmth of feeling, while fervent suggests stronger intensity.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a fervent Cardinals fan, so he never misses a game.
examples.professional: She is a fervent advocate for better testing in our data pipelines.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that a fervent faith must still be tested by reason and communal discernment.

nuance.analogy: A fervent person is like a campfire that keeps burning strongly even in the cold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fervens, from fervere, 'to boil'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fervent' for weak interest, which contradicts the strong sense of the word.
Confusing 'fervent' with 'fervid'; 'fervid' is more literary and less common.

fervent.etymology: From Middle English *fervent*, from Old French *fervent*, from Latin *ferventem*, the or form of *fervēns* (“burning, fiery; hot; zealous; etc.”), the of *ferveō* (“to burn; to be hot; to be agitated, fired up, or inflamed; etc.”), ultimately from…

senses.definition: A thin strip of any material, in various technical uses.
A heavy bead of waterproofing compound or sealant material generally installed at the point where vertical and horizontal surfaces meet.
A rounded relief or cut at an edge, especially an inside edge, added for a finished appearance and to break sharp edges.
A strip or compact piece of meat or fish from which any bones and skin and feathers have been removed.
A thin featureless moulding/molding used as separation between broader decorative mouldings.
An ordinary equal in breadth to one quarter of the chief, to the lowest portion of which it corresponds in position.
The thread of a screw.
A colored or gilded border.
The raised moulding around the muzzle of a gun.
Any scantling smaller than a batten.
The loins of a horse, beginning at the place where the hinder part of the saddle rests.
The space between two flutings in a shaft.
A fascia; a band of fibres; applied especially to certain bands of white matter in the brain.
(rare) A headband; a ribbon or other band used to tie the hair up, or keep a headdress in place, or for decoration.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To slice, bone or make into fillets.
To apply, create, or specify a rounded or filled corner to.

core.definition: A boneless piece of meat or fish cut from the side of an animal; as a verb, to remove the bones from fish or meat to make fillets.

pronunciation.tip: In the cooking sense Americans stress the second syllable: "fih-LAY." The spelling suggests "FIL-it," which is not the standard American pronunciation for the food word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes food and cooking, often in restaurant or grocery contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say "fish fillet" or "salmon fillet" at the grocery store. Menus often spell the steak cut "filet mignon," so "filet" is the common American spelling for that cut, while "fillet" is used for fish and general cooking. Ordering a "fillet of salmon" is natural and polite.

distinctions.note: "Filet" is the common American spelling for steak cuts like filet mignon, while "fillet" is standard for fish and cooking.
"Bone" means removing bones from meat or fish in general, while "fillet" means cutting the meat into clean, boneless pieces.

examples.everyday: I'll have the salmon fillet, medium, please.
examples.professional: Our new menu uses a standardized portion for each salmon fillet to control costs.
examples.analytical: Yield loss during filleting is a key variable in comparing supplier costs.

nuance.analogy: Like taking the bones out of a fish and leaving only the clean, boneless meat.
nuance.etymology: From French filet, meaning a thin strip or thread.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "FILL-it" in the food sense.
Using "filet" for fish in careful writing; "fillet" is standard for fish.
Confusing "fillet" with "fill it" in spoken orders.

fillet.etymology: From Middle English *filet*, *vylette*, *felet*, *filette*, *flette*, from Old French *filet*, diminutive of *fil* (“thread”), from Latin *fīlum* (“thread”).

senses.definition: To obtain, arrange, or achieve by indirect, complicated and/or intensive efforts.
senses.example: finagle a day off work

senses.definition: To obtain, arrange, or achieve by deceitful methods, by trickery.
senses.example: finagled his way out of a ticket by pretending to be on the way to a funeral, distraught

senses.definition: To cheat or swindle; to use crafty, deceitful methods. (often with "out of" preceding the object)
senses.example: shady stockbrokers who finagle their clients out of fortunes.

core.definition: To get or achieve something through clever, sometimes dishonest, maneuvering or manipulation of people or rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAY. The final syllable is reduced to a light 'gul,' not 'gel.'

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in casual talk to describe someone who gets what they want through clever or slightly underhanded means, often with a hint of humor. It sounds playful in conversation, but it can be an accusation at work. Use it with friends or colleagues you know well; calling someone a finagler to their face can sound rude.

distinctions.note: Manage is neutral and means handle or achieve, while finagle implies cleverness that bends rules or the truth.
Wangle is a close synonym, mostly British, meaning to obtain through cunning; Americans prefer finagle.

examples.everyday: My brother somehow finagled us a table at the packed restaurant without a reservation.
examples.professional: She finagled an extra budget line by bundling the request with a more popular project.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the committee finagled the statistics to make the policy look more successful than it was.

nuance.analogy: Finagling is like picking a lock with a bent paper clip: you get through a door that was meant to stay shut, using ingenuity rather than the proper key.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly from a dialect word 'fainaigue,' meaning to cheat.
common_mistakes: Using 'finagle' for honest effort; it implies a shady or clever workaround, not just hard work.
Mispronouncing the second syllable as 'fi-NAG-gul' rather than 'fi-NAY-gul.'

finagle.etymology: Americanism from the 1920s, perhaps combining an alteration of *fainaigue* (“to renege”) with the suffix *le*, possibly influenced by *inveigle*; compare *haggle*.

senses.definition: The first play in a series that has a maximum of four downs.
The act of getting a first down by advancing the ball more than ten yards ahead of the field position where the team took possession.

core.definition: In American football, one of up to four plays a team has to advance the ball ten yards; gaining those ten yards earns a new set of downs.

pronunciation.tip: In this football compound the stress falls on FIRST, with down lighter, so say FURST down rather than furst DOWN. Keep the rhotic r in FURST and do not add a vowel after the st cluster.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means progress for the offense; neutral in general sports talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term constantly during football games and in fan conversation, and it is nearly always about the sport. Fans also use it figuratively for a small step forward, which is informal. A natural reply to 'Nice first down!' is 'Finally, we needed that.'

distinctions.note: A touchdown scores six points; a first down only moves the offense forward and resets the four-down count.
A set of downs is the group of up to four plays; a first down is the moment the offense earns a new set.

examples.everyday: Did you see that? We got a first down on the last play, so we're still in this game.
examples.professional: Our sales team finally got a first down this quarter, closing the account we had been chasing for months.
examples.analytical: A first down is a discrete checkpoint in the rules of the game, and its conversion rate is a standard measure of offensive efficiency.

nuance.analogy: Like a checkpoint on a hike where you earn a fresh allowance of time before you must push on.
nuance.etymology: Down comes from Old English adūne, 'off the hill'; football uses it for a play in the count.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the first down' for a single play when fans usually just say 'first down'
Putting the main stress on down, which sounds unnatural to American fans

conversation.text: They just need two more yards for a first down.
That's a first down! The drive is still alive.
They went for it on fourth down and got the first down.

senses.definition: To mend, to repair.
senses.example: That heater will start a fire if you don't fix it.

senses.definition: To prepare (food or drink).
senses.example: She fixed dinner for the kids.

senses.definition: To make (a contest, vote, or gamble) unfair; to privilege one contestant or a particular group of contestants, usually before the contest begins; to arrange immunity for defendants by tampering with the justice system via bribery or extortion.
senses.example: A majority of voters believed the election was fixed in favor of the incumbent.

senses.definition: To render (a photographic impression) permanent by treating with such applications as will make it insensitive to the action of light.
(Of a piercing look) to direct at someone.
senses.example: He fixed me with a sickly grin, and said, "I told you it wouldn't work!"

senses.definition: To attach; to affix; to hold in place or at a particular time.
senses.example: A dab of chewing gum will fix your note to the bulletin board.

senses.definition: To focus or determine (oneself, on a concept); to fixate.
senses.example: She's fixed on the idea of becoming a doctor.

senses.definition: To be immensely pleasurable to.
senses.example: Some pizza rolls would fix me right now.

senses.definition: To surgically render an animal, especially a pet, infertile.
senses.example: Rover stopped digging under the fence after we had the vet fix him.

senses.definition: To map (a point or subset) to itself.
senses.example: The function f:ℝ→ℝ;f(x):=4x−3 fixes the point 1∈ℝ, since f(1)=4(1)−3=1.

senses.definition: To take revenge on, to best; to serve justice on an assumed miscreant.
senses.example: He got caught breaking into lockers, so a couple of guys fixed him after work.

senses.definition: To become fixed; to settle or remain permanently; to cease from wandering; to rest.
To become firm, so as to resist volatilization; to cease to flow or be fluid; to congeal; to become hard and malleable, as a metallic substance.
To shoot up; to inject a drug.
To arrange (an event etc.).
senses.example: Could you fix it for me to meet the band backstage?

senses.definition: To prevent enemy pawns from advancing by directly opposing the most advanced one with one of one's own pawns so as to threaten to capture any advancing backward pawns.
To convert into a stable or available form.
senses.example: Legumes are valued in crop rotation for their ability to fix nitrogen.

senses.definition: A repair or corrective action.
senses.example: That plumber's fix is much better than the first one's.

senses.definition: A non-waypoint terrain feature used to make a determination of location.
A difficult situation; a quandary or dilemma; a predicament.
senses.example: It rained before we repaired the roof, and were we in a fix!

senses.definition: A single dose of a narcotic drug, especially when injected.
Something that satisfies a yearning or a craving.
A compulsive desire or thrill.
A prearrangement of the outcome of a supposedly competitive process, such as a sporting event, a game, an election, a trial, or a bid.
An understanding, grasp of something.
A determination of location.
senses.example: We have a fix on your position.

senses.definition: Fettlings (mixture used to line a furnace).

core.definition: To repair something that is broken or not working properly, or to make it right.

pronunciation.tip: Short vowel /ɪ/ as in 'sit', not 'seat'. Final /ks/ is a single consonant cluster, so say the k clearly before the s.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it describes making something work again. It is also used in everyday speech for preparing food, as in 'fix a sandwich'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fix' constantly for household and car repairs: 'Can you fix the sink?' or 'My car needs fixing.' In the US it also means 'to prepare' food or drink, so 'Let me fix you some coffee' is a friendly offer. Avoid it for formal reports on damage; 'repair' sounds more precise there.

distinctions.note: 'Repair' is more formal and precise, often for technical or expensive work, while 'fix' is the everyday word.
'Mend' suggests sewing, clothing or small tears, and is less common in everyday American speech for machines.

examples.everyday: Our dishwasher broke again, so we're going to call someone to fix it.
examples.professional: The team agreed to fix the failing data pipeline before Monday's release.
examples.analytical: To fix a flaw in an argument is not merely to restate it, but to identify the premise that makes it fail.

nuance.analogy: Like a mechanic putting a broken engine back together, 'fix' brings something back to working order.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'fixus', past participle of 'figere', 'to fasten'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fix' for 'fix in place' in formal writing, where 'fasten' or 'attach' is clearer.
Saying 'I will fix to the store'; the correct phrase is 'I will go to the store'.

fix.etymology: From Middle English *fixen*, borrowed from Old French **fixer* (attested only as *ficher*, *fichier*; > English *fitch*), from *fix* (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin *fīxus* (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from *fīgō* (“to drive in; stick; fasten”),…

conversation.text: Can you fix the drawer? It keeps falling off the track.
The landlord finally fixed the heater after two weeks.
Let me fix you something to eat before you go.

senses.definition: Full of flavor.

core.definition: Having a strong, pleasant, or interesting taste.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is a reduced 'fuhl' sound, not a full 'full,' and the middle 'er' is weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment for food, and in some contexts for writing, music, or ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flavorful' to praise food, especially in restaurant reviews or conversation with friends. It is a common, friendly word that you can use in everyday talk. For a dish that is too strong, Americans would say 'bold' or 'intense' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Delicious' describes how good something tastes, while 'flavorful' focuses on how rich or distinct the flavor is.
'Tasty' is more casual and simpler, while 'flavorful' sounds a little more descriptive and is often used in cooking or reviews.

examples.everyday: This soup is so flavorful that I want a second bowl.
examples.professional: The menu team wants more flavorful options for the vegetarian line.
examples.analytical: A flavorful argument is one that has depth, though its persuasive force still depends on its logic.

nuance.analogy: A flavorful dish is like a song with many layers that all work together.
nuance.etymology: Formed from flavor and the suffix -ful, meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Using 'flavorful' for food that is just strong or spicy, where 'bold' or 'spicy' may be better
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'full' rather than a reduced 'fuhl'

conversation.text: This curry is really flavorful; what spices did you use?
The chicken was juicy and flavorful.
Fresh herbs make any dish more flavorful.

senses.definition: Having four feet.

core.definition: Having four feet; describing an animal that walks on four legs, such as a dog, horse, or cow.

pronunciation.tip: Both words get stress, with the main stress on FOOT, the second word. Say the first word as one clear syllable, 'fohr,' with a strong American r, and do not add an extra vowel between 'four' and 'footed.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain descriptive term for animals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use four-footed mostly in descriptions, teaching, or writing about animals, often in contrast with birds or people. In casual speech people more often say 'a dog' or 'a horse,' or 'four-legged' for everyday talk. Four-footed is a common word in Bible study contexts, where it translates Hebrew terms for livestock and land animals.

distinctions.note: Four-legged is the more common everyday American term for animals; four-footed sounds slightly more formal or traditional.
Quadruped is a technical zoological term for an animal with four limbs, used in science writing.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's four-footed friend, a big golden retriever, greets everybody at the park.
examples.professional: The zoo's new exhibit features several four-footed animals that were moved from the old habitat.
examples.analytical: The author distinguishes the two-footed human from the four-footed beast, a contrast that shapes the moral order of the creation account.

nuance.analogy: Like a table that stands on four legs, a four-footed animal has a steady, sturdy base.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fēower and fōt; compounded as an adjective describing animals with four feet.
common_mistakes: Saying 'four foots' or treating 'foot' as a plural in the adjective form.
Stressing 'four' too weakly, so it sounds like 'for.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 1:24-25 God creates land animals, which the RSV renders as beasts of the earth, cattle, and creeping things, and the Hebrew term behemah (livestock, beast) covers many four-footed animals. Leviticus 11 separates clean and unclean animals, and four-footed creatures that walk on paws are unclean in that chapter. Acts 10:12 describes a vision of many animals, showing that Peter should not treat any creature as unclean.

senses.definition: Containing the maximum possible amount that can fit in the space available.
senses.example: The jugs were full to the point of overflowing.

senses.definition: Complete; with nothing omitted.
senses.example: Our book gives full treatment to the subject of angling.

senses.definition: Surjective as a map of morphisms.
Including all morphisms. Formally: Such that for every pairs of objects (X, Y) in S, the hom-sets HomS(X,Y) and HomC(X,Y) are equal.
Total, entire.
senses.example: She had tattoos the full length of her arms. He was prosecuted to the full extent of the law.

senses.definition: Completely empowered, authorized or qualified (in some role); not limited.
senses.example: full member

senses.definition: Having eaten to satisfaction, having a "full" stomach; replete.
senses.example: "I'm full," he said, pushing back from the table.

senses.definition: Replete, abounding with.
senses.example: This movie doesn't make sense; it's full of plot holes.

senses.definition: Carrying as much as possible.
senses.example: Hang on - my hands are full; just let me put these down.

senses.definition: Plump, round.
senses.example: full lips; a full face; a full figure

senses.definition: Having its entire face illuminated.
Of a size that is ample, wide, or having ample folds or pleats to be comfortable.
senses.example: a full pleated skirt; She needed her full clothing during her pregnancy.

senses.definition: Having depth and body; rich.
senses.example: a full singing voice

senses.definition: Having the attention, thoughts, etc. absorbed in any matter, and the feelings more or less excited by it.
senses.example: She's full of her latest project.

senses.definition: Filled with emotions.
Said of the three cards of the same rank in a full house.
senses.example: nines full of aces

senses.definition: Drunk, intoxicated.
Utmost measure or extent; highest state or degree; the state, position, or moment of fullness; fill.
senses.example: I was fed to the full.

senses.definition: The phase of the moon when its entire face is illuminated, full moon.
A flip involving a complete turn in midair.
An aerialist maneuver consisting of a backflip in conjunction and simultaneous with a complete twist.
To become full or wholly illuminated.
To baptize.
To make cloth denser and firmer by soaking, beating and pressing; to waulk or walk.

core.definition: Containing as much as can fit; having no room left. Also used to say you have eaten enough and cannot take more.

pronunciation.tip: Full rhymes with pull and wool, not with fool or cool. The vowel is short and relaxed, and the final l is clear, with the tongue touching the top of the mouth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Saying you are full after a meal is a polite, ordinary way to show satisfaction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use full constantly in everyday talk, such as 'I'm full, thanks' at a dinner or 'The parking lot is full.' For a stronger informal feeling after eating, Americans often say 'I'm stuffed' or 'I'm so full I could burst.' Full is also used with 'up' in 'I'm full up' for casual emphasis.

distinctions.note: Stuffed is informal and suggests you are uncomfortably full after eating a lot, while full is neutral and polite.
Complete means nothing is missing from a whole, while full describes a container or space that holds as much as it can.

examples.everyday: Thanks for dinner, but I'm full, so I'll skip dessert.
examples.professional: Sorry, the conference room is full, so let's move the meeting to the small room on the second floor.
examples.analytical: A container is full when no further material can be added without exceeding its capacity, which makes fullness a limit rather than a quantity.

nuance.analogy: A glass filled to the brim: once the water touches the rim, there is no room left for more.
nuance.etymology: From Old English full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz, related to fill.
common_mistakes: Using 'full with' instead of 'full of', as in 'The room was full with people' rather than 'full of people'.
Saying 'I am full' when you mean you are very full and uncomfortable; Americans would say 'I'm stuffed' in that case.
patterns: full (= not hungry; not before a noun)

full.etymology: From Middle English *ful*, from Old English *full* (“full”), from **full*, from Proto-Germanic **fullaz* (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European **pl̥h₁nós* (“full”).

conversation.text: I'm full, but that was really good.
Don't fill up on bread, or you'll be full before dinner.
The restaurant is full tonight, so we'll have to wait.
No more for me, thanks; I'm full.
I'm too full to eat dessert.
The fridge is full of leftovers.

core.definition: A Judean official whom the Babylonians appointed governor of Judah after 586 BC; he was assassinated soon after taking office.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, LYE. Say the first syllable as 'ged' and the middle as a weak 'uh.' The final 'ah' is a soft 'uh' or 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Gedaliah' in Bible study, Jewish history and seminary contexts. It is a personal name, so it is not used in everyday talk. When discussing him, say he was governor after Jerusalem fell.

distinctions.note: Gedalia is an alternate English spelling of the same name in some translations.

examples.everyday: In our Bible reading this week, Gedaliah was appointed governor after Jerusalem fell.
examples.professional: The historical timeline in the lecture notes places Gedaliah's governorship at Mizpah just after the destruction of Jerusalem.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah's account of Gedaliah's assassination by Ishmael shows the fragility of the remnant community after the exile.

nuance.analogy: Gedaliah is like a caretaker manager appointed after a company collapses, trying to hold things together until it is clear who is in charge.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew Gedalyahu, meaning Yahweh is great, from the root gadal, to be great, and Yah, a short form of the divine name.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'GED-uh-LY-uh'; the stress is on the third syllable.
Confusing Gedaliah with Gedalia, the same name in different spellings.
nuance.biblical_note: Gedaliah (Hebrew Gedalyahu, meaning Yahweh is great) was the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan. The Babylonians made him governor over the remnant in Judah, based at Mizpah, after the fall of Jerusalem. Key passages: 2 Kings 25:22-25, which describes his appointment and his murder by Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Jeremiah 40:5-6, where Gedaliah encourages the people to serve the Babylonians and settle in the land. Jeremiah 41:1-3, which tells how Ishmael kills Gedaliah and others at Mizpah.

core.definition: The New Testament letters not attributed to Paul, namely James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, and Jude, addressed to wider Christian audiences.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'JEN' in 'General' and 'PIS' in 'Epistles'. The first syllable of 'General' is a reduced 'uh' and the 'r' is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: A standard term in Bible study, seminary courses and scholarly writing. Americans use it when discussing New Testament organization, usually in a church or academic setting.

distinctions.note: Pauline Epistles are letters traditionally attributed to Paul; General Epistles are the letters not attributed to him.
An epistle is any letter in this sense; General Epistles is the name for a specific group of New Testament letters.

collocations: the letters of the General Epistles

examples.everyday: Our small group is reading through the General Epistles this summer, starting with James.
examples.professional: In the New Testament survey, I will cover the General Epistles after the Pauline letters.
examples.analytical: The General Epistles address wider communities than the Pauline letters, which shapes their concerns with perseverance and ethics.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of open letters sent to many churches rather than private letters to one congregation.
nuance.etymology: 'Epistle' from Greek epistolē, 'letter'; 'general' from Latin generalis, 'common to all'.
common_mistakes: Calling them the 'Catholic Epistles', which is an older term; Americans in Protestant settings usually say 'General Epistles'.
Including Hebrews in the group, which is usually treated separately.
nuance.biblical_note: The General Epistles are the New Testament letters of James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John and Jude. They are called 'general' because they are not addressed to a specific congregation or individual, though 2 and 3 John are short letters to named recipients. Hebrews is usually placed separately, since its authorship and genre differ from these letters.

senses.definition: Another common thing Americans say when someone sneezes.

core.definition: A German word said to someone who has just sneezed, wishing them good health.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, ZOONT. The 'nd' is pronounced as a 't' before 'h', and the final syllable is one 'hite' with a strong 'ai' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly, with a light, playful tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Bless you' far more often; Gesundheit is a lighthearted alternative, popular among friends and in offices. After a sneeze, the usual reply is simply 'Thank you.' Saying it to a stranger in a very formal setting can sound unusual.

examples.everyday: Achoo! Oh, gesundheit.
examples.professional: Someone sneezed during the call, and Dana quickly said, 'Gesundheit!' to lighten the mood.
examples.analytical: The custom of blessing a sneeze is older than the German word, though many Americans use gesundheit without knowing its German meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a quick nod, it acknowledges the sneeze in a warm way without making a fuss.
nuance.etymology: German for 'health', from gesund (healthy) with the noun suffix -heit.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable or pronouncing it from the spelling as 'guh-ZOON-dite'.
Replying 'Gesundheit' to the sneezer's thanks; the usual reply is 'Thank you'.

conversation.text: Gesundheit! That was a big one.
Every time I sneeze, my coworker says, "Gesundheit."
Gesundheit. Are your allergies acting up again?

senses.definition: To move softly, smoothly, or effortlessly.
To fly unpowered, as of an aircraft. Also relates to gliding birds and flying fish.
To cause to glide.
To pass with a glide, as the voice.
The act of gliding.
A transitional sound, especially a semivowel.
An attack or preparatory movement made by sliding down the opponent’s blade, keeping it in constant contact.
A bird, the glede or kite.
A kind of cap affixed to the base of the legs of furniture to prevent it from damaging the floor while being moved.
The joining of two sounds without a break.
A smooth and sliding step in dancing the waltz.

core.definition: To move smoothly and effortlessly, without visible effort, as on ice, through the air, or through traffic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable, with a clear diphthong that moves from 'ah' toward 'ee'. End with a clear 'd', not an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests smooth, calm, and skilled movement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glide in everyday speech for cars moving through traffic, skaters on ice, or birds in the air. People also say 'glide into a parking spot' or 'glide through a meeting' when something goes smoothly. It is less common for fast or forceful movement.

distinctions.note: Slide usually involves contact with a surface and may be uncontrolled. Glide suggests smooth, controlled movement, often without much friction.
Float means staying on or in a fluid or air with little effort, usually without a clear direction. Glide suggests a direction and a controlled path.

examples.everyday: The swan glided across the pond while we ate lunch by the water.
examples.professional: Thanks to the new process, approvals glide through the system without needing manual review.
examples.analytical: The essay's transitions glide from one argument to the next so smoothly that the reader rarely notices the seams.

nuance.analogy: Like a skater who pushes off the ice and coasts with no visible effort.
nuance.etymology: From Old English glidan, meaning to slip or glide.
common_mistakes: Using glide for fast, forceful motion. The word implies smoothness and control.
Adding an extra syllable, as in 'glide-uh'. The word has one syllable.

glide.etymology: From Middle English *gliden*, from Old English *glīdan*, from **glīdan*, from Proto-Germanic **glīdaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **gʰleydʰ-*.

senses.definition: A cooking device comprising a source of radiative heat from above and a means of holding food under it; a broiler in US English.
A cooking device comprising a source of radiative heat from below and a means of holding food above it; a barbecue.
senses.example: I put some peppers and mushrooms on the grill to go with dinner.

senses.definition: A grating; a grid of wire or a sheet of material with a pattern of holes or slots, usually used to protect something while allowing the passage of air and liquids. Typical uses: to allow air through a fan while preventing fingers or objects from passing; to allow people to talk to somebody, while preventing attack.
The criss-cross pieces that separate panes of glass in a window.
On a vehicle, a slotted cover as above, to protect and hide the radiator, while admitting air to cool it.
Food (designed to be) cooked on a grill.
senses.example: a packet of frozen cauliflower cheese grills

senses.definition: A grillroom; a restaurant serving grilled food.
senses.example: These coupons will get you a discount at Johnny's Bar and Grill.

senses.definition: A type of jewelry worn on the front teeth.
The front teeth regarded collectively.
Deliberate misspelling of girl.
senses.example: r u a grill?

senses.definition: To cook (food) on a grill; to barbecue.
senses.example: Why don't we get together Saturday and grill some burgers?

senses.definition: To cook food under the element of a stove or only under the top element of an oven – broil, salamander.
To interrogate; to question aggressively or harshly.
senses.example: The police grilled him about his movements at the time of the crime.

senses.definition: To feel very hot; to swelter.
To stamp or mark with a grill.
To stare at.

core.definition: A metal rack or appliance with grates that cooks food over direct heat, often outdoors on charcoal or gas.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short i and a clear final l. Do not add a vowel before the l, and do not stretch the vowel into a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes cooking equipment and everyday summer cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grill for outdoor cooking equipment and for cooking on it, as in we're grilling burgers tonight. For the heat source in an oven, Americans usually say broiler, so reserve grill for outdoor cooking with grates. Restaurants also use grill for a cooking station or a casual menu.

distinctions.note: In American usage barbecue often means slow-smoked meat, and as a noun it can also name the event, while grill means cooking over direct heat.
A broiler is the heat source above food in an oven, while grill is usually outdoor cooking from below.

examples.everyday: Can you fire up the grill? The burgers should be ready in twenty minutes.
examples.professional: The restaurant's grill station can prepare the chicken for the event menu.
examples.analytical: The grill's direct radiant heat gives food a sear that an enclosed oven cannot easily reproduce.

nuance.analogy: A grill is like a campfire with a grate laid over it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle French gril, from Latin craticula, a small grate.
common_mistakes: Calling the oven's heat source a grill, when Americans say broiler.
Confusing grill, to cook, with grill, to question someone harshly.

grill.etymology: 1655, from French *gril*, from Middle French *gril*, from Old French *greïl*, *graïl* (“gridiron”), from *graïlle* (“grate, grating”), from Latin *crātīcula* (“gridiron”), diminutive of *crātis* (“hurdle, wickerwork”).

conversation.text: Let's grill some burgers this weekend.
Mike is out back firing up the grill.
My parents grilled me about where I was last night.
Can you fire up the grill? I'll get the burgers.
Does the campsite have a grill?
We grilled hot dogs and corn for dinner.

senses.definition: Having a rough, surly, and harsh demeanor and nature.
Hoarse-voiced.
senses.example: a gruff woman

senses.definition: Hoarse.
senses.example: a gruff voice

senses.definition: To speak gruffly.

core.definition: Rough, harsh, or brusque in manner, often sounding unfriendly, though the person may not be unkind underneath.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, relaxed U like the vowel in 'cup' and end with a clear, voiceless F. Do not add a vowel after the F.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it suggests a rough or curt manner, but a gruff person can be kind underneath.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often describe an older man or a tough-acting worker as gruff, meaning he speaks bluntly but may be kind. It is used in stories, reviews, and casual descriptions of people. Calling someone gruff is usually not an insult, but describing a customer service worker as gruff suggests a complaint.

distinctions.note: Blunt describes direct honesty without softening, while gruff describes a rough tone or manner.
Curt describes very short, impolite speech, while gruff can describe a rough voice or a tough personality.
Surly is stronger and more hostile, suggesting bad temper, while gruff is less hostile.

examples.everyday: The old mechanic was gruff, but he fixed my brakes for free and wouldn't take a tip.
examples.professional: Our gruff senior engineer rarely smiles in meetings, but his code reviews are the most helpful on the team.
examples.analytical: The prophet is portrayed as a gruff figure who speaks with blunt authority, yet his words reveal a deep concern for justice.

nuance.analogy: A gruff manner is like a rough wooden door: it looks hard to open, but it often protects something warm inside.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'grof', perhaps from Middle Low German or Dutch words meaning coarse or rough.
common_mistakes: Using gruff to mean angry or violent, when it usually means rough in manner or voice.
Adding an extra vowel sound after the F, which makes the word sound like 'gruh-fuh.'

gruff.etymology: 16th century, from Dutch *grof* and/or *grof* (both “rough, coarse, rude”), from **grof* or **grof*, both from **grob*, from Proto-Germanic **grubaz* (“coarse, rough”), possibly from an earlier **gahrubaz* and then related with **hreubaz* (“scabby, rough,…

core.definition: A priest of Aaron's line, head of the eighth priestly division in King David's time, and an ancestor of families listed after the exile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ck' is a single hard K sound, and the final 'z' is voiced, not 'hack-ohs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a name from the Bible used in historical and genealogical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible study, lectures on Old Testament priests, or genealogical lists. It is not a common personal name in everyday life. Pronounce it as the Hebrew name, with the stress on the first syllable.

examples.everyday: My friend asked me about a name in her Bible reading, and I said Hakkoz was a priest's family name from the Old Testament.
examples.professional: The Sunday school curriculum includes a lesson on the priestly families, so the Hakkoz list is on the handout.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Hakkoz in Ezra and Nehemiah shows how the post-exilic community verified priestly descent before admitting families to temple service.

nuance.analogy: Like a name in a family tree that a historian has to check before deciding who belongs to the family.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Haqqoz, probably meaning 'the thorn'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'hack-ose' with an 'oh' vowel.
Confusing Hakkoz with Hakkatan, another name in the Old Testament.
nuance.biblical_note: Hakkoz is the head of the eighth priestly course in 1 Chronicles 24:10, one of the twenty-four divisions that served in the temple in David's time. Ezra 2:61 lists descendants of Hakkoz among priests who could not prove their genealogy after the exile and were excluded. Nehemiah 3:4 names Meremoth son of Uriah son of Hakkoz as one of the workers who repaired the wall of Jerusalem.

senses.definition: Causing or likely to cause harm or damage; injurious.
senses.example: Wear a hat to protect your skin from harmful sunlight.

core.definition: Likely to cause damage, injury, or harm to people, animals, things, or health.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HARM. The ending -ful is a syllabic l with no full vowel, so the word has only two syllables, the second sounding like 'fl'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that damages or endangers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harmful for things that damage health, safety, or relationships, such as harmful chemicals or the harmful effects of smoking. It is common in warnings, medical advice, and everyday talk. For slight or temporary effects, 'bad for' or 'not good for' sounds more natural.

distinctions.note: Dangerous stresses immediate risk to life or safety, while harmful is broader and can describe slow or long-term damage.
Hurtful describes words or actions that cause emotional pain, while harmful covers physical, social, or financial damage as well.

examples.everyday: Smoking is really harmful, so I'm trying to quit this year.
examples.professional: The security team flagged a harmful script in the attachment and blocked the email before it reached anyone.
examples.analytical: Some ethical theories hold that an action is wrong only when it is harmful to a person, not merely unpleasant.

nuance.analogy: Harmful is like a small leak in a roof: it does damage slowly and quietly, long before the storm arrives.
nuance.etymology: From harm plus -ful, from Old English hearm and the suffix meaning full of.
common_mistakes: Saying 'harmful for' people; the usual phrase is 'harmful to' someone or something.
Giving the ending a full vowel, as in 'HARM-ful'; the second syllable is a syllabic l.

harmful.etymology: From Middle English *harmful*, from Old English **hearmful* (suggested by *hearmfullīċ* (“harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to *harm* + *ful*.

core.definition: A Levite in the post-exilic period of Israel, named as a leader in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, BY. The ending is a light 'uh' sound, and the sh is clear. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name in a biblical list, used in scholarly or church contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly encounter Hashabiah in Bible study, sermons, or academic commentary on Ezra and Nehemiah. It is a formal name and is rarely used in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Hashabneiah is a different name for a different man, appearing in Nehemiah 3:10 as the father of Hattush, so keep them separate.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study, someone asked who Hashabiah was, and we found him in a list of Levites.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Hashabiah is cited as an example of Levitical leadership after the exile.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists in Ezra and Nehemiah name Hashabiah to establish the legitimacy of the restored Levitical families.

nuance.analogy: Hashabiah is like one name in a roll call of community leaders, recorded so that each family's role is remembered.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥashavyāh, meaning Yahweh has reckoned or considered.
common_mistakes: Confusing Hashabiah with Hashabneiah, who is a different person in Nehemiah 3:10.
Stressing the first syllable, saying 'HASH-uh-by-uh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hashabiah (Hebrew Ḥashavyah, meaning Yahweh has reckoned) is a Levite named in the post-exilic books. Ezra 8:19 lists him among Levites, sons of Merari, whom Ezra recruited to return to Jerusalem with the exiles. Nehemiah 12:24 names him as a head of the Levites in the days of Joiakim, the high priest's successor, and in the time of Nehemiah's dedication of the walls. These passages show Levites performing leadership and worship roles after the exile.

senses.definition: A strip of fabric worn around the head.
A hair accessory, made of a flexible material and curved like a horseshoe, for holding one's hair back.
A strip of fabric attached to the top of the spine of a book; used as decoration and reinforcement.
A thin slip of iron on the tympan of a printing press.

core.definition: A strip of fabric or elastic worn around the head to keep hair back or to hold sweat away, such as during exercise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HED, and the second syllable is lighter. Keep the d sound clear at the end of head and band, since Americans often link the two words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday item with no particular emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use headband for both athletic and fashion accessories, such as a sweatband for running or a fabric band for keeping hair out of the face. Someone might say they need a headband for a workout. Do not confuse it with a headdress, which is a ceremonial or decorative covering.

distinctions.note: A headscarf is a square or rectangular cloth tied over the head and usually covers more of the hair, while a headband is a narrow band worn across the forehead.
Hairband is a less common, somewhat informal synonym; headband is the standard American term in most contexts.

examples.everyday: I wore a headband to keep the sweat out of my eyes during my run.
examples.professional: The marketing team chose a moisture-wicking headband for the new fitness product line.
examples.analytical: The headband functions less as a garment than as a boundary between the body and its surroundings, managing sweat and visibility at once.

nuance.analogy: A headband is like a belt for your forehead: narrow, flexible, and wrapped around one part of the body to hold things in place.
nuance.etymology: From head plus band, a strip of material; the compound is recorded in English from the 1600s.
common_mistakes: Saying hedband with a weak d sound; the final d in both words should be pronounced.
Using headband for a ceremonial crown or decorative head covering, which is a headdress.

headband.etymology: From Middle English **hedband*, from Old English *hēafodbænd*, *hēafodbend* (“headband”), equivalent to *head* + *band*.

senses.definition: An employee who is hired, often to perform unpleasant tasks with little independence.
Someone who does a job purely for money, rather than out of interest in the work itself.
A horse for hire.

core.definition: A person who works for wages, especially one seen as serving only for pay rather than from loyalty or commitment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HY, and the 'r' is strongly rhotic before the 'l' in the second syllable. Learners often insert a vowel after the r, saying 'HY-ruh-ling'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying someone works only for money and lacks commitment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use hireling in everyday speech; they say employee, worker or contractor. The word appears mainly in Bible passages, sermons and literary writing, where it suggests a worker who does not care about the people or cause. Calling a colleague a hireling in an office would sound harsh and old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Employee is the neutral everyday term; hireling is negative and suggests a person serving only for pay.
A mercenary is a soldier or fighter paid to serve, often a foreigner; a hireling is a broader term for any paid worker with weak commitment.

examples.everyday: When the company replaced the whole crew, one of the old workers said they had been treated like hirelings.
examples.professional: Our leadership program emphasizes ownership, so we avoid building a team of hirelings who only do the minimum.
examples.analytical: In John 10, Jesus contrasts the good shepherd, who cares for the sheep, with the hireling, who runs away when the wolf comes.

nuance.analogy: A hireling is like a substitute teacher who shows up for the paycheck but never really cares whether the students learn.
nuance.etymology: From hire and the suffix -ling, a noun ending indicating a person connected to the stated thing.
common_mistakes: Using hireling as a neutral word for an employee, which can insult a colleague.
Stressing the second syllable instead of HY-ling.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word sakir (שָׂכִיר) means hired worker or day laborer. Job 7:2 compares the hard life of man to a hireling who waits for his wages. John 10:12-13 contrasts the good shepherd, who risks himself for the sheep, with a hireling who flees when the wolf comes. Malachi 3:5 denounces those who oppress the hireling in his wages, showing God's concern for fair treatment of workers.

hireling.etymology: From Middle English *hirlyng*, from Old English *hȳrling* (“hireling, employee”), from **hūʀijuling*.

senses.definition: Exaggerated, overemotional behavior, especially when calculated to elicit a response; melodramatics.

core.definition: Exaggerated, overly emotional behavior meant to attract attention or get a reaction from others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AH, the third syllable. It is almost always used in the plural form, so do not add an article like 'a histrionics'. The final 'ks' is a clear unvoiced sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests an emotional display that is excessive or insincere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use histrionics mostly in the plural, as in 'Enough histrionics' or 'all the histrionics'. It describes showy emotional behavior in arguments, family conflicts, or workplace complaints. It is informal but understood widely, and it is often said with a sigh or an eye roll.

distinctions.note: Drama can mean an exciting event or an emotional situation, while histrionics refers specifically to the exaggerated behavior of the people involved.
A tantrum is a sudden outburst, usually from a child or someone frustrated, while histrionics is more deliberate and performed.

examples.everyday: Can we skip the histrionics and just talk about what happened with the car?
examples.professional: Let's keep the histrionics out of the postmortem and focus on the root cause of the outage.
examples.analytical: Much of the political debate was dominated by histrionics, which obscured the substantive policy questions beneath the outrage.

nuance.analogy: Histrionics are like a smoke machine at a concert: a lot of visible effect that can hide what is actually happening on stage.
nuance.etymology: From Latin histrionicus, from histrio meaning actor, of uncertain origin, possibly Etruscan.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a histrionics' instead of 'histrionics' or 'some histrionics'.
Using the singular 'histrionic' as a noun for the behavior.

core.definition: A member of an ancient people of Anatolia, or in the Bible, one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel's settlement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HIT, and the final syllable rhymes with 'bite.' Learners often pronounce the second syllable as 'tee' or stress the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical or biblical term with no negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: In American English it is mainly used in Bible study, history, and archaeology. In everyday speech it would sound unusual. In Scripture it refers to a Canaanite people, distinct from the later Anatolian empire, though scholars debate the connection.

distinctions.note: Both are biblical Canaanite peoples, but the Hittites are named more often and include individuals like Uriah, while the Hivites are linked to Shechem and the Gibeonites.
The Anatolian Hittites were a historical empire; the biblical Hittites are a Canaanite group, and scholars debate whether they are related.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group was reading about Uriah the Hittite, and everyone was shocked by the story.
examples.professional: In the seminar, I explained that the Hittites in Genesis are not the same people as the Anatolian empire.
examples.analytical: The biblical references to Hittites raise questions about the relationship between Canaanite population groups and the Hittite kingdom of Anatolia.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name shared by different branches of a family, the same word can point to different groups in different contexts.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ḥittî (of Heth), the name of Heth, a son of Canaan in Genesis 10:15.
common_mistakes: Confusing the biblical Hittites with the Anatolian empire without noting the difference.
Pronouncing 'Hittite' as 'HIT-eye-t' with three distinct syllables instead of two.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is Ḥittî (Hittite), a people descended from Heth, a son of Canaan (Genesis 10:15). Key passages: Genesis 23 describes Abraham buying the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite, showing them as established landholders in Canaan. In 2 Samuel 11:3 Uriah the Hittite is a loyal soldier of David whose death David arranges. In 1 Kings 11:1 Solomon's foreign wives include Hittite women, a warning about intermarriage.

hittite.etymology: From Biblical Hebrew *חִתִּי*, from *𒄩𒋾*, perhaps ultimately an exonym related to *Hatti*.

senses.definition: One who refuses to give consent to an agreement in the hope of an improved offer; one who holds out; one who clings to a cause that has been mostly abandoned.
A device for cheating at card games by covertly holding a card out of play until it is wanted.

core.definition: A person or group that refuses to agree to a deal or to give up an old position.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on HOLD, and the second word out is lighter. Say the final t clearly, and avoid turning owt into a long o sound.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, since it suggests stubbornness, though it can be neutral or positive when the person refuses for principled reasons.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use holdout in news, politics, labor disputes and business, such as 'a holdout senator' or 'a holdout homeowner.' In data science, holdout also refers to a set of data kept back for testing a model, so say the context clearly. A natural reply is 'Who is the holdout?' or 'Why are they holding out?'

distinctions.note: A holdout set is a sample of data kept separate for model testing, while a holdout is a person or group that refuses to agree.
Dissenter is more formal and principled, while holdout suggests refusing to accept a deal or change.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is the holdout on the fence project, but he finally agreed.
examples.professional: We used a holdout set to check whether the model generalized beyond the training data.
examples.analytical: The holdout in the debate became the decisive figure because the rest of the committee could not move without him.

nuance.analogy: Like the last player at the table who will not fold, a holdout keeps refusing while others move on.
nuance.etymology: Formed from hold out plus the noun ending.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, hold out, when used as a noun.
Confusing the everyday meaning with the data science meaning in technical meetings.

core.definition: A town in the Negev desert in southern Judah, whose name recalls the Israelites' vow to destroy the Canaanite cities there.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final vowel is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'muh' rather than 'mah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it refers to a historical place, though the name recalls the idea of total destruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the name mainly in Bible study, church teaching or academic discussion of biblical geography. It is not used in ordinary conversation. Its meaning ties into the Hebrew idea of devoting something to destruction.

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher said Hormah was a town in the desert, and I wrote it down to look up later.
examples.professional: When teaching the wilderness narratives, I always map Hormah so students see the southern route of Israel's journey.
examples.analytical: The naming of Hormah in Numbers 21 is a wordplay on the Hebrew root for devotion to destruction, which shapes the story's meaning.

nuance.analogy: Hormah is like a place name that became a permanent memorial to a dreadful promise, so the name carries the memory of what happened there.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew hormah, related to the root haram, to devote to destruction.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'hor-MAH'.
Confusing it with Horon or Hormah's similarly sounding biblical places.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Hormah (hormah), named from the root haram, meaning to devote to destruction. Numbers 14:45 records that Amalekites and Canaanites defeated Israelites there. Numbers 21:1-3 tells how the king of Arad fought Israel, and Israel vowed to devote the cities to destruction, after which the place was called Hormah. Judges 1:17 says Judah and Simeon destroyed Zephath and renamed it Hormah.

senses.definition: A geometric figure in four or more dimensions, which is analogous to a cube in three dimensions. Specifically, the n-dimensional equivalent of a cube for any non-negative integer n.
Such a figure in four dimensions; a tesseract.
A data cube with more than three dimensions.
A computer architecture in which each processor is connected to n others, by analogy with a hypercube of n dimensions.

core.definition: A geometric shape in four or more dimensions, the generalization of a cube to higher dimensions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HY. The word is pronounced as three syllables with a clear 'er' sound in the middle, and the final syllable rhymes with 'tube'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in mathematics, computer science, and data science, especially when discussing high-dimensional spaces. In casual talk, people would say four-dimensional cube or tesseract. In data science, the term sometimes refers to a multidimensional data cube in databases.

distinctions.note: Tesseract is the specific name for a four-dimensional hypercube, while hypercube covers any number of dimensions.
A cube is three-dimensional, while a hypercube generalizes the idea to any dimension.

examples.everyday: My kid asked what a hypercube is, and I said it is basically a cube that exists in four directions.
examples.professional: We store the sales metrics in a data hypercube so analysts can slice by region, product, and month at once.
examples.analytical: A hypercube in n dimensions has 2^n vertices, which shows how quickly the structure grows in complexity.

nuance.analogy: A cube is a square extended one step further, and a hypercube is that same extension repeated again and again.
nuance.etymology: From hyper- meaning beyond, plus cube, from Greek kubos, a die or cube.
common_mistakes: Confusing hypercube with hyperplane, which is a different concept of one dimension less than its space.
Stressing the wrong syllable as hy-PER-cube.

senses.definition: A term of endearment, often a diminutive; a pet name.
The formation of terms of endearment or pet names.
Baby talk, such as bow-wow for dog and choo-choo for train.

core.definition: A pet name or diminutive form of a name, such as Bobby for Robert, used to show affection.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PAH, the second syllable. Pronounce the final -ism as a reduced schwa plus m, not as a full vowel. The r in the middle is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes affectionate naming, but it is a technical linguistic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside linguistics or literary study. In conversation they would say pet name, nickname, or diminutive. Use hypocorism when writing about naming patterns.

distinctions.note: A nickname can be any alternative name, including ones based on personality, while a hypocorism is a shortened or diminutive form of a given name.
Diminutive is broader and includes any word form showing smallness or affection, while hypocorism refers specifically to names.

examples.everyday: My grandma still calls me Bebe, which is a hypocorism she made up when I was little.
examples.professional: In our naming study, we coded each hypocorism separately so that Bobby and Robert were counted as variants.
examples.analytical: Hypocorisms reveal how affection reshapes a formal name into something smaller, warmer, and more intimate.

nuance.analogy: A hypocorism is like a name wearing a cozy sweater: the same person, dressed for closeness.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hypokorisma, 'a pet name', from hypokorizesthai 'to call by a pet name'.
common_mistakes: Confusing hypocorism with hypocrisy, which means pretending to have virtues you lack.
Placing the stress on the last syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Characterized by hypocrisy or being a hypocrite.

core.definition: Showing hypocrisy, meaning claiming to hold standards that you do not actually follow.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KRIT, the third syllable. The final -al is a reduced syllable, so say it as kuhl, not as a separate ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It judges someone's words or conduct as dishonest, and it is more polite than calling someone a hypocrite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hypocritical in both casual and formal speech, often to comment on a specific action rather than a whole person. 'That's hypocritical' is a clear, less personal statement than 'You're a hypocrite.' It is common in politics, news, and workplace discussions.

distinctions.note: Inconsistent describes any mismatch, while hypocritical adds a moral judgment that the person knows better and is pretending otherwise.
Two-faced is more informal and emphasizes deception toward different people, while hypocritical emphasizes the gap between stated and real standards.

examples.everyday: It's a bit hypocritical to complain about traffic when you text while you drive.
examples.professional: It's hypocritical to push for flexible hours in every meeting and then deny every remote request that comes to you.
examples.analytical: The argument is hypocritical because it applies one moral standard to others and a more lenient one to the speaker himself.

nuance.analogy: A hypocritical statement is like a referee who calls fouls on everyone except his own team.
nuance.etymology: Formed from hypocrite, from Greek hupokrites, 'stage actor'.
common_mistakes: Using hypocritical as a noun; the noun is hypocrisy or hypocrite.
Confusing it with hypocrite when you mean the person, not the behavior.
patterns: it's hypocritical (of sb) to do sth

hypocritical.etymology: From *hypocritic* + *-al*, from Ancient Greek *ὑποκριτικός*, from *ὑποκριτής* (“actor, hypocrite”), from *ὑποκρίνομαι* (“I play a part on stage”), from *ὑπό* (“below”) + *κρίνω* (“I choose”).

senses.definition: Saying you haven't watched the latest episodes.

core.definition: Saying you have not yet seen or done the latest episodes, updates, or work that others have already reached.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'yet', with 'caught up' secondary-stressed; 'caught' sounds like 'kot' in General American, not 'kawt'. Link the words so 'not caught up' runs together smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a casual admission with no shame attached, and Americans say it about TV shows, sports, emails, or group projects.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in group chats, with coworkers, and with friends who want to avoid spoilers, for example 'Don't spoil it, I'm not caught up yet.' A natural reply is 'No worries, take your time' or 'Okay, I won't say anything.' You can also say 'caught up on' followed by the topic, such as 'caught up on emails' or 'caught up on the show'.

distinctions.note: 'I'm behind' often suggests falling short of a schedule or expectation, while 'not caught up yet' simply means you have not reached the current point.
'I haven't seen it yet' refers to one specific item, while 'not caught up' describes being behind on an ongoing series or stream of updates.

examples.everyday: Don't spoil the finale for me, I'm not caught up yet.
examples.professional: Sorry, I'm not caught up yet on the sprint board, so I'll review the open tickets after standup.
