senses.definition: A function which satisfies a particular set of formal conditions, created to generalize the notion of the length of a vector. Formally, a real-valued function on a vector space, generally denoted v↦|v| or v↦‖v‖, that satisfies the following properties:
Any of several generalizations of the above: a field norm, ideal norm, etc.
senses.example: A quaternion algebra (a,b) over ksplits if and only if b is a norm from the field extension k(a)/k, i.e. if and only if there is some x in k(a) which has field norm exactly equal to b.

senses.definition: An element of the image of some (generalized) norm, the element then said to be from the norm in question, or from the structure which gave rise to the norm.
senses.example: A quaternion algebra (a,b) over ksplits if and only if b is a norm from the field extension k(a)/k, i.e. if and only if there is some x in k(a) which has field norm exactly equal to b.

senses.definition: That which is normal or typical.
senses.example: Unemployment is the norm in this part of the country.

senses.definition: A rule that is imposed by regulations and/or socially enforced by members of a community.
senses.example: Not eating your children is just one of those societal norms.

senses.definition: A sentence with non-descriptive meaning, such as a command, permission, or prohibition.
If v≠0 then ‖v‖≠0;
Given a scalar k, ‖kv‖=|k|⋅‖v‖, where |k| is the absolute value of k;
Given two vectors v,w, ‖v+w‖≤‖v‖+‖w‖ (the triangle inequality).
A high level of performance in a chess tournament, several of which are required for a player to receive a title.
To endow (a vector space, etc.) with a norm.

core.definition: A standard or typical way people behave or things are done, often unwritten, that a group expects others to follow.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with an open vowel like the 'aw' of 'law,' and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech. Don't add an extra vowel and say 'nor-um.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a norm describes what is expected, though 'social norms' can sound restrictive when criticized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use norm in everyday talk and in social science; 'the norm' means what is typical, as in 'Remote work is the norm now.' Plural forms like 'social norms' and 'cultural norms' are common. In casual speech 'usual' or 'the way things are' may sound more natural.

distinctions.note: A rule is explicit and often written; a norm is an expected pattern of behavior that may never be written down.
A standard is a formal, measurable benchmark often set by an authority; a norm is an informal group expectation.
A custom is a traditional practice in a community; a norm can be broader, such as the expected way to act at work.

examples.everyday: It's the norm around here to bring a dish when you visit someone for dinner.
examples.professional: Our team follows industry norms for code reviews, so every change gets a second look before it merges.
examples.analytical: Sociologists argue that shared norms make everyday cooperation possible even where no law requires it.

nuance.analogy: Norms are the unwritten rules of a group, like people lining up for coffee in order without a sign telling them to.
nuance.etymology: From Latin norma, 'carpenter's square' or 'rule,' via French norme.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in norm' or 'as a norm' to mean 'as usual'; the natural phrase is 'the norm' or 'normally.'
Confusing norm with normal; norm is the standard, while normal is the adjective describing something typical.

norm.etymology: From Latin *norma* (“a carpenter's square, a rule, a pattern, a precept”).

senses.definition: Sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (also called top-p sampling).

core.definition: A method for generating text in which the model samples only from the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to a threshold p.

pronunciation.tip: The word nucleus is stressed on its first syllable, while sampling has primary stress on SAM. In fast speech, the final 's' of 'nucleus' often blends into the 'nu' sound, so it sounds like 'nu-klee-us SAM-pling'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in machine learning discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nucleus sampling mainly among machine learning engineers and researchers discussing how language models choose their next word. It is usually explained as top-p sampling, and it is compared with top-k sampling. It is not used in everyday conversation, and it should be introduced with a brief definition when speaking to non-specialists.

distinctions.note: Top-k keeps a fixed number of the most likely tokens, while nucleus sampling keeps a varying set whose probabilities reach p.
Greedy decoding always picks the single most probable token, while nucleus sampling introduces randomness within a probability threshold.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the chatbot sounds more natural because it uses nucleus sampling.
examples.professional: Let's switch the generation settings to nucleus sampling with p equal to 0.9 and compare the output quality.
examples.analytical: Nucleus sampling trades a degree of determinism for diversity by truncating the tail of the distribution adaptively at each step.

nuance.analogy: Nucleus sampling is like choosing a team from the people who make up most of the candidate pool, while ignoring the long tail of unlikely candidates.
nuance.etymology: Nucleus is from Latin, 'kernel'; the term was adopted in machine learning for a sampling method that keeps the core of the probability mass.
common_mistakes: Confusing nucleus sampling with top-k sampling and assuming both use a fixed number of tokens.
Stressing nucleus on its second syllable instead of the first.

conversation.text: Nucleus sampling picks from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p.
Unlike top-k, nucleus sampling adapts: the candidate set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it isn't.
Nucleus sampling with p set to 0.9 is a common default for open-ended generation.

senses.definition: Extremely overweight, especially: weighing more than 20% (for men) or 25% (for women) over their conventionally ideal weight determined by height and build; or, having a body mass index over 30 kg/m.
A person who is obese.

core.definition: Extremely overweight, with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, to a degree that poses serious health risks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BEES. The final s is a voiceless 's', not a 'z', and the first syllable is 'oh' as in 'go'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical; it can be hurtful in casual conversation, so Americans often prefer 'overweight' or 'living with obesity' in polite settings.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, health reports, and government statistics use 'obese' as a medical category. In everyday talk, Americans often avoid it because it sounds harsh and stigmatizing. Saying 'overweight' is usually more polite, but 'obese' is common in health contexts.

distinctions.note: Overweight is a milder term for a BMI of 25 to 29.9; obese is a stronger medical category for a BMI of 30 or higher.
Fat is blunt and informal, and often considered rude; obese is clinical and more precise.

examples.everyday: My doctor said I'm not obese, but I should lose a few pounds to lower my blood pressure.
examples.professional: The study tracks how many obese adults in the sample develop type 2 diabetes over ten years.
examples.analytical: Defining obesity by BMI alone raises questions about whether a single numerical threshold can fairly describe health across different body compositions.

nuance.analogy: Obese is like a warning light on a car dashboard: it does not describe the whole engine, but it signals that something needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obesus, 'eaten away, stout', from obedere, 'to eat up'.
common_mistakes: Using obese as a casual insult; it sounds harsh and can be hurtful.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ob' as in 'obey'; it is 'oh-BEES'.

obese.etymology: From Latin *obēsus*, derived from *obedō* (“to devour, eat away”), from *ob* (“away”) + *edō* (“to eat”).

senses.definition: An immediate inference that denies the opposite of something previously affirmed.
senses.example: All men are mortal, so, by obversion, no men are immortal.

senses.definition: The act of turning toward or downward.

core.definition: In logic, an immediate inference that turns a statement into an equivalent one by changing its quality and negating its predicate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable 'vur.' The ending '-sion' is pronounced 'zhun' after the r in this word, so avoid saying 'ob-VER-shun.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in logic without emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter obversion mainly in philosophy and logic courses, often alongside conversion and contraposition. Outside of those fields, the word is almost never used. The second sense, turning toward or downward, is rare and mostly archaic.

distinctions.note: Conversion swaps the subject and predicate of a statement. Obversion changes the quality of the statement and negates the predicate, without swapping terms.
Contraposition swaps and negates both terms. Obversion keeps the same terms in their original order and only changes the quality and the predicate.

examples.everyday: My logic professor said that obversion turns 'all dogs are animals' into 'no dogs are non-animals,' which still means the same thing.
examples.professional: The rules engine applies obversion before matching, so the negated condition is written in a standard form.
examples.analytical: Obversion preserves logical equivalence, which is why it counts as an immediate inference rather than a new premise.

nuance.analogy: Like rewriting a sign that says 'open' as 'not closed,' obversion keeps the meaning while flipping the wording.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obversio, 'a turning toward,' from obvertere, 'to turn toward or against.'
common_mistakes: Confusing obversion with conversion, which swaps terms.
Mispronouncing the ending as 'shun' instead of 'zhun.'

senses.definition: Away from a main location; in a place not owned by a particular organization.
Away from a particular site.
A group outing or meeting that takes place outside of the office.
senses.example: They went bowling for their team offsite.

core.definition: Located away from the main workplace, such as at a hotel, another building, or a retreat venue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OFF, with a lighter stress on SITE. The word 'site' rhymes with 'light' and has the long i of 'bite'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals a change of setting for a meeting, event, or project.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'offsite' means a meeting or retreat held somewhere away from the usual workplace, such as a hotel or a lake house. It is common in emails and meeting invitations. Use 'remote' for people working from home, and use 'offsite' for events or locations.

distinctions.note: Remote describes working from home or from anywhere, while offsite refers to a location away from the office for meetings or work.
Off-campus is used for schools and universities; offsite is the common business term.

examples.everyday: Next week the whole team is going to an offsite at a lake house.
examples.professional: Let's move the planning discussion to an offsite session so we can focus without interruptions.
examples.analytical: An offsite location separates an organization's decisions from its daily routines, which changes how people reason about them.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a board game to the park: the same pieces, but a different table.
nuance.etymology: Compound of off and site, meaning away from the site.
common_mistakes: Writing 'off site' as two words in formal memos; the one-word form is standard in business writing.
Using offsite to mean remote, as in an employee working from home.

conversation.text: The leadership team is at an offsite in Napa all week.
We're planning a two-day offsite to work on next year's strategy.
Let's save the big-picture discussion for the offsite.

senses.definition: In AI: The algorithm that updates a model's parameters during training, such as stochastic gradient descent or Adam.
A compiler or assembler that produces optimized code.
A program that uses linear programming to optimize a process.
A person in a large business whose task is to maximize profits and make the business more efficient.

core.definition: In machine learning, the algorithm that updates a model's parameters during training to reduce its error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the 'my' in the middle as a full diphthong. The final '-er' is a reduced rhotic 'er' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term that carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Machine learning engineers and data scientists use 'optimizer' every day, often naming specific ones such as Adam or SGD. Outside technical work, the word is rarely used. In programming tools, it can also mean a compiler component that makes code run faster, so the context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Optimization' is the process; 'optimizer' is the algorithm or component that carries it out.
A loss function measures error; the optimizer uses that measure to adjust the model's weights.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says the optimizer choice matters more than people think.
examples.professional: We switched the optimizer to Adam, and the training loss dropped much faster in the first epoch.
examples.analytical: The choice of optimizer shapes which minima a network converges to, so the inductive bias is partly an algorithmic decision.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who checks the slope under their feet and takes a step downhill, again and again, until they reach a valley.
nuance.etymology: From 'optimize' with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'optimizer' with 'optimization' when talking about the process rather than the algorithm.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'air' instead of a reduced 'er.'

conversation.text: The optimizer decides how to update the weights from the gradients; Adam and SGD are common choices.
Remember to reset the optimizer state when you load new weights for fine-tuning.

senses.definition: A shrine dedicated to some prophetic deity.
A person such as a priest through whom the deity is supposed to respond with prophecies or advice.
A prophetic response, often enigmatic or allegorical, so given.
A person considered to be a source of wisdom.
senses.example: a literary oracle

senses.definition: A wise sentence or decision of great authority.
A fortune-teller.
One who communicates a divine command; an angel; a prophet.
The sanctuary, or most holy place in the temple; also, the temple itself.
A theoretical entity capable of answering some collection of questions.
A third-party service that provides smart contracts with information from the outside world.

core.definition: A person or sacred place through which a god was believed to give authoritative answers, predictions, or advice; a trusted source of wise guidance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r strong. The final -cle is a syllabic l with no extra vowel, so say OR-uh-kul in two beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; can be humorous when someone is jokingly called the oracle.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oracle for someone whose knowledge is trusted, like the office oracle for computer problems, often with light humor. In the literal sense it refers to ancient Greek shrines such as Delphi or to a prophetic message. Calling a friend the oracle is a compliment, but using it for a casual guess sounds overly dramatic.

distinctions.note: A prophet speaks a divine message as a person; an oracle can be the message itself or the shrine where it was given.
Expert describes skill; oracle implies a trusted authority whose answers seem almost mysterious.
Guru suggests spiritual teaching or a following; oracle focuses on answers and predictions.

examples.everyday: Ask Dana about the printer; she's the office oracle when it comes to tech problems.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is the oracle for the legacy billing system, so check with her before changing anything.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Delphic oracle gave ambiguous answers on purpose or because the questions were poorly phrased.

nuance.analogy: An oracle is like a weather forecaster whose forecasts people treat as final, even when the forecast is cryptic.
nuance.etymology: From Latin oraculum, from orare, 'to speak, pray'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable in the middle; say OR-uh-kul, not OR-uh-ku-ul.
Using oracle for any expert; the word implies authority and sometimes mystery.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word debir refers to the inner sanctuary of the temple, the most holy room where the ark was placed and where God's presence was believed to dwell. In 1 Kings 6:19 Solomon sets up the inner sanctuary for the ark of the covenant, and 1 Kings 8:6 describes the priests bringing the ark into that inner place. In the New Testament, the Greek word logion, meaning 'utterance' or 'oracle', appears in Romans 3:2, where Paul says the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God, and in Acts 7:38, where Stephen calls the law the living oracles given to Moses.

oracle.etymology: From Middle English *oracle*, from Old French *oracle*, from Latin *ōrāculum*.

senses.definition: A Hesychast, an intellectual leader of the Hesychasts.
Hesychastic.

core.definition: A follower of Gregory Palamas, a 14th-century Byzantine monk and theologian who defended hesychast prayer and the distinction between God's essence and energies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'light'. Non-native speakers often add an extra syllable or stress the second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized historical and theological term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Used almost only in academic writing on Byzantine theology, Orthodox mysticism, or church history. In American seminaries and graduate courses you might hear it in lectures on hesychasm. Outside those settings it would puzzle most listeners, so explain it when you use it. The adjective is Palamite or Hesychastic depending on the emphasis of the discussion.

distinctions.note: A Hesychast is anyone who practices the contemplative prayer of stillness; a Palamite specifically defends Palamas's theology of that prayer and God's energies.
Barlaam of Calabria was Palamas's opponent in the 14th-century debate; a Barlaamite was on the other side of the controversy.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies Orthodox history said the Palamite debate is why some monks still talk about prayer as stillness.
examples.professional: In the seminar on Byzantine spirituality, the professor framed the reading list around the Palamite position on the energies of God.
examples.analytical: The Palamite distinction between God's unknowable essence and his communicable energies allowed the hesychast tradition to claim direct experience of God without violating divine transcendence.

nuance.analogy: Think of a Palamite as a defense attorney for a particular way of prayer: the case is about whether God can truly be encountered, not just known by reasoning.
nuance.etymology: Named after Gregory Palamas, the 14th-century Byzantine theologian, from Greek Palamas.
common_mistakes: Confusing Palamite with Hesychast, which is a broader term for the practice itself.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'puh-LAM-ite'.

traditions.view: Palamas is honored as a defender of the faith. His distinction between God's essence and uncreated energies is affirmed as a safeguard for real communion with God.
Catholic theology has generally upheld divine simplicity and has not accepted a real distinction between God's essence and energies. Palamas's teaching is therefore viewed with reservation.

Protestant traditions have rarely engaged Palamas's theology directly. Reformed thinkers generally affirm divine simplicity, while some Pietist and contemplative traditions show interest in the hesychast practice of prayer.

senses.definition: Having the properties of a panacea; solving everything.

core.definition: Able to cure everything or solve every problem; claimed to be a universal remedy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, -SEE-, and make the final syllable a reduced 'un'. The word is related to panacea but has a different ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it usually criticizes an overly broad claim.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use panacean in ordinary speech; it appears mostly in essays, reviews or academic writing. Most people would say 'a cure-all' or 'a solution for everything.' If you use it, make sure your listener will understand the connection to panacea.

distinctions.note: Universal means applying to everything or everyone; panacean specifically suggests a cure or remedy for all problems.
Panacea is the noun for the remedy itself; panacean is the adjective describing its character.

examples.professional: The vendor's panacean pitch promised to fix every workflow problem with one tool.
examples.analytical: The essay critiques the panacean assumption that a single principle can resolve every moral dilemma.

nuance.analogy: Like a label that promises a cure for everything on the shelf.
nuance.etymology: Derived from panacea, from Greek panakeia, a universal remedy.
common_mistakes: Using panacean as a noun instead of an adjective.
Stressing the first syllable as PAN-uh-see-un.

senses.definition: Miscellaneous items, especially the set of equipment required for a particular activity.
senses.example: drug paraphernalia

core.definition: Equipment, tools or accessories needed for a particular activity, often a large, miscellaneous collection of small items.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third-from-last syllable, NAY. Americans reduce the middle syllables heavily, so the -ia ending sounds like 'ee-uh' and the first syllables are quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest clutter or a lot of unnecessary stuff, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for gear or belongings, like camping paraphernalia, smoking paraphernalia, or a photographer's paraphernalia. It is often said with a slightly humorous or dismissive tone about a messy pile of things. For simple everyday items, 'stuff' or 'gear' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Equipment is specific and purposeful for a task; paraphernalia is a looser collection of accessories and related items.
Gear is the more casual American word for equipment, especially outdoors or sports; paraphernalia suggests a broader or more cluttered set.

examples.everyday: We need to pack all the camping paraphernalia into the back of the car before we leave.
examples.professional: Before the site visit, the engineering team collected all the testing paraphernalia and sensors from the lab.
examples.analytical: The ritual's paraphernalia, from incense to vestments, reveals how material objects mediate the sacred for the community.

nuance.analogy: Like a toolbox that holds everything from wrenches to rubber bands, paraphernalia is a mixed collection of gear.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin paraphernalia, from Greek parapherna, property beyond a dowry, from para (beside) and phernē (dowry).
common_mistakes: Saying 'a paraphernalia' as a countable noun; say 'a piece of equipment' or 'a set of paraphernalia' instead.
Mispronouncing the stress as PAIR-uh-fer-nay-lee-uh; the main stress is on NAY.

paraphernalia.etymology: Medieval Latin *paraphernālia* (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for *paraphernālia bona* (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of *paraphernālis*, from *parapherna* + *-ālis*, from Ancient Greek *παράφερνα*, a…

senses.definition: A package wrapped, as for shipment or transport.
senses.example: I saw a brown paper parcel on my doorstep.

senses.definition: An individual consignment of cargo for shipment, regardless of size and form.
An individual item appearing on an invoice or receipt (only in the phrase bill of parcels).
A division of land bought and sold as a unit.
senses.example: I own a small parcel of land between the refinery and the fish cannery.

senses.definition: An indiscriminate or indefinite number, measure, or quantity; a collection; a group.
A small amount of food that has been wrapped up, for example a pastry.
A portion of anything taken separately; a fragment of a whole; a part.
senses.example: A certain piece of land is part and parcel of another piece.

senses.definition: To wrap something up into the form of a package.
To wrap a strip around the end of a rope.
senses.example: Worm and parcel with the lay; turn and serve the other way.

senses.definition: To divide and distribute by parts or portions; often with off, out or into.
To add a parcel or item to; to itemize.

core.definition: To divide something into portions and give them out, often with off or out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The verb has the same pronunciation as the noun, so the second syllable is a reduced 'l' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes dividing tasks, resources, or land.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use parcel out most often for tasks, money, or responsibilities being distributed among people. The phrasal form is more natural than parcel alone. In a meeting, 'Let's parcel out the research tasks' sounds natural and organized.

distinctions.note: Divide is neutral and general; parcel out suggests distributing portions deliberately to several people.
Allocate is a formal business term; parcel out is more concrete and informal.

examples.everyday: Let's parcel out the chores so nobody ends up doing all the dishes.
examples.professional: I'll parcel out the testing work across the three teams so each owns a module.
examples.analytical: The Byzantine administration parceled out imperial land among loyal officials, binding their status to the state.

nuance.analogy: To parcel out is like dealing cards from a deck: each person gets a share, and the whole is divided among them.
nuance.etymology: From the noun parcel, from Old French parcelle, small part.
common_mistakes: Omitting out or off when the sense is distribution; say 'parcel out the work' rather than 'parcel the work.'
Confusing parcel with particle or partial, which are unrelated.

parcel.etymology: From Middle English *parcel*, from Old French *parcelle* (“a small piece or part, a parcel, a particle”), from Late Latin *particella*, diminutive of Latin *particula* (“particle”), diminutive of *pars* (“part, piece”).

senses.definition: To celebrate at a party, to have fun, to enjoy oneself.
senses.example: We partied until the early hours.

senses.definition: To engage in flings, to have one-night stands, to sow one's wild oats.
To take recreational drugs.
To form a party (with).
senses.example: If you want to beat that monster, you should party with a healer.

senses.definition: A social gathering, usually of invited guests, which typically involves eating, drinking, and entertainment and often held to celebrate a particular occasion.
senses.example: I'm throwing a huge party for my 21st birthday.

senses.definition: A person or group of people constituting one side in a legal proceeding, such as in a legal action or a contract.
senses.example: The contract requires that the party of the first part pay the fee.

senses.definition: A political group considered as a formal whole, usually organized on a national basis, which contests elections and aims to form or take part in a government; a political party.
senses.example: The green party took 12% of the vote.

senses.definition: Active player characters organized into a single group.
A group of characters controlled by the player.
A group of people gathered together, especially temporarily, for a specific purpose such as travel or sport.
senses.example: We're expecting a large party from the London office.

senses.definition: A small group of birds or mammals.
(rare) A group of people forming one side in a given dispute, contest, etc. or united in maintaining a cause, policy, or opinion in opposition to others; a faction.
senses.example: The green party took 12% of the vote.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: With to: someone who takes part in an action or affair; an accessory.
senses.example: I can't possibly be (a) party to that kind of reckless behavior.

senses.definition: The Communist Party, especially as the sole political party of a communist state.
A gathering of acquaintances so that one of them may offer items for sale to the rest of them.
senses.example: Tupperware party

senses.definition: A detachment of troops selected for a particular service or duty.
senses.example: boarding party

senses.definition: (dated) A person; an individual.
senses.example: He is a queer party.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated, rare) The feeling of solidarity with and support for one's political party; partisanship, especially in political matters.
senses.label: dated, rare

senses.definition: (clarification of this definition is needed) Favoring one party; partisan.
Divided into parts of different tinctures, usually equal, and especially following the lines of one of the ordinaries.
senses.example: an escutcheon party per pale

senses.definition: (rare) Shared by two properties and serving to divide them.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A social gathering, usually of invited guests, with food, drinks and entertainment, often held to celebrate an occasion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the r clear. The final vowel is a light American 'ee', not a long 'ee' as in 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It usually suggests fun, friendship and celebration, though the political and legal senses are neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use party constantly for birthdays, holidays, housewarmings and casual get-togethers, and it is informal but polite. Saying 'Are you going to the party?' is natural. For a small, low-key gathering, Americans might say get-together or hangout, and for a formal event they might say reception or dinner.

distinctions.note: Gathering is a more general and neutral word for any group of people meeting; party implies food, drinks and fun.
Celebration focuses on marking an occasion; a party is the social event where that celebration happens.

examples.everyday: Do you want to come to my birthday party on Saturday?
examples.professional: We're planning a team party for the end of the quarter, so please send me your availability.
examples.analytical: A party in the older sense was a group of people who joined together for a common purpose, and the sense of social celebration developed later.

nuance.analogy: A party is like a pot that brings people together, with food, music and conversation filling it up.
nuance.etymology: From Old French partie, meaning a part or side, from Latin partita, meaning divided.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a party' instead of 'throw a party' or 'have a party'.
Using party for a formal event like a dinner speech, where Americans would say reception or dinner.

party.etymology: From Middle English *party*, *partye*, *partie*, from Anglo-Norman *partie*, from Old French *partie* (“side, part; portion, share; separation, division”), noun use of feminine of past participle of Old French *partir* (“to divide, separate”), from Latin…

conversation.text: Are you going to Jake's birthday party on Friday?
The party didn't really get going until after ten.
"How many in your party?" "Four, please."
Those guys love to party on the weekends.

senses.definition: A theory of the atonement holding that Christ, in his death, took on himself the punishment due to sinners, satisfying God's justice in their place.

core.definition: The view of the atonement that Christ died in sinners' place, bearing the punishment their sins deserved and so satisfying God's justice.

pronunciation.tip: Penal is PEE-nul, like 'penalty' without its short 'e'. In substitution, stress TOO; Americans say 'too', not 'tyoo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a label; for many evangelicals it is the heart of the gospel, while critics see it as too legal or violent.
nuance.usage_note: This is a common term in American evangelical theology, seminary courses and debates about the cross. It is often shortened to 'PSA' (penal substitutionary atonement). It is one of several 'atonement theories' along with Christus Victor, satisfaction and moral influence, and many theologians hold more than one together.

distinctions.note: Anselm's satisfaction theory says Christ restored the honor due to God; penal substitution, developed by the Reformers, says Christ bore the penalty for sin.
Christus Victor stresses Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil; penal substitution stresses his bearing judgment in our place.
The moral influence view says the cross changes us by showing God's love, rather than dealing with a debt or penalty.

examples.everyday: Our small group got into a long talk about penal substitution after the pastor said Jesus took our punishment.
examples.professional: The systematic theology course devotes two weeks to penal substitution and its critics.
examples.analytical: Penal substitution assumes that forgiveness without justice would compromise God's holiness, an assumption its critics challenge.

nuance.etymology: Penal from Latin poena 'penalty, punishment'; substitution from Latin substituere 'to put in place of'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing penal as 'PEN-ul'; say PEE-nul.
nuance.biblical_note: Supporters cite Isaiah 53:5-6, where the servant is wounded for our transgressions and the Lord lays on him the iniquity of us all; 2 Corinthians 5:21, where God made him to be sin who knew no sin; Galatians 3:13, where Christ became a curse for us; and 1 Peter 2:24, where he bore our sins in his body on the tree. In Romans 3:25 the RSV translates the key Greek word hilasterion as 'expiation', where some other versions say 'propitiation', a difference at the center of this debate.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology generally does not frame the cross in terms of the Father punishing the Son. It speaks of Christ trampling down death by death, healing human nature and opening the way to theosis, and many Orthodox writers criticize penal substitution as a Western legal framework.

Catholic teaching describes Christ's death as a sacrifice of atonement and as satisfaction for sin, drawing on Anselm and Aquinas, but it does not teach that the Father punished the Son. It stresses Christ's loving obedience offered on our behalf.

Penal substitution is central for Reformed and most evangelical Protestants and is taught by many Lutherans and Anglicans. Some Anabaptist, Wesleyan and mainline Protestants criticize it or place it beside other views such as Christus Victor.

senses.definition: Miserly; excessively cheap.
senses.example: The old man died a penurious wretch; eighty-thousand dollars in the mattress and as many holes in the roof.

senses.definition: Not bountiful; thin; scant.
senses.example: The penurious stew would have been more accurately labeled broth.

senses.definition: Impoverished; wanting for money.
senses.example: The poor penurious horde, naught in the cooking pot and naught in the belly.

core.definition: Extremely stingy with money, or very poor and short of money.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NYOOR, the second syllable. The yoo sound is one syllable in American English, and the ending is -ee-us, not -ee-ous.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies meanness or deprivation, so it can be harsh when describing a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use penurious in casual speech. In conversation they say stingy, cheap or tight-fisted. Penurious sounds formal or literary, and it often appears in fiction, editorials and formal writing about poverty or meanness.

distinctions.note: Stingy is common and informal, describing a reluctance to spend; penurious is formal and can also describe actual poverty.
Frugal is positive and means careful with money; penurious is negative and suggests meanness or deprivation.

examples.everyday: My uncle is so penurious that he reuses the same tea bag twice.
examples.professional: The penurious budget left the team no room for testing or training.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays the penurious household as a moral system in which every coin is weighed against dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like a wallet that refuses to open even when the price is fair.
nuance.etymology: From Latin penuria (want, need), with the English suffix -ous.
common_mistakes: Using penurious as a casual word for cheap in everyday talk, where stingy sounds more natural.
Pronouncing it with three syllables (pen-yoo-ri-us) instead of puh-NYOOR-ee-us.

senses.definition: A general belief that bad things will happen.
The doctrine that this world is the worst of all possible worlds.
The condition of being pessimal.

core.definition: The tendency to expect bad outcomes and to see the worst side of situations or people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PES. The last syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like zum, not zam or zim.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a gloomy outlook and can sound like criticism if you say someone has it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pessimism in everyday conversation and at work, often about the economy, a project, or a sports team. Calling someone a pessimist can sound judgmental, so people often say they are being realistic. The opposite is optimism, and you can name the mood in a friendly way.

distinctions.note: Cynicism is a distrust of people's motives; pessimism is an expectation that things will go badly.
Realism is an honest view of how things are; pessimism is a more negative expectation that may go beyond the evidence.

examples.everyday: I can't shake this pessimism about the weather; I'm sure it's going to rain on our picnic.
examples.professional: There's some pessimism on the team about the launch date, but the testing numbers look good.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's pessimism rests on the claim that suffering outweighs any good in human life.

nuance.analogy: Pessimism is like wearing gray-tinted glasses: everything still looks the same, but it all seems darker.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pessimus, the worst, with the suffix -ism, coined in the 1700s as the opposite of optimism.
common_mistakes: Using pessimism to mean realism when you only mean caution.
Saying pessimist as an adjective instead of pessimistic.

senses.definition: Concise and meaningful.
Of, like, or abounding in pith; spongy or having small holes or pits.

core.definition: Expressing a lot in few words; concise, forceful and meaningful. Used of speech or writing that is brief but memorable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The th is voiceless, as in think, and the final -y is a light /i/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises speech or writing that is clear and well chosen.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pithy to praise a short, clever comment, a speech or a headline, such as 'a pithy summary' or 'a pithy quote.' It is a somewhat formal word, so it sounds natural in writing, teaching or media. A typical reply is 'That's pithy, I like it.'

distinctions.note: Brief only means short, while pithy means short and also meaningful or sharp.
Concise is neutral and technical, while pithy adds a sense of wit or memorable force.

examples.everyday: My dad always has a pithy comment about the weather.
examples.professional: Give me a pithy summary of the project status for the executive slide.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues its thesis in pithy sentences that reward slow, careful reading.

nuance.analogy: A pithy remark is like a well-cut gem: small, but clear and bright.
nuance.etymology: From pith, from Old English pitha, meaning the core or essence of something.
common_mistakes: Using pithy to mean small or short in size.
Confusing pithy with pitiful, which has a very different meaning.

senses.definition: The spirit or soul.
One of three levels of a human being, the spirit, along with the body and soul.
A neume.

core.definition: In Christian theology, the Spirit or breath of God, or the spiritual life-giving principle in a human being.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'p' is silent, so start with the 'n' sound. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'a' is a reduced 'uh' sound, not 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pneuma outside theology, philosophy, and classics. In a church or Bible study you might hear it in a sermon or lecture, where it refers to the Greek word behind spirit or breath in the New Testament. In casual conversation, people say 'spirit' or 'breath' instead. Using it in everyday speech may sound overly academic.

distinctions.note: Psyche usually means the mind or personality in psychology, while pneuma refers to the breath or spirit as a divine or life-giving principle in theology.
Spirit is the everyday English word with a wide range of meanings, while pneuma is a technical term tied to the Greek of the New Testament and early Christian philosophy.

examples.everyday: In Bible study, our pastor said the Greek word pneuma can mean either breath or spirit.
examples.professional: For the seminar handout, I translated pneuma as spirit and noted that it also means breath in John 3.
examples.analytical: Paul's use of pneuma distinguishes the animating divine breath from the merely natural life of the body and soul.

nuance.analogy: Pneuma is like the wind that fills a sail: invisible, life-giving, and felt in its movement.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pneuma (breath, wind, spirit), from pneein (to breathe).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent initial 'p' as a separate sound.
Confusing pneuma with the more common English word spirit, which has broader everyday meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word pneuma means breath, wind, or spirit and is used throughout the New Testament for the Holy Spirit and for the spirit of a person. John 3:8 uses the same word for both wind and the Spirit, so the image of invisible movement is central. Romans 8:16 says the Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 lists spirit, soul, and body as parts of a person to be kept sound.

pneuma.etymology: From Ancient Greek *πνεῦμα* (“wind, breath, spirit”), from *πνέω* (“I blow, breathe”).

senses.definition: To pay a visit in an impromptu manner.

core.definition: To visit someone briefly, usually without a formal plan, as in 'I'll pop in on you later.'

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'in,' not 'pop,' because it is a phrasal verb. In fast speech, the two words run together to sound like 'pop-IN.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It suggests a relaxed, welcome visit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pop in' among friends, neighbors, and coworkers for a quick, unplanned visit. It is casual, so avoid it in formal invitations. A natural reply is 'Sure, pop in anytime,' or 'Come on in, it's open.' Saying 'Can I pop in?' by text message is also very common.

distinctions.note: Drop by is nearly identical and equally common; pop in often suggests an even shorter visit.
Visit is neutral and can be planned; pop in always suggests a quick, spontaneous stop.
Stop by is very close in meaning, and both are common in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: I'm going to pop in at my neighbor's house to drop off some tomatoes from the garden.
examples.professional: I can pop in at your desk after the meeting if you have a minute to review the draft.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'pop in' reveals an American expectation of informality, where a quick visit is seen as a sign of friendship rather than an imposition.

nuance.analogy: Pop in is like a quick knock on a door: brief, friendly, and without a formal invitation.
nuance.etymology: Pop is imitative of a sharp sound, and the sense of a quick, sudden visit is a figurative extension.
common_mistakes: Using 'pop in' for a long, planned stay; it always means a short visit.
Putting the stress on 'pop' and reducing 'in,' which makes the phrasal verb sound unnatural.

conversation.text: I'll just pop in to say hi, but I can't stay long.
My neighbor popped in to borrow some sugar.
Feel free to pop in if you're ever in the neighborhood.

senses.definition: Meriting praise; worthy of high praise.

core.definition: Deserving praise or admiration; good enough that people should openly approve of it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PRAYZ, and the last two syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like 'thee' with a quick, soft vowel. Do not say each syllable equally.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a person, action or effort, and it is often used for work, behavior or character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use praiseworthy in writing, speeches, reviews and formal feedback, such as 'Her efforts on the project were praiseworthy.' In casual talk people more often say 'great' or 'impressive.' It can sound stiff in a text message but fits a performance review, a thank-you note or a toast.

distinctions.note: Admirable focuses on the feeling of respect a person has for someone; praiseworthy focuses on the thing deserving public praise.
Commendable is slightly more formal and bureaucratic, often used for effort that is good but not outstanding.

examples.everyday: Your mom would say it was praiseworthy that you drove her to the airport at five in the morning.
examples.professional: Dana's work on cleaning the training data was praiseworthy, and the team should recognize it in the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: Aquinas held that a virtuous act is praiseworthy because it proceeds from a well-ordered will, not merely because it produces good results.

nuance.analogy: A praiseworthy act is like a gold star on a report card: it shows that the work earned approval.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English praise and worthy, from Old French and Old English roots meaning value and deserving.
common_mistakes: Saying 'praiseable' or 'praisable' instead of praiseworthy.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'prayz-WUR-thee'.

senses.definition: Comparisons showing which of two or more outputs a person preferred, used to train reward models.

core.definition: Records of comparisons showing which of two or more AI outputs a person preferred, used to train reward models.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PREF in the first word and DAY in the second. The middle syllable of 'preference' is nearly silent, so say 'PREF-er-ens', and 'data' is 'DAY-tuh' in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in machine learning with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in AI research and engineering use preference data as standard jargon for human rankings of model responses, especially in reinforcement learning from human feedback. Outside technical teams it is rarely used. In a meeting, say 'preference data' only if others share the context, and explain it briefly otherwise.

distinctions.note: Labeled data assigns a fixed category or value to each example, while preference data records relative judgments between outputs.
Training data is the broad term for any data used to train a model; preference data is a specific type of human comparison data.

examples.everyday: My friend who works at an AI company said their chatbot improves mainly from people choosing which answer they like better.
examples.professional: We need to audit the preference data before retraining, because the annotators disagreed on a large share of pairs.
examples.analytical: Preference data encodes human judgments that may reflect the annotators' cultural assumptions rather than objective quality.

nuance.analogy: Preference data is like a taste test where people say which of two dishes they like more, and the chef learns from those choices.
common_mistakes: Saying preference data means personal settings or user profiles; in AI it means human comparisons of outputs.
Stressing the middle of 'preference' as 'pref-ER-ence'; the usual stress is on PREF.

conversation.text: Preference data consists of prompts with two or more responses and a label saying which one is better.
Noisy preference data with lots of rater disagreement makes the reward model unreliable.
We collected preference data from domain experts, not general crowdworkers.

senses.definition: A menu in which the entire meal is offered at a single fixed price.
The price of such a meal.

core.definition: A restaurant menu offering a full meal, usually several courses, for one set price, with limited choices.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress the second word, 'fix', and pronounce it like English 'fix', not with the French nasal or rounded vowel. The first word is 'pree', not 'pricks'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests good value and an easy meal, though choices are limited.
nuance.usage_note: You will see 'prix fixe' on menus at mid-range and upscale American restaurants, especially for lunch or a special dinner. Americans often say 'the three-course prix fixe' or 'the prix fixe menu' when talking to a server. A natural reply when ordering is 'I'll have the prix fixe, please,' and the server may ask which options you want for each course.

distinctions.note: 'À la carte' means each dish is priced separately and you choose freely, while 'prix fixe' bundles the courses into one price.
A tasting menu is usually a long, chef-chosen series of small dishes, while a prix fixe has a set number of courses you pick from.

examples.everyday: We're getting the prix fixe tonight, so we can try three courses for thirty-five dollars.
examples.professional: Our team dinner is at a restaurant with a prix fixe menu, so we should confirm the headcount by Friday.
examples.analytical: The prix fixe format limits the diner's choices, yet it shifts the restaurant's risk toward predictable costs and waste.

nuance.analogy: A prix fixe is like a bundle deal at a store: several items for one price, with less freedom to pick.
nuance.etymology: From French, literally 'fixed price'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'prix FEKS' with a French vowel or as 'prick fix'.
Treating 'prix fixe' as meaning any fixed-price item, when it refers to a whole multi-course meal.

conversation.text: They have a prix fixe menu: three courses for forty-five dollars.
The prix fixe is a good deal if you want dessert anyway.
On weekends they only serve the prix fixe menu.

senses.definition: Inclined to waste resources or behave extravagantly.
Immoral; abandoned to vice.
Overthrown, ruined.
An abandoned person; one openly and shamelessly vicious; a dissolute person.
An overly wasteful or extravagant individual.

core.definition: Recklessly wasteful with money or resources; or, of a person, shamelessly immoral and dissolute.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ate is a reduced schwa, 'uht' or 'ut', not the 'gate' of a verb. The verb form with -ate is rare and archaic.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses strong disapproval, and it can describe a person, a habit or a government.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use profligate mostly in formal writing, journalism and literature, such as 'profligate spending' in a news story. In everyday speech they would say 'wasteful', 'spendthrift' or 'reckless'. As a noun, it describes a dissolute person and sounds old-fashioned in conversation.

distinctions.note: Wasteful is the everyday word for using resources badly; profligate is more formal and implies habitual, reckless extravagance or moral laxity.
Extravagant can be neutral or even positive when describing a generous gift; profligate is almost always negative.

examples.everyday: My brother is so profligate with his paycheck that he is always asking to borrow money.
examples.professional: The team's profligate use of compute credits was flagged in the quarterly budget review.
examples.analytical: Her argument is that a profligate culture of debt eventually undermines the moral authority of institutions.

nuance.analogy: A profligate spender is like someone pouring water on the ground at a well: the supply is there, but it is thrown away carelessly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin profligatus, 'overthrown, ruined', from profligare, 'to strike down'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as the verb 'gate'; the adjective ends in a reduced schwa.
Using profligate for mild overspending; the word implies a strong moral or practical failure.

profligate.etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1535, the verb in 1542; Latin *prōflīgātus*, perfect passive participle of *profligo* (“to strike down, cast down”) (see *-ate* and *pro-*), from *prō-* (“forward”) + *flīgō* (“to strike, dash”) + *-ō*.

senses.definition: A forecast of the future course or outcome of a situation based on what is presently known; a prediction.
A forecast of the future course or outcome of a disease or disorder based on current medical knowledge.

core.definition: A forecast of how a situation or disease is likely to develop, based on present knowledge; a prediction of outcome.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NOH, and the vowel in the first syllable is the open GA 'ah' sound, as in 'cot'. The plural 'prognoses' is pronounced prahg-NOH-seez.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a factual term, but a doctor's prognosis can sound grave when the news is bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prognosis most often in medical settings, where a doctor gives a patient a prognosis, such as 'The prognosis is good.' Outside medicine it appears in business and policy writing, but 'forecast' or 'outlook' is often more natural there. In casual talk, people say 'What's the outlook?' or 'What did the doctor say?' instead.

distinctions.note: A diagnosis identifies what the condition is now; a prognosis predicts how it will develop.
Forecast is a general word for predicting anything, while prognosis is specific to a disease or a serious situation's likely course.

examples.everyday: My uncle had surgery last week, and the doctor said the prognosis is really good.
examples.professional: Given the churn data, the prognosis for the subscription line is weak unless we fix onboarding.
examples.analytical: A prognosis is only as reliable as the models and base rates behind it, so its uncertainty must be stated openly.

nuance.analogy: A diagnosis is a photograph of where you are; a prognosis is the weather forecast for where you are headed.
nuance.etymology: From Greek prognōsis, 'foreknowledge', from pro- 'before' and gignōskein 'to know'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prognosis' for the present condition; that is the diagnosis.
Using the singular 'prognosis' for plural meaning; the plural is 'prognoses'.

prognosis.etymology: Late Latin *prognōsis* (“forecast, prediction; forecast of the course and outcome of a disease”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek *πρόγνωσις* (“forecast of the course and outcome of a disease; foreknowledge, perceiving beforehand, prediction”), from…

senses.definition: Any place to which one eagerly seeks to go and which one expects to greatly improve one's situation.

core.definition: In the Bible, the land of Canaan that God promised to Abraham's descendants; figuratively, a place or state of great hoped-for happiness or fulfillment.

pronunciation.tip: 'Promised' is pronounced 'PRAH-mist' with a final 't' sound, not 'promise-ed'. In this phrase, main stress falls on 'land', with a light stress on 'prah'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and hopeful, evoking long struggle and eventual reward. It can be ironic when the 'promise' falls short.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'the Promised Land' both for the biblical land and metaphorically, as in Martin Luther King Jr.'s last speech, which spoke of seeing the Promised Land. It appears in songs and in everyday talk about a longed-for place such as a job or city. Usually capitalized.

distinctions.note: Paradise is a place of perfect happiness, often heaven, while the Promised Land is a destination reached after journey and struggle.
Utopia is an imagined perfect society, while the Promised Land is a specific hoped-for place.
This is a biblical phrase describing the land's abundance and is often used as a synonym.

collocations: the road to the Promised Land
lead someone to the Promised Land

examples.everyday: After years of cold winters, Florida felt like the Promised Land to my parents when they retired.
examples.professional: Don't treat the new platform as the Promised Land; migrations always bring their own problems.
examples.analytical: In the Exodus narrative, the Promised Land is both a geographic gift and a covenantal test of Israel's faithfulness.

nuance.analogy: It's the finish line at the end of a long wilderness road.
nuance.etymology: From 'promise' (Latin promittere, 'send forth, assure') + 'land', a phrase popularized in English Bible translations.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'promised' as 'PRAH-mized' or 'PRAH-mi-sed'.
Writing it without capitals when it refers to the biblical land.
Using it for any good place, when it implies a goal reached after hardship.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible describes God's promise of Canaan to Abraham in Genesis 12:7 and 15:18-21. Moses leads Israel through the wilderness but sees the land only from Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 34:1-4), and Joshua leads the entry (Joshua 1-4). Hebrews 11:8-16 reads the promise as pointing to a better, heavenly country.

senses.definition: The technique of formulating instructions (prompts) for a generative AI, in order that it produce the expected output.

core.definition: The practice of writing and refining instructions (prompts) for a generative AI model to get the output you want.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word (PROMPT) and the -NEER- syllable of 'engineering'. Keep the 'en' short and unstressed, and say the final -ing as a reduced syllable, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in tech companies, universities and job postings, and it is now common in general business talk about AI tools. It does not mean building software; it is mostly writing, testing and iterating on instructions. People often say 'good prompt engineering' or 'prompt engineering skills' in résumés and meetings.

distinctions.note: Fine-tuning changes the model's internal weights with new training data; prompt engineering changes only the input and leaves the model unchanged.
Prompt design is a broader, sometimes more informal term for planning how a prompt is structured; prompt engineering implies systematic testing and iteration.

examples.everyday: My cousin does prompt engineering for a marketing firm, and she says the trick is just being very specific.
examples.professional: We hired a contractor for prompt engineering to tune the support chatbot before the product launch.
examples.analytical: Prompt engineering raises a methodological question: how do we tell whether a model reasons or merely responds to cues in the wording?

nuance.analogy: It is like learning to ask a reference librarian the right question so they find the exact book you need.
nuance.etymology: 'Prompt' from Latin promptus; 'engineering' from Latin ingenium, 'cleverness, talent'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prompt engineer' as a verb ('I prompt engineered it'); it is more natural to say 'I wrote a better prompt'.
Stressing 'ENG-ineer-ing' with the stress on the first syllable of engineering; the stress is on -NEER-.

prompt-engineering.etymology: Likely coined in 2020 by AI researcher Gwern Branwen.

conversation.text: Prompt engineering closed most of the gap before we touched fine-tuning.
A lot of prompt engineering is just writing clear instructions, which is still a real skill.
Prompt engineering means carefully wording your requests so the AI gives better, more reliable answers.

senses.definition: A prediction, especially one made by a prophet or under divine inspiration.
senses.example: French writer Nostradamus made a prophecy in his book.

senses.definition: The public interpretation of Scripture.

core.definition: A message that predicts future events, especially one believed to come from God. In religious usage, it can also mean the public interpretation of Scripture.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PRAH. The second syllable is weak and reduced, so 'fih' is quick, and the final vowel is a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use; it can be positive in religious contexts and negative when describing a doomsday forecast or someone's bold predictions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prophecy in religious conversation, in the news, and in movies and books about the future. In casual talk, people sometimes use it jokingly, as in 'That's a prophecy' for a dire prediction. Religious settings may use the second sense of Scripture interpretation.

distinctions.note: Prediction is a neutral forecast based on data or reasoning, while prophecy implies a claim of divine inspiration or uncanny foresight.
A forecast is a technical or scientific estimate, while prophecy is a religious or dramatic claim about the future.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's prophecy about the snowstorm came true, so now she thinks she's a weather expert.
examples.professional: The analyst's market prophecy looked impressive, but we could not reproduce the reasoning behind it.
examples.analytical: Prophecy in the Hebrew Bible is best understood as a message from God that addresses the present community as well as the future.

nuance.analogy: A prophecy is like a weather report from a source you trust without checking the instruments: it is a claim about the future that rests on authority rather than measurement.
nuance.etymology: From Greek prophēteia, 'inspired utterance, prediction', from prophētēs.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun prophecy with the verb prophesy, which is pronounced with a final 'eye' sound.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pruh-FEE-see'.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew nabi (נָבִיא) is the usual word for prophet, meaning one who speaks for God; the Greek prophēteia (προφητεία) means prophecy. In Scripture, prophecy is primarily God's word spoken through a human messenger, often to the present community, and only secondarily prediction. Revelation 19:10 in the RSV says 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy', linking prophecy with witness to Christ. 2 Peter 1:20-21 teaches that no prophecy of Scripture comes from human will but from men moved by the Holy Spirit. 1 Corinthians 14:1 encourages believers to desire the gift of prophesying, which Paul explains in terms of building up the church.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church recognizes a continuing gift of prophecy, understood as inspired speech that must be discerned within the life of the Church, and it honors many saints as having prophetic insight.
The Catholic Church teaches that public revelation ended with the apostles, while the charism of prophecy can be exercised in the Church under the authority and discernment of the magisterium.

Many Protestants, especially Reformed and some Lutheran groups, hold that prophecy as revelation ceased with the apostolic age, while Pentecostal and charismatic Christians affirm contemporary prophetic gifts.

prophecy.etymology: From Middle English *prophecie*, from Old French *prophetie*, from Latin *prophētīa*, from Ancient Greek *προφητεία* (“prophecy”), from *προφήτης* (“speaker of a god”), from *πρό* (“before”) + *φημί* (“to tell”).

senses.definition: Likely or expected to happen or become.
senses.example: Prospective students are those who have already applied to the university, but have yet to be admitted.

senses.definition: Anticipated in the near or far future.
Of or relating to a prospect; furnishing a prospect.
Looking forward in time; acting with foresight.
Indicating grammatically an activity about to begin.
senses.example: What some other languages convey with prospective aspect, English conveys with expressions like going to drive the car home.

senses.definition: Being a study that starts with the present situation and follows participants into the future.
A prospective (potential) member, student, employee, date, partner, etc.
senses.example: Would you like to show the prospective around?

core.definition: Expected or likely to happen or become in the future; potential.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'spek', and the first syllable is a reduced vowel. Do not say 'PRO-spective' with stress on the first syllable, and do not pronounce the final 'ive' as a long 'eve'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a person or thing that is expected to become something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'prospective' mainly in business, real estate, education and hiring, such as 'prospective buyer' or 'prospective student'. In casual talk, people say 'potential' or 'future', and 'prospective' can sound stiff in everyday conversation. A natural reply in a meeting is simply to continue the topic, since the word is descriptive rather than a question.

distinctions.note: Potential suggests a possibility or ability to develop, while prospective suggests a person or thing that is expected to take a particular role.
Future refers to time, while prospective refers to someone or something that is expected to fill a role, such as a future employer.

examples.everyday: My sister is visiting prospective colleges this month, so she's been reading their websites every night.
examples.professional: We sent the proposal to three prospective clients, and two of them asked for a follow-up call.
examples.analytical: A prospective study follows participants forward in time, which allows researchers to observe outcomes that a retrospective study could only infer.

nuance.analogy: A prospective employee is like a seed that has been planted but has not yet grown into a plant.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin prospectivus, 'looking forward', from prospicere, 'to look ahead'.
common_mistakes: Using 'prospective' to mean 'perspective', which is a different word.
Confusing it with 'prospect', the noun, when the adjective is needed before a noun.

prospective.etymology: From Middle French *prospectif*, from Late Latin *prospectivus*.

senses.definition: The act or condition of prostrating oneself (lying face-down), as a sign of humility.
A part of the ordination of Catholic and Orthodox priests, in which the ordinand lies prostrate in a gesture of submission to the will of God.
senses.example: The ordination ceremony includes a variety of rituals, rich in meaning and history, e.g., the prostration, laying on of hands, anointing of hands, giving of the chalice and paten, and sign of peace. — Diocese of Rochester, NY

senses.definition: The state of lying face down (prone).
The condition of being prostrated, as from heat; complete loss of strength.
A reverential bow performed in Middle Eastern cultures.

core.definition: The act or position of lying face-down on the ground, usually as a sign of humility, submission or worship.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -STRAY-, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun. Keep the middle vowel reduced so it does not sound like pros-TRAY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn. It is used in religious and historical descriptions and is not common in ordinary conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prostration mainly in religious studies, theology, church history and descriptions of worship. In everyday speech they would say bowing down or lying face-down. In Orthodox settings, prostrations are a regular part of worship, so the word may be heard in parish talk.

distinctions.note: A bow is a brief inclination of the head or body; prostration is a fuller act in which the whole body lies down.
Kneeling keeps the body upright on the knees, while prostration puts the whole body flat on the ground.

examples.everyday: At the Orthodox church my friend invited me to, people kept doing full prostrations during the service, and I didn't know what to expect.
examples.professional: The liturgy guide explains the timing of each prostration so visitors can follow along without confusion.
examples.analytical: Prostration in Scripture expresses worship and submission, as when the elders fall down before the throne in Revelation 4 and 5.

nuance.analogy: Prostration is like a flat stone set on the ground in front of a king: the whole body makes itself low and still.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prostratio, from prosternere, to throw down, from pro- forward and sternere to spread out.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying PRAH-stray-shun.
Confusing the noun prostration with the adjective prostrate in writing, since the noun needs the -tion ending.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, hishtachawah (הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה) means to bow down or worship, and in Greek proskyneo (προσκυνέω) means to prostrate oneself in reverence or worship. Genesis 17:3 describes Abram falling on his face before God. Matthew 2:11 says the magi fell down and worshiped the child Jesus. Revelation 7:11 describes angels falling on their faces before the throne to worship God.

traditions.view: Prostrations are a regular part of worship, often done during prayer and liturgy as an expression of repentance and reverence before God.
Prostration is used in specific rites, such as the ordination of priests and on Good Friday; kneeling is the more common posture in daily worship.
Most Protestant churches favor standing, sitting, kneeling or bowing in worship, and full prostration is rare; Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Baptist practice varies widely.

prostration.etymology: From Middle English *prostracioun,prostracyon*, from Middle French *prostration* and its etymon Latin *prōstrātiō*, from *prōstrātus*, past participle of *prōsternō*.

core.definition: An ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast of Galilee, the Greek name for Acco, now Akko in northern Israel.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'P' is silent, so start with the 't' sound. The main stress falls on the 'MAY' syllable, and the final 'is' is a short, weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans know this name mainly from Bible study, ancient history and Christian geography. In modern conversation, most people would say 'Akko' or 'Acre' for the same city. Using 'Ptolemais' in a church setting is natural if you are reading Acts.

distinctions.note: Acco is the Hebrew name used in the Old Testament, while Ptolemais is the Greek name given after the Hellenistic period.
Acre is the Crusader-era and English name for the same city, so naming it Ptolemais points to the ancient Greek period.

examples.everyday: We stopped in Ptolemais, the old name for Akko, on our trip to Israel.
examples.professional: In our church history class, we traced how Ptolemais served as a port for early Christian travel.
examples.analytical: Luke's mention of Ptolemais in Acts shows the coastal route Paul followed toward Jerusalem.

nuance.analogy: Like a town that has changed its name over centuries, so a single place appears on different maps under different labels.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Ptolemaïs, named after the Ptolemaic king Ptolemy II Philadelphus, who refounded the city.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial 'P' in Ptolemais, which is silent.
Confusing Ptolemais with Ptolemy, which is a person's name rather than a place.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament the city appears as Acco, a Hebrew name, and Judges 1:31 says that Asher did not drive out its inhabitants. In the New Testament, Acts 21:7 describes Paul's ship arriving at Ptolemais on the way from Tire to Jerusalem, where the believers greeted him. The city is the Greek name of Acco, so the Old Testament and New Testament names refer to the same place.

senses.definition: Inflicting punishment; punishing.
senses.example: Beijing imposed punitive sanctions on Canada.

core.definition: Intended to punish, or involving punishment, especially a fine, penalty or legal measure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PYOO. The later syllables are short and reduced, so say nih-tiv quickly, with the t as a clear sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes measures meant to punish, and it often appears in legal and policy discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use punitive mainly in legal, political and business contexts such as punitive damages or punitive tariffs. In casual speech they would more often say a punishment or a harsh penalty. Punitive can sound stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Corrective aims to fix a behavior, while punitive aims to make the offender suffer.
Penal refers to the criminal justice system and prisons; punitive describes the purpose or quality of a measure.

examples.everyday: The city council wants a punitive fine for people who dump trash on the street.
examples.professional: Legal counsel advised that the proposed punitive clause could expose the company to large damages.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the punitive logic of the system neglects the goal of restoring offenders to society.

nuance.analogy: A punitive measure is like a fine on a parking ticket: it is designed to make the offender pay for the wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin punitivus, from Latin punire, to punish.
common_mistakes: Using punitive as a synonym for punishment in everyday speech; punishment is the noun.
Pronouncing the first vowel as in PUNCH; the stress vowel is a long oo.

punitive.etymology: From Middle French *punitif*, from Medieval Latin *pūnitīvus*, from *pūniō* (“to punish”).

senses.definition: The pouring of wine into the chalice to rinse it after communion, the wine being then drunk by the priest.
The act or process of purifying; the removal of impurities.
senses.example: air purification

senses.definition: A religious act or rite in which a defiled person is made clean or free from sin.
senses.example: purification of the soul

core.definition: The process of removing impurities or sin from something or someone, making it clean, pure, or ritually acceptable.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAY, with a lighter secondary stress on pyoor. Say the first syllable as PYOOR with a clear American r, and don't reduce the middle vowels too much.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually describes a serious or meaningful process of cleaning or cleansing, and can refer to religious or moral renewal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use purification mainly in formal, technical, religious, or literary contexts, such as water purification, a purification rite, or a purification process in chemistry. In everyday speech, people usually say cleaning, filtering, or making clean. The word can sound elevated if used for ordinary tasks, so match it to a serious topic.

distinctions.note: Cleaning is everyday and general. Purification implies removing specific impurities, often through a deliberate process.
Filtration is a specific technical method of passing something through a filter. Purification is broader and can include distillation, chemical treatment, or ritual cleansing.
Sanitation focuses on removing germs and keeping areas hygienic. Purification focuses on removing impurities from a substance or person.

examples.everyday: The campground has a water purification system, so you can fill your bottle from the tap.
examples.professional: Our purification unit removes most of the chlorine before the water reaches the cooling system.
examples.analytical: For Paul, the purification of the heart is not achieved by ritual washing alone but by a transformation of the will.

nuance.analogy: Purification is like pouring muddy water through layers of sand and charcoal until only clear water is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin purificatio, from purificare, to make pure, from purus pure and facere to make.
common_mistakes: Saying PUR-ih-fih-KAY-shun with the stress in the wrong place.
Confusing purification with purity, the quality, when you mean the process.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, purification refers to ritual cleansing that made a person or object acceptable for worship or community life. The Hebrew word tahar means to be clean or pure, and the Greek katharismos means cleansing or purification. Leviticus 12:4 describes the days of a woman's purifying after childbirth. Luke 2:22 mentions the purification of Mary and Joseph according to the law of Moses. John 2:6 describes stone water jars used for Jewish rites of purification at Cana.

senses.definition: A small bag for carrying money.
A handbag (small bag usually used by women for carrying various small personal items)
A quantity of money given for a particular purpose.
(historical) A specific sum of money in certain countries: formerly 500 piastres in Turkey or 50 tomans in Persia.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To press (one's lips) in and together so that they protrude.
To draw up or contract into folds or wrinkles; to pucker; to knit.
To put into a purse.

core.definition: A small bag for carrying money. In the Bible, a money bag or pouch carried by travelers, and in everyday American English, a handbag.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one stressed syllable with a rhotic r, so the vowel is the r-colored sound in 'nurse'. Many learners add an extra vowel, saying 'pur-se' with two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is ordinary and carries no strong emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, purse usually means a handbag a woman carries personal items in, while wallet means the flat case for cash and cards. Americans may also say 'pocketbook' or 'handbag' in some regions, but 'purse' is the standard word. A man's small case for cash is usually called a wallet, not a purse.

distinctions.note: A wallet is a flat case for cash, cards and IDs, usually carried in a pocket; a purse is a larger bag for carrying more items.
Handbag is a more general and slightly more formal term for a bag carried by hand; purse is the more common everyday word in American speech.

examples.everyday: I left my purse on the kitchen counter, so I can't pay for the groceries yet.
examples.professional: Please bring your employee badge and a photo ID, because security will check every purse at the front desk.
examples.analytical: In the Gospel of Luke, the purse signifies the material provision that the disciples must now leave behind.

nuance.analogy: A purse is like a small room that holds your everyday belongings, while the wallet is more like a single drawer for cards and cash.
nuance.etymology: From Old English purs, from Late Latin bursa, meaning a leather bag or sack.
common_mistakes: Saying 'purse' for a men's wallet; Americans usually say wallet for a man's money case.
Adding a vowel and saying 'pur-see' instead of one syllable /pɝs/.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture a purse is a small bag or pouch for money, often carried by travelers. The Greek word is balantion.
