The raw material from which things are made, such as feedstock.
senses.example: They make beef stock from the butchery scraps that they otherwise might not have used.

senses.definition: Broth made from meat (originally bones) or vegetables, used as a basis for stew or soup.
senses.example: They make beef stock from the butchery scraps that they otherwise might not have used.

senses.definition: The type of paper used in printing.
senses.example: The books were printed on a heavier stock this year.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of film stock.
Plain soap before it is colored and perfumed.
Stock theater, summer stock theater.
The trunk and woody main stems or limbs of a tree; the base from which something grows or branches.
The plant upon which the scion is grafted.
Lineage; family; ancestry.
A larger grouping of language families: a superfamily or macrofamily.
Any of the several species of cruciferous flowers in the genus Matthiola.
A handle or stem to which the working part of an implement or weapon is attached.
The part of a rifle or shotgun that rests against the shooter's shoulder.
The handle of a whip, fishing rod, etc.
Part of a machine that supports items or holds them in place.
The headstock of a lathe, drill, etc.
The tailstock of a lathe.
A bar, stick, or rod. A ski pole.
A ski pole.
A type of (now formal or official) neckwear.
A necktie or cravat, particularly a wide necktie popular in the eighteenth century, often seen today as a part of formal wear for horse riding competitions.
A piece of black cloth worn under a clerical collar.
A bed for infants; a crib, cot, or cradle.
A piece of wood magically made to be just like a real baby and substituted for it by magical beings.
A block of wood; something fixed and solid; a pillar; a firm support; a post.
The frame or timbers on which a ship rests during construction.
Red and gray bricks, used for the exterior of walls and the front of buildings.
The beater of a fulling mill.
A thrust with a rapier; a stoccado.
A bar going through an anchor, perpendicular to the flukes.
The axle attached to the rudder, which transfers the movement of the helm to the rudder.
A pipe (vertical cylinder of ore)
In tectology, an aggregate or colony of individuals, such as trees, chains of salpae, etc.
To provide with material requisites; to store; to fill; to supply.
senses.example: to stock a warehouse with goods

senses.definition: To have on hand for sale.
senses.example: The store stocks all kinds of dried vegetables.

senses.definition: To allow (cows) to retain milk for twenty-four hours or more prior to sale.
To put in the stocks as punishment.
To fit (an anchor) with a stock, or to fasten the stock firmly in place.
(dated) To arrange cards in a certain manner for cheating purposes; to stack the deck.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Of a type normally available for purchase/in stock.
senses.example: stock items

senses.definition: Having the same configuration as cars sold to the non-racing public, or having been modified from such a car.
Straightforward, ordinary, just another, very basic.
senses.example: He gave me a stock answer.

core.definition: A flavorful liquid made by simmering bones, meat or vegetables, used as a base for soups, sauces and gravies.

pronunciation.tip: Americans pronounce the vowel as a short open ah, with no glide, and the final k is crisp and unaspirated. Most American speakers do not distinguish it from stalk in everyday speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and everyday. It is a positive word in cooking, suggesting homemade quality.
nuance.usage_note: In American cooking, stock usually means a liquid made from bones or vegetables, while broth is often a lighter, seasoned liquid meant to be sipped or used as is. Recipes call for chicken stock or vegetable stock, and cooks often make it at home. A natural conversation about soup is Did you use homemade stock or store-bought?

distinctions.note: Broth is usually a thinner, seasoned liquid that can be eaten on its own, while stock is a base ingredient that is rarely served plain.
Bouillon is often a clear, seasoned broth, and in American stores it usually means concentrated cubes or powders.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a carton of chicken stock on your way home? I want to make soup tonight.
examples.professional: For the catering order, we'll use a veal stock base so the sauces stay consistent across locations.
examples.analytical: The stock reduces during simmering, concentrating its flavor the way long reflection concentrates a thought.

nuance.analogy: Like the foundation of a house: you never serve it alone, but everything rests on it.
nuance.etymology: Old English stocc, a tree trunk or stump.
common_mistakes: Confusing stock with broth when ordering in a restaurant.
Saying stocks when you mean one carton of stock, since stocks usually means shares or investments.

stock.etymology: From Middle English *stok*, from Old English *stocc*, from **stokk*, from Proto-Germanic **stukkaz* (“tree-trunk”).

conversation.text: Use chicken stock instead of water for the rice.
Homemade stock is better than canned.
Sorry, that item is out of stock right now.
My dad has been buying tech stocks for years.

senses.definition: A subset of a space which is a space in its own right.
Any (often unspecified) method of communicating or traveling faster than light speed.
An alternative dimension or universe, access to or use of which permits faster-than-light travel or communications; hyperspace.
The psychological state of the submissive or bottom during sadomasochistic activity.

core.definition: In mathematics, a subset of a larger space that itself satisfies the rules of a space, such as a line inside a plane.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SUB. Keep the word as one smooth unit with no pause between sub and space, and make the final s clearly voiceless.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical term with no emotional charge in mathematics.
nuance.usage_note: In American mathematics courses and research, subspace is standard for a subset that is closed under the space's operations, especially in linear algebra and topology. Outside technical work, the word is rare, and in science fiction it sometimes refers to hyperspace. When talking with colleagues, specify which kind of subspace you mean, such as a linear subspace or a topological subspace.

distinctions.note: Every subspace is a subset, but a subset need not satisfy the structural rules of the larger space, so subspace is the stronger term.
In mathematics, subspace is a precise term for part of a space, while hyperspace in science fiction is an imagined dimension for faster-than-light travel.

examples.everyday: My kid asked what a subspace was, so I told her it's like a flat sheet inside a bigger room.
examples.professional: Before we apply the regression, we need to confirm that the feature vectors lie in a subspace of lower dimension.
examples.analytical: A subspace is defined by closure under addition and scalar multiplication, and this definition is what makes it inherit the structure of the ambient space.

nuance.analogy: A subspace is like a flat sheet of paper placed inside a room: it is smaller, but it has its own geometry.
nuance.etymology: From sub- (under, within) and space, a term used in mathematics from the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using subspace to mean any smaller set, without requiring that it keep the structure of the larger space.
Confusing the word with hyperspace in science fiction when speaking about mathematics.

senses.definition: The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.
senses.example: In this football tournament, three substitutions can be made during the match.

senses.definition: A substitute or replacement.
senses.example: Gary is off this weekend, so Jeff will be his substitution.

senses.definition: The expansion of the lexicon of a language by native means in correspondence to a foreign term.
The replacement of an atom, or group of atoms, in a compound, with another.

core.definition: The act of replacing one thing, person, or item with another, often to fill a gap or achieve the same result.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, TOO. The sh in -tion is pronounced like 'sh' in shoe, and the -tion ending is one syllable 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a replacement without judgment, though context can make it positive or negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use substitution in sports, cooking, math, and formal writing, for example making a substitution in a game or a substitution in a recipe. In everyday talk, people often say swap, replacement, or sub. Substitution is slightly formal, so it fits announcements, instructions, and reports better than casual chats.

distinctions.note: Replacement is usually the thing that takes the place of something broken or missing, while substitution emphasizes the act of swapping one thing for another.
An alternative is one option among several choices, while a substitution means one thing has replaced another that was intended to be used.

examples.everyday: The restaurant made a substitution and gave me sweet potato fries instead of regular fries because they ran out.
examples.professional: The vendor proposed a substitution of one component, so we need to check that it meets the same specification before approval.
examples.analytical: A substitution in an argument is valid only if the replacement term preserves the truth of the premises.

nuance.analogy: A substitution is like swapping a stand-in actor into a role: the part still needs to be filled, but the performer is different.
nuance.etymology: From Latin substitutio, from substituere (to put in place of), from sub- (under) and statuere (to set up).
common_mistakes: Using substitution as a verb; the verb is substitute.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a long vowel, so the word sounds like 'sub-stih-TYOO-shun'.
patterns: [C, U] substitution of X for Y

substitution.etymology: From Middle French *substitution*, from Late Latin *substitutio*.

senses.definition: A movie about superheroes.

core.definition: A movie whose main characters are superheroes with extraordinary powers, often based on comic book stories.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEER in superhero and on MOO in movie, so say soo-per-HEER-oh MOO-vee. The -er and -o syllables are quick and reduced, and the rhotic r stays clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lighthearted; it can be praised or mocked depending on the speaker's taste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superhero movie constantly in everyday conversation and entertainment news, usually when discussing films from Marvel or DC. People often say "superhero film" in writing, but movie is more natural in speech. A typical reply is to name a favorite or ask whether someone has seen the latest one.

distinctions.note: An action movie emphasizes fights and stunts in realistic settings, while a superhero movie centers on characters with extraordinary powers.
Comic book movie is a broader category that includes non-superhero stories, while superhero movie refers specifically to films about superheroes.

examples.everyday: Do you want to watch a superhero movie tonight, or something more relaxing?
examples.professional: The studio wants the next superhero movie to open before the summer schedule fills up, so we need the rough cut by Friday.
examples.analytical: The rise of the superhero movie reflects anxieties about institutional power that are expressed through fantasy spectacle.

nuance.analogy: A superhero movie is like a big family cookout: everyone brings a favorite dish, and the flavor comes from the shared spectacle.
nuance.etymology: Superhero comes from super (beyond) plus hero, first used in the 1910s for characters with extraordinary abilities.
common_mistakes: Saying super-hero movie with the wrong stress, putting equal weight on every word.
Dropping the r in hero, as in soo-per-HEE-oh.

conversation.text: Another superhero movie? There's a new one every month.
The kids want to see the new superhero movie.
I'm kind of tired of superhero movies.

senses.definition: An irrational number, especially one expressed using the √ symbol.
A voiceless consonant.
Involving surds, or irrational numbers; not capable of being expressed in rational numbers.
senses.example: a surd expression or quantity; a surd number

senses.definition: Unvoiced; voiceless.

core.definition: An irrational number that cannot be written as a simple fraction, especially a root such as the square root of 2, usually shown with a radical sign.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with the r-colored vowel of 'word' and 'heard', so do not add an extra vowel before the r. Do not confuse it with 'sword' (SORD) or 'absurd' (ab-SURD) when speaking.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use surd in algebra and mathematics courses, often in phrases like 'simplify the surd'. In many US classrooms students more often hear 'irrational number' or 'radical', so surd may sound specialized outside algebra. Teachers use it mainly with radical expressions like √2 or √3.

distinctions.note: Irrational number is the general term for any real number that cannot be a ratio of integers, while surd is used mainly for irrational roots and radical expressions.
A radical is the √ symbol or a root expression, while a surd is the irrational value that the radical expresses.
In phonetics, surd is a separate sense meaning a voiceless consonant, which is the same word with a different meaning.

examples.everyday: My kid's homework has surds in it, and honestly I've forgotten what those are.
examples.professional: In the numerical solver we flag any surd result and round it before storing it as a float.
examples.analytical: The Greek discovery that the diagonal of a unit square is incommensurable with its side amounts to recognizing a surd, which shook their assumption that all magnitudes are ratios.

nuance.analogy: Like a decimal that never ends and never repeats, a surd keeps going without settling into a pattern.
nuance.etymology: From Latin surdus, 'deaf' or 'mute', a translation of an Arabic term asamm, 'deaf', used for irrational numbers.
common_mistakes: Confusing surd with absurd or sword, which are different words with different sounds.
Using surd for any root, when it refers specifically to irrational roots.

surd.etymology: from Latin *surdus* (“deaf, mute”), used in mathematics for “irrational,” reflecting *ἄλογος* (“irrational, speechless”) as found in Euclid, apparently transmitted via Arabic *جِذْر أَصَمّ* (“deaf root”).

senses.definition: Tawny, dusky, dark.
Dark-skinned; black.
Darker-skinned than white, but lighter-skinned than tawny; tan.
A dark gray color.
senses.example: swarthy:

senses.definition: A swarthy person.

core.definition: Having a dark complexion, often describing skin that is naturally tanned or olive-toned.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly. The final syllable is a light 'thee' sound, with the th voiced as in 'this'.

nuance.connotation: Potentially offensive; it can describe appearance neutrally in older writing but is often associated with stereotyped descriptions of people of Mediterranean or other backgrounds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use swarthy in everyday speech because it can sound dated and sometimes insensitive when applied to people. It appears in older novels and descriptions. For a modern and respectful description, say 'dark-complexioned' or 'olive-skinned' if you are describing someone's skin tone.

distinctions.note: Tan describes skin darkened by sun exposure; swarthy describes a naturally dark complexion, often with a more old-fashioned tone.
Olive-skinned is a more common modern description of a naturally warm, medium-to-dark complexion, and is preferred in polite speech.

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a quiet, swarthy man who spent every summer working outside.
examples.professional: Avoid describing applicants by skin tone; swarthy is outdated and can read as biased in any report.
examples.analytical: The novel's swarthy villain reflects the racial stereotypes of its era, which modern critics read as a warning about the genre's assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Swarthy is like an old painting's dark wood: it describes a tone, but its frame is dated.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English swarty, from swart, meaning black or dark.
common_mistakes: Using swarthy in polite modern conversation about people's appearance.
Pronouncing the w as silent or the r too weakly.

swarthy.etymology: Alteration of obsolete *swarty*, from *swart* + *y*, from Old English *sweart* (“black”).

senses.definition: Synonym of swimming trunks.

core.definition: Short, close-fitting shorts worn by men and boys for swimming.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TRUNKS. Pronounce the r clearly after t, and finish with the -nks cluster, with a clear k sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Ordinary shopping and summer-trip vocabulary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say swim trunks or trunks for men's swimwear, and swimming trunks is also common. Surf-style longer shorts are called board shorts. Women usually say swimsuit or bathing suit.

distinctions.note: Board shorts are longer, looser surf-style shorts; swim trunks are usually shorter and closer-fitting.
Swimsuit is the general word for swimwear, usually for women; swim trunks are for men and boys.

examples.everyday: Did you pack your swim trunks for the lake trip?
examples.professional: Please bring swim trunks and a towel for the team retreat at the pool.
examples.analytical: The history of swim trunks shows beach fashion moving from long, modest cuts toward shorter styles over the twentieth century.

nuance.analogy: They are basically running shorts that learned to swim.
nuance.etymology: Trunks comes from Latin truncus, trunk of a tree; the garment sense is a later development.
common_mistakes: Saying swim pants or swim shorts; Americans say swim trunks
Dropping the k in trunks, which makes it sound like trunz

conversation.text: He forgot his swim trunks, so he swam in his shorts.
These swim trunks dry really fast.
I bought new swim trunks for the trip to Mexico.

senses.definition: Of a relation R on a set S, such that xRy if and only if yRx for all members x and y of S (that is, if the relation holds between any element and a second, it also holds between the second and the first).
senses.example: "Is a sibling of" is a symmetric relation.

senses.definition: Synonym of symmetrical.
Using the same key (or keys that are trivially related) for both encryption and decryption.

core.definition: In math, describing a relation where if x relates to y, then y also relates to x, or describing a mirror-like balance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'MEH', the second syllable. The 'r' is American and rhotic, and the final '-ic' is short, as in 'trick'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics and computing.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists use 'symmetric' in its technical sense, especially for relations, matrices and encryption. Americans in everyday talk prefer 'symmetrical' for visual balance, as in 'a symmetrical face.' In math, 'symmetric' is the standard term, and it does not always mean the same thing as the everyday sense.

distinctions.note: Symmetric is preferred in technical math and computing; symmetrical is more common in everyday descriptions of balanced shapes.
Asymmetric means not symmetric; in encryption, an asymmetric key system uses different keys for encryption and decryption.

examples.everyday: The two wings of the house look symmetrical, which is why my wife liked the design.
examples.professional: We use symmetric encryption for the internal traffic, so the same key encrypts and decrypts.
examples.analytical: A relation is symmetric when xRy implies yRx, and this property distinguishes it from reflexive and transitive relations.

nuance.analogy: Like a mirror image, where the left and right match exactly.
nuance.etymology: From Greek summetria 'commensurability', from sun- 'together' and metron 'measure'.
common_mistakes: Using 'symmetric' for everyday visual balance when 'symmetrical' sounds more natural.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SIM-uh-trik'; the stress is on the second syllable.

symmetric.etymology: From *symmetry* + *ic*, from Latin *symmetria*, from Ancient Greek *συμμετρία*.

senses.definition: A signal; anything that indicates, or is characteristic of, the presence of something else, especially of something undesirable.
senses.example: Lying, hiding one's true feelings, and having affairs are typical symptoms of a doomed marriage.

senses.definition: A perceived change in some function, sensation or appearance of a person that indicates a disease or disorder, such as fever, headache or rash; strictly, a symptom is felt or experienced by the patient, while a sign can be detected by an observer.
senses.example: The doctor told that his coughing and sneezing was the symptom of standing for too long in the rain.

core.definition: A change in your body or mind that shows you may have an illness, such as a fever, cough, or pain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SIMP. The p is often silent in fast speech, so many Americans say 'SIM-tum,' but both are acceptable. The final syllable is a weak schwa, not 'mahs'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a medical or general sign, but it can also be negative when describing problems in a situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'symptom' in everyday health talk, such as 'What are your symptoms?' or 'My symptoms started yesterday.' In medical settings, doctors distinguish symptoms, which the patient feels, from signs, which the doctor observes. Outside medicine, 'symptom' can refer to any sign of a bigger problem, as in 'a symptom of poor management.'

distinctions.note: A sign is something a doctor can observe, such as a rash or a fever, while a symptom is something the patient feels, such as pain or nausea.
A syndrome is a group of symptoms that occur together, while a symptom is a single indication.

examples.everyday: I have a sore throat and a slight cough, but no fever, so I hope those are just early symptoms of a cold.
examples.professional: The monitoring tool flagged a symptom of server overload, so the on-call engineer checked the memory usage.
examples.analytical: A symptom is significant only insofar as it points to an underlying cause, which is why diagnosis requires interpretation rather than observation alone.

nuance.analogy: A symptom is like a check-engine light in a car: it tells you something is wrong underneath, but the light itself is not the problem.
nuance.etymology: From Greek symptōma, 'chance occurrence, that which befalls', from sympiptein, 'to fall together'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'symptom' when the word you need is 'sign' for something a doctor observes.
Pronouncing the p in casual speech if you want to sound natural; most Americans drop it, though it appears in careful speech.
Using 'symptoms' as a singular noun with a plural verb; say 'a symptom is' or 'the symptoms are'.

symptom.etymology: From Middle English *sinthoma*, from Medieval Latin *sinthoma*, altered by *symptoma*, from Ancient Greek *σύμπτωμα* (“a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of *συμπίπτω* (“Ι befall”), from *συν-* (“together”) + *πίπτω* (“to fall”).

core.definition: An Egyptian city in the Nile Delta, where Judean refugees settled and where the prophet Jeremiah was taken after Jerusalem fell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced 'uh,' and the final syllable rhymes with 'keys.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a place in biblical history and carries no positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Tahpanhes is used in Bible study, historical studies, and sermons on Jeremiah. Americans would not use it in everyday conversation. In a sermon or class, you might say 'the Judeans fled to Tahpanhes in Egypt.'

distinctions.note: Tahpanhes is a city in Egypt, while Tahath is a Levite named in the genealogies.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group talked about Jeremiah's time in Tahpanhes, the Egyptian city where the refugees ended up.
examples.professional: The historical note in the study Bible explains that Tahpanhes was an important frontier city in the Delta.
examples.analytical: The prophecy against Tahpanhes shows Jeremiah confronting the Judean exiles' hope for safety in Egypt.

nuance.analogy: Tahpanhes is like a border town where people go to escape their homeland but find that trouble follows them.
common_mistakes: Confusing Tahpanhes with Tahath, which is a person's name.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Tahpanhes is an Egyptian city in the Nile Delta, identified with the Greek Daphnae and modern Tell Defenneh. Judean survivors fled there after Gedaliah's murder, and Jeremiah was taken with them, as described in Jeremiah 43:7 and 44:1. Jeremiah also prophesies against the city in Jeremiah 43:8-13, where he says Nebuchadnezzar will set up his throne at its entrance, and Ezekiel 30:18 mentions Tahpanhes in a prophecy of judgment on Egypt.

senses.definition: A three-line stanza in a poem.

core.definition: A group of three lines of verse forming one stanza, often linked by rhyme.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the 'er' be a single r-colored vowel, not 'ur-ray'. The final syllable is a reduced 'it', so do not say 'tur-SEET'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term of poetics with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tercet' mainly in poetry classes, literary criticism and discussions of verse forms such as terza rima. In casual speech people say 'three-line stanza' or 'triplet', although 'triplet' can also mean three notes played in the time of two or three children or objects. Stanzas of four lines are called quatrains.

distinctions.note: A quatrain has four lines, and a tercet has three.
In poetry 'triplet' is a loose synonym, but in everyday American speech it more often means a group of three children or three musical notes.

examples.everyday: My daughter's poetry homework was just one tercet, so she finished it in ten minutes.
examples.professional: The editor asked us to format each stanza as a tercet so the layout matches the printed anthology.
examples.analytical: Dante's terza rima is built from interlocking tercets, where the middle line of each rhymes with the first and third lines of the next.

nuance.analogy: A tercet is like a three-step staircase in verse: it carries the poem up one stanza at a time.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'terzetto', diminutive of 'terzo', 'third'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tur-SET'.
Confusing 'tercet' with 'quatrain', which has four lines.

senses.definition: A mathematical statement of some importance that has been proven to be true. Minor theorems are often called propositions. Theorems which are not very interesting in themselves but are an essential part of a bigger theorem's proof are called lemmas.
A syntactically correct expression that is deducible from the given axioms of a deductive system.
To formulate into a theorem.

core.definition: A mathematical statement that has been proven true from axioms and previously established results.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THEE, the first syllable. Americans say it in two syllables, with a rhotic r and a reduced final vowel, so it sounds like 'THEE-ruhm,' not 'THEE-or-em.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It names a result that has been rigorously proven.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theorem in mathematics, statistics, computer science and logic classes. The word refers to a proven result, so people do not call an untested idea a theorem. In everyday talk, theorem is rare, though people might say it in jokes about proof or logic.

distinctions.note: A lemma is a smaller result proven mainly to help prove a larger theorem, while a theorem is usually more important in itself.
A hypothesis is an assumption or conjecture that has not been proven, while a theorem has been proven.

examples.everyday: My brother is a math teacher, and he still gets excited when he explains the Pythagorean theorem to his kids.
examples.professional: Our data science team used the central limit theorem to justify the sample size for the survey analysis.
examples.analytical: The proof of the theorem relies on a lemma showing that every bounded sequence in this space has a convergent subsequence.

nuance.analogy: A theorem is like a bridge that has been load-tested: it has been shown to hold weight, so you can build on it without checking again.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin theorema, from Greek theorema 'contemplation, speculation,' from theorein 'to look at, consider.'
common_mistakes: Using theorem for any idea or guess, when it refers only to a proven mathematical result.
Pronouncing it as 'THEER-em' with a long e and a dropped r.

theorem.etymology: From Middle French *théorème*, from Late Latin *theōrēma*, from Ancient Greek *θεώρημα* (“speculation, proposition to be proved”), from *θεωρέω* (“to look at, view, consider, examine”), from *θεωρός* (“spectator”), from *θέα* (“a view”) + *ὁράω* (“to see,…

senses.definition: The state of being under the control of another person.
senses.example: Today's kids are in thrall to their phones.

senses.definition: A shelf; a stand for barrels, etc.

core.definition: The state of being completely controlled by another person, a habit, or a powerful feeling, usually used in 'in thrall to'.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with a rhotic 'r' after 'th'. In General American the vowel is the 'aw' of 'law', and the final 'l' is clear.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dramatic. It implies loss of freedom or will, though it can be used lightly for fascination.
nuance.usage_note: 'Thrall' is mostly found in set phrases such as 'in thrall to' or 'held in thrall'. Americans say it in books, reviews, and serious writing, rarely in casual speech. In everyday conversation, 'under the spell of' or 'completely hooked on' is more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Slave' is a literal legal status. 'Thrall' is figurative or historical and describes control by a person, force, or emotion.
'Spell' can mean a brief enchantment or a period of time. 'Thrall' suggests a deeper, longer-lasting control over a person.

examples.everyday: Since the new show came out, my whole family has been in thrall to it every night.
examples.professional: The executives seemed to be in thrall to the vendor's dashboard, and no one questioned the numbers.
examples.analytical: Many critics argue that the reader is held in thrall by the narrator, who controls what we are allowed to see.

nuance.analogy: A person in thrall is like a boat caught in a strong current, moving wherever the water pushes it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'thrǣl', meaning slave or servant, from Old Norse 'þræll'.
common_mistakes: Using 'thrall' as a verb, as in 'He thralled the crowd'; the verb is 'enthrall'.
Saying 'in thrall of' instead of 'in thrall to'.

thrall.etymology: From Middle English *thral*, *thralle*, *threl*, *threlle*, from Old English *þrǣl* (“thrall, slave, servant”), from Old Norse *þræll* (“slave”), from Proto-Germanic **þrahilaz*, **þragilaz*, **þrigilaz* (“runner, gofer, servant”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: A song or poem of lamentation or mourning for a dead person; a dirge; an elegy.

core.definition: A slow, solemn song or poem of mourning for someone who has died; a lament or elegy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a weak 'dee' with a reduced vowel. Non-native speakers often stress the second syllable or say 'three-NOD-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn; the word always implies grief and a formal, artistic expression of sorrow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use threnody mainly in literary criticism, music writing, and formal eulogies, not in casual speech. In everyday talk, people say 'a sad song for her' or 'a eulogy'. It can describe a poem, a piece of music, or a speech that mourns someone.

distinctions.note: An elegy is a broader term for any poem of mourning or reflection on death, while threnody stresses the wailing, lamenting character of the sound itself.
A dirge is a slow funeral song, often sung or played at a burial, and is plainer and more everyday than threnody.
A eulogy is a spoken tribute praising a dead person, while a threnody is primarily an expression of grief.

examples.everyday: Her grief at the funeral sounded like a long, quiet threnody.
examples.professional: The conference organizer asked the choir to perform a short threnody in memory of our late colleague.
examples.analytical: The poem functions as a threnody, transforming private grief into a public ritual of lament.

nuance.analogy: A threnody is to a funeral what a storm warning is to a coming storm: a sound that signals the loss before anyone speaks of it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thrēnōidia, from thrēnos 'wailing, lament' plus ōidē 'song'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (thre-NOD-ee) instead of the first (THREN-uh-dee).
Using threnody for any sad event or mood, when it specifically means a song or poem of mourning.

senses.definition: A group of people crowded or gathered closely together.
A group of things; a host or swarm.
To crowd into a place, especially to fill it.
To congregate.
To crowd or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of living beings.
Filled with persons or objects; crowded.
Busy; hurried.

core.definition: A large crowd of people pressed closely together, moving or gathered in one place.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable, with the aw vowel of law, which most Americans also use for cot-caught words. The ng is a single nasal sound, so do not add a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; suggests a large, lively crowd, often at an event.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use throng mostly in writing or formal speech, such as news reports and literary descriptions: a throng of fans outside the stadium. In everyday talk people would more often say a big crowd. Throng can also be a verb, as in crowds thronged the square, and it is used in that form in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Crowd is the everyday word for any group of people; throng is more formal and suggests a dense, dramatic mass.
Mob suggests an angry or disorderly group, while throng is neutral and can be festive.

examples.everyday: There was a throng of shoppers at the mall the day after Thanksgiving.
examples.professional: The conference keynote drew a throng so large that we had to open a second room.
examples.analytical: The public square was a throng of voices, each claiming to speak for the nation.

nuance.analogy: Like a throng at a concert, people moving together until they form one body.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gethrang, a crowd, related to thringan, to press.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with thong, a type of sandal or underwear.
Using throng in everyday conversation where crowd is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Gospels great crowds press around Jesus. The Greek word ochlos (ὄχλος) means a crowd or multitude. Mark 5:24 describes a great crowd following Jesus, and Luke 8:42 says the crowds thronged him as he went.

throng.etymology: From Middle English *throng*, *thrang*, from Old English *þrang*, *ġeþrang* (“crowd, press, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic **þrangwą*, **þrangwō* (“throng”), from **þrangwaz* (“pressing, narrow”), from **þrinhwaną* (“to press, to push; to force”), from…

senses.definition: Emotionally moved (by), made to feel emotion (by).
senses.example: I was touched that he should remember my birthday.

senses.definition: Slightly mentally deficient; touched in the head.

core.definition: Emotionally moved by something kind or meaningful, often in a warm or grateful way.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable ending in a hard t sound. Do not add a vowel between ch and t; it should sound like "tuhcht."

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing being moved by kindness; negative or dismissive when used to mean mentally unstable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say "I'm touched" or "That touched me" to express gratitude or emotion after a kind gesture. The meaning "touched in the head" is informal and can sound rude, so avoid it. The emotional sense is warm and common in everyday talk and writing.

distinctions.note: Moved is slightly stronger and more serious; touched is lighter and often used for small kindnesses.
Touching describes the thing that causes emotion; touched describes the person who feels it.

examples.everyday: I was really touched when my neighbor brought over soup after my surgery.
examples.professional: Our team was touched by the client's handwritten thank-you note after the project launch.
examples.analytical: Readers are often touched by the narrator's honesty, though the novel's moral claims remain ambiguous.

nuance.analogy: Like a bell that rings when struck, a touched person resonates emotionally when something kind reaches them.
nuance.etymology: From touch, referring to making contact with the feelings.
common_mistakes: Saying "I am touching" to mean being moved; use "touched" for the feeling.
Using "touched" in the head sense in polite company, which can offend.

conversation.text: I was really touched that you remembered my birthday.
We were so touched by all the cards and flowers.
Who touched my phone? The screen is all smudged.

senses.definition: Of a place: not having tracks or paths; pathless, untrodden; also, having had all tracks removed.
senses.example: a trackless desert a trackless forest

senses.definition: Leaving no track or trace when moving; also, not following any track or path.
Of a train, tram, etc.: not running on tracks.
senses.example: a trackless trolley

core.definition: Having no marked paths or tracks, so that the ground is untouched and no one has passed through.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending '-less' is short and unstressed, so say it as 'lis' rather than 'less'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to evocative. It often suggests wilderness, emptiness, or a place no one has mapped.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'trackless' in everyday speech. You will meet it in literature, travel writing, or descriptions of deserts, forests, and snow. In normal conversation, say 'no trail' or 'no paths' instead.

distinctions.note: Pathless is very close in meaning but more common in literary description of land, while trackless also suggests the absence of footprints or traces.
Uncharted means not yet mapped, while trackless describes the physical absence of tracks or marks on the ground.

examples.everyday: We drove for hours across the trackless desert, with no road signs anywhere.
examples.professional: The survey crew mapped the trackless forest before the engineers laid out the access road.
examples.analytical: In many psalms the wilderness is portrayed as trackless, a place where human paths end and divine guidance becomes necessary.

nuance.analogy: A trackless field is like fresh snow with no footprints in it: the surface is untouched and shows that no one has crossed it yet.
nuance.etymology: From track (noun) plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without'.
common_mistakes: Using 'trackless' for trains without tracks in everyday speech, where 'off-track' or 'not on rails' is clearer.
Stressing the final syllable, as in 'track-LESS'.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often describes the wilderness as a dry, uninhabited place that people cross with difficulty, and the word trackless fits this image. The RSV does not use 'trackless' itself, so the idea appears in descriptive phrases. Deuteronomy 8:15 describes the wilderness as a great and terrible place of drought, where Israel was led by God. Deuteronomy 32:10 speaks of God finding Israel in a desert land and in a howling waste. Jeremiah 2:6 describes a land of deserts and pits, where no man crossed and no man dwelt, the setting for Israel's wandering.

senses.definition: In a treacherous manner.
senses.example: The former spy behaved treacherously.

core.definition: In a way that betrays someone's trust or hides a danger.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ous ending becomes a reduced 'us', and the final -ly is a light 'lee'. Keep the r in the middle syllable, which is typical of American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It emphasizes deliberate betrayal or deception.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb mostly in writing, news reports, and dramatic or formal speech. In everyday talk, people usually say 'behind someone's back' or 'sneakily'. It is a strong word, so use it only for serious betrayal.

distinctions.note: Deceitfully stresses lying or misleading, while treacherously adds the idea of betraying a trust or loyalty.
Dangerously refers to risk, while treacherously can refer to hidden risk or betrayal.

examples.everyday: He treacherously told my boss about the plan we had made together.
examples.professional: The contractor treacherously shared confidential pricing with a competitor.
examples.analytical: The text describes how the king treacherously broke his oath to his own people.

nuance.analogy: Acting treacherously is like a friend who smiles at you while quietly locking the door behind you.
nuance.etymology: From treacherous, from Old French trecherie, 'deceit'.
common_mistakes: Using it for simple mistakes or bad luck, since it implies deliberate betrayal.
Stressing the last syllable or saying 'tree-cher-US-ly'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew root bagad means 'to deal treacherously' or 'to betray', and it is used for faithless dealing between people and toward God. Isaiah 24:16 describes the treacherous as dealing treacherously, showing the repeated word as a judgment on betrayers. Jeremiah 3:20 compares Israel's unfaithfulness to a wife who leaves her husband, describing treachery as broken loyalty. Psalm 25:3 speaks of those who act treacherously without cause, and it contrasts them with those who wait for the Lord.

senses.definition: A medical disorder where someone compulsively pulls their own hair out.

core.definition: A mental health disorder in which a person has a repeated, compulsive urge to pull out their own hair.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -MAY-, with the other syllables lighter. Many learners stress the early syllables or add an extra vowel in '-mania.' Say it as 'nee-uh' with a soft ending.

nuance.connotation: Clinical and neutral. It describes a medical condition and can be sensitive, so it should be used respectfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in medical, psychological, and health contexts. In everyday talk, people often say 'hair-pulling disorder' or simply describe the behavior. It is part of a group of body-focused repetitive behaviors, and the term appears in the DSM-5.

distinctions.note: Dermatillomania is compulsive skin picking, while trichotillomania is compulsive hair pulling.
Alopecia is hair loss from any cause, including disease or genetics, while trichotillomania is a behavioral disorder caused by pulling hair out.

examples.everyday: My cousin has trichotillomania, so she wears a hat when she feels stressed and keeps her hands busy.
examples.professional: Our school counselor attended a workshop on trichotillomania so that she could support students with hair-pulling habits.
examples.analytical: Trichotillomania is often analyzed as a body-focused repetitive behavior, linking compulsive urges to anxiety, tension relief, and reward.

nuance.analogy: Trichotillomania is like a nervous habit of tapping a pen that has grown into a compulsion, where the body acts to relieve tension even when the person wants to stop.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thrix (hair), tillein (to pull), and mania (madness, compulsion).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress by putting it on the first syllable.
Using it as a casual word for any habit of touching hair, which overstates the clinical meaning.

trichotillomania.etymology: From *tricho-* + Ancient Greek *τίλλω* (“I pull out, pluck”) + *-mania*.

senses.definition: Division or separation into three groups or pieces.

The property of an order relation whereby, given an ordered pair of elements (of a given algebraic structure), exactly one of these is true: the first element is 'less than' the second one, the second is 'less than' the first, or the two elements are equal.

core.definition: A division of something into three parts, or, in theology, a view of the human person as body, soul, and spirit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KAH, the second syllable. The last syllable is a light 'mee,' and the middle syllables are weak, so don't pronounce each one fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In theology it is a descriptive term, and in mathematics and logic it is a precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trichotomy in logic, mathematics, theology, and philosophy when discussing three-part divisions. In theology it often refers to the body, soul, and spirit view. In math it describes the trichotomy property of order relations. In everyday English, people more often say 'three parts' or 'three categories.'

distinctions.note: A dichotomy divides something into two opposed parts, while a trichotomy divides it into three.
Trichotomy is the general idea of a three-part division, while trichotomism is the specific theological belief that a person has body, soul, and spirit.

examples.everyday: The article describes a trichotomy of work, family, and hobbies, which sounds like a useful way to think about a balanced life.
examples.professional: In our ordering rules, the trichotomy property tells us that for any two values, exactly one of the three comparisons holds.
examples.analytical: The trichotomy of body, soul, and spirit in some Christian anthropologies offers a richer account of human nature than a simple dualist division.

nuance.analogy: A trichotomy is like a three-way traffic light, where every situation falls into exactly one of three states.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tricha (in three) and tomē (cutting or division).
common_mistakes: Confusing trichotomy with dichotomy, which divides into two parts.
Using trichotomy for any three items in a list, when the word implies a formal division with precise categories.
nuance.biblical_note: Trichotomy as a theological term is not a Bible word, but it is linked to New Testament passages that name spirit, soul, and body. 1 Thessalonians 5:23 prays that the whole spirit and soul and body be kept sound and blameless. Hebrews 4:12 describes God's word as dividing soul and spirit. These verses are central to debates about whether human nature has two or three parts.

senses.definition: Deserving of trust, reliable.

core.definition: Deserving of trust; reliable, honest and likely to do what you expect.

pronunciation.tip: Stress trust, with a lighter secondary stress on worthy. The r is pronounced in American speech, and the final -y sounds like ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's or something's reliability and honesty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trustworthy for people, businesses, sources and products, as in a trustworthy mechanic or a trustworthy news source. It is friendly and natural in everyday talk, and it is also common in business and professional settings. Saying someone is trustworthy is a high compliment, so use it sincerely.

distinctions.note: Reliable emphasizes consistent performance, while trustworthy emphasizes honesty and moral confidence.
Dependable is close to reliable and often describes behavior over time, while trustworthy also covers character and integrity.

examples.everyday: My sister found a trustworthy plumber who showed up on time and didn't overcharge us.
examples.professional: We want to work with a trustworthy vendor who delivers data on schedule and documents every change.
examples.analytical: A trustworthy witness is not merely accurate but is disposed to disclose the limits of what she knows.

nuance.analogy: A trustworthy person is like a sturdy bridge: you can walk across it without checking every board first.
nuance.etymology: From trust with the adjective -worthy, meaning deserving of.
common_mistakes: Using trustworthy for things that are merely accurate; it implies character or dependable behavior.
Pronouncing it trust-worth-ee with equal stress on each syllable.

senses.definition: Swollen, enlarged, bulging.
Cancerous, unhealthy.
Pompous, bombastic.

core.definition: Swollen, enlarged, or bulging; in writing, also describes pompous or overblown language.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel is 'oo' as in 'too,' not the British 'tyoo.' The final syllable is a short 'id.'

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests unhealthy swelling or inflated, pompous style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tumid mainly in medical writing or literary and critical prose, where swelling or pomposity is being described. In everyday speech, people say 'swollen' or 'puffy.' Do not confuse it with timid, which means shy.

distinctions.note: Swollen is the everyday word for enlarged by fluid or injury, while tumid is more formal and often literary.
Turgid describes overblown, pretentious writing or speech, while tumid can describe physical swelling or inflated style.

examples.everyday: The doctor said my ankle looked tumid, so she ordered an X-ray to check for a fracture.
examples.professional: The clinical note describes tumid lymph nodes in the patient's neck, which need follow-up imaging.
examples.analytical: His tumid rhetoric swells with self-importance, mistaking size for substance.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon blown up past its normal size, stretched tight and bulging.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tumidus, from tumere, 'to swell.'
common_mistakes: Confusing tumid with timid, which means shy or fearful.
Pronouncing it 'TYOO-mid' in General American speech.

senses.definition: Confused, agitated noise as made by a crowd.
A violent commotion or agitation, often with a confusion of sounds.
senses.example: the tumult of the elements

senses.definition: A riot or uprising.

core.definition: A loud, confused noise or violent commotion, often from a crowd, or a state of inner emotional agitation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak 'uh,' so do not stress the second syllable as 'MULT.'

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests disorder, noise and agitation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tumult in formal writing, journalism, and literature to describe crowds, political unrest, or emotional turmoil. In everyday speech, people say 'uproar,' 'commotion,' or 'chaos.' Tumult sounds elevated, so it fits well in a news report or essay.

distinctions.note: Uproar is an everyday word for loud, angry noise, while tumult is more formal and can describe inner feelings too.
A riot is a violent public disturbance by a group, while tumult can describe noise or agitation without violence.

examples.everyday: After the buzzer, the whole gym broke into a tumult, and nobody could hear the announcer.
examples.professional: During the outage, the chat channel descended into a tumult of conflicting instructions.
examples.analytical: Beneath the calm surface of his argument lay a tumult of doubts he never fully resolved.

nuance.analogy: Like a storm at sea, where waves, wind, and noise all crash together at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tumultus, 'uproar, commotion,' probably from tumere, 'to swell.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'tu-MULT.'
Confusing tumult with multitude, which is a large number of people.

tumult.etymology: From Old French *tumulte*, from Latin *tumultus* (“noise, tumult”).

senses.definition: That does not believe; incredulous, skeptical.

core.definition: Not believing, especially refusing to accept something, often in a religious sense, or doubtful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LEE, and the first two syllables are reduced to short uh sounds. The final ing is a light, quick sound, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. It can suggest stubbornness or refusal to accept proof.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unbelieving in religious and literary contexts, and also to describe a person who looks doubtful in a reaction, as in 'an unbelieving stare.' In everyday talk people more often say 'skeptical' or 'disbelieving.' It can sound judgmental about a person, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Disbelieving describes someone who does not accept a claim in the moment, while unbelieving can describe a settled or religious refusal to believe.
Skeptical is a neutral, intellectual word for questioning claims, while unbelieving is more often religious or literary.

examples.everyday: He gave me an unbelieving look when I said I had finished the whole marathon.
examples.professional: The stakeholders were unbelieving at first, so we showed them the raw data before presenting the forecast.
examples.analytical: In John's account, Thomas is portrayed as unbelieving until he sees the risen Christ, and then his confession becomes central.

nuance.analogy: An unbelieving mind is like a door that stays shut, even when someone knocks with good evidence.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus believing, the present participle of believe, from Old English geliefan.
common_mistakes: Using unbelieving as a noun, as in 'the unbelieving' for a single person, which is possible but usually sounds literary.
Confusing it with unbelievable, which means impossible to believe or amazing.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind unbelieving is apistos, meaning without faith or trust. In John 20:27 Jesus tells Thomas to stop being doubting and to believe. In Mark 16:14 Jesus rebukes the disciples for their unbelief and hardness of heart after they refused to trust reports of his resurrection. In Romans 11:20 Paul notes that some branches were broken off because of unbelief.

senses.definition: A Christian who denies the doctrine of the Trinity, usually stressing some distinctions between God the Father and God the Son without denying the divinity of Jesus.
Synonym of Muwahhid, a Muslim advocating God's strict unity.
Synonym of monotheist, a believer in the unity of God, particularly non-Christians (Muslims, Jews, etc.) discussed from a Christian perspective.
A person who rejects dualism in other contexts.
Espousing a unitary view of something.
senses.example: the unitarian position on deity

senses.definition: Espousing a unitary view of God.
senses.example: the unitarian position on deity

senses.definition: Espousing a unitary view of national government.
senses.example: the unitarian position on executive power

core.definition: A person who denies the Trinity and believes God is one person, not three.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAIR, the third syllable, with a strong r before the vowel. The ending is 'ee-un,' not 'ee-an.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a religious label; calling someone a Unitarian is factual, but some churches may see it as a theological critique.
nuance.usage_note: In the US the word often refers to Unitarian Universalism, a liberal, non-creedal religious movement whose members may not call themselves Christian or Trinitarian. In a theology class it refers to the historic denial of the Trinity. Avoid using it as an insult.

distinctions.note: Universalists teach that all people will be saved; Unitarians deny the Trinity. The two traditions merged in 1961 as the Unitarian Universalist Association.
A Trinitarian affirms that God is one being in three persons; a Unitarian denies this.

examples.everyday: My neighbor goes to the Unitarian church downtown, and they always have a wonderful potluck.
examples.professional: Our seminary course traces the history of Unitarian thought, from early Arian controversies to nineteenth-century New England.
examples.analytical: The Unitarian rejection of the Trinity rests on the claim that the Father alone is the one God, a claim that reads Scripture within a different Christological frame.

nuance.etymology: From Latin unitas 'oneness', from unus 'one', with the suffix -arian for an adherent.
common_mistakes: Using 'Unitarian' to mean any monotheist; the word refers to the specific denial of the Trinity.
Stressing the wrong syllable; say yoo-nuh-TAIR-ee-un, not YOO-nuh-tair-ee-un.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew echad (אֶחָד), one, appears in Deuteronomy 6:4 (RSV), which says the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Greek heis (εἷς), one, appears in 1 Corinthians 8:6 (RSV), which speaks of one God, the Father. John 17:3 (RSV) calls the Father the only true God, a verse that Unitarian readers emphasize while Trinitarian readers also read it alongside the Son's sending.

senses.definition: Lacking awareness; oblivious.
Failing to remember, recognize, or pay attention to something; heedless.
senses.example: unmindful of his promise

core.definition: Not paying attention to something, or failing to remember or consider it, often with a sense of carelessness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MIND, the second syllable. The -ful ending is reduced to 'fuhl', not 'ful' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It suggests carelessness or forgetfulness, sometimes with a moral tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use unmindful in formal writing, sermons or literature, not in everyday talk. In normal conversation they say 'forgetful', 'careless' or 'not paying attention'. It can sound old-fashioned if used casually.

distinctions.note: Mindless means thoughtless or dull, and is often insulting. Unmindful means not attending to something specific.
Forgetful describes a habit of losing memory. Unmindful describes failing to pay attention in the moment or to a duty.

examples.everyday: I was so unmindful of the time that I missed the bus again.
examples.professional: The team became unmindful of security warnings, and that oversight caused the outage.
examples.analytical: The psalmist warns against becoming unmindful of God's works, which the community must keep in memory.

nuance.analogy: Being unmindful is like walking through a familiar park with your eyes on your phone: the path is there, but you do not notice it.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus mindful, from mind (Old English gemynd, memory) plus -ful.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for 'mindless' in insults, which changes the tone.
Forgetting the preposition: 'unmindful of' is standard.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb zakar means to remember, and the RSV uses 'mindful' in Psalm 8:4, asking what man is that God is mindful of him. Deuteronomy 8:11 warns Israel to take heed lest they forget the LORD. The contrast between being mindful and unmindful of God runs through the Old Testament.

senses.definition: Not supervised; not being constantly observed.
senses.example: unsupervised learning

core.definition: Done without a supervisor watching or directing; in data science, not guided by labeled examples or human oversight.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SU, and the -ed after a z sound is just /d/ with no extra syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'pur' sound, so say 'SOO-pur-vyzd' not 'SOO-per-vi-zed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in everyday talk it can suggest a child left alone, which may sound worrying depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American talk, unsupervised describes children playing alone or teenagers left at home for a while. In data science and AI it describes methods that work without labels. In a meeting, a natural question is 'Is this supervised or unsupervised?' and a common answer is 'Unsupervised, since we have no labels yet.'

distinctions.note: Supervised describes work done with someone overseeing it, or in machine learning, training on labeled data; unsupervised is its opposite.
Self-supervised learning creates its own labels from the data, so it is technically a form of supervision, not unsupervised learning.

examples.everyday: My kids are old enough to stay home for an hour unsupervised, but I still check in by phone.
examples.professional: We left the anomaly detector running unsupervised on last month's logs to see what patterns it found.
examples.analytical: An unsupervised method cannot tell us which groups matter, only that the data separates into patterns that a human must interpret.

nuance.analogy: Sorting a box of mixed buttons by color and shape without any sample card to guide you.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus supervised, from Latin supervidere, to oversee.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable or adding an extra syllable to the -ed
Using unsupervised to mean 'without a manager' in technical discussion, where unlabeled is more precise

senses.definition: Of or relating to the viscera or bowels regarded as the origin of a person's emotions; hence, relating to or having deep internal feelings or sensibility.
Having to do with the response of the body as opposed to the intellect, as in the distinction between feeling and thinking.
Of or relating to, made up of, or positioned among or within, the viscera (“internal organs of the body, especially those contained within the abdominal and thoracic cavities”).
senses.example: visceral remains

senses.definition: Of a disease: involving the viscera.

core.definition: Felt deeply in the body and emotions rather than through careful thought; instinctive and intense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'al' is a reduced 'uhl' sound. The r is strong and clear, and the middle vowel is a quick 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to intense. It describes strong, direct feeling; it can be positive or negative depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'visceral' in reviews, journalism, and everyday talk about strong reactions, as in 'a visceral reaction' or 'a visceral fear'. It is more emotional than 'intellectual' and suggests the response comes before thinking. In casual speech people might say 'gut reaction', which carries a similar meaning.

distinctions.note: Intuitive means understood without reasoning, but visceral emphasizes strong emotional or bodily feeling.
Emotional is a broad term for feelings, while visceral suggests a raw, immediate, almost physical response.

examples.everyday: When I saw the car accident on the news, I had a visceral reaction and had to turn it off.
examples.professional: The user feedback showed a visceral response to the new interface, so the design team changed the color scheme and layout.
examples.analytical: Hume's account of sympathy relies on a visceral response, which he treats as more basic than reasoned judgment.

nuance.analogy: A visceral reaction is like a hand jerking away from a hot stove before the mind has even registered the word 'hot'.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin visceralis, from Latin viscera 'internal organs'.
common_mistakes: Using 'visceral' to mean 'vicious', which is a different idea.
Pronouncing the middle as 'vis-ser-al' with a heavy 's' and no clear 'uh'.

visceral.etymology: From Middle French *viscéral*, or from its etymon Medieval Latin *viscerālis* (“internal”) + *-al*.

senses.definition: To remove (or be removed) by washing; to clean off (dirt or the thing that it is besmirching) by washing.
senses.example: I'm trying to wash off this equipment.

core.definition: To remove dirt, paint, or stains from something by washing, or for dirt to come away when washed.

pronunciation.tip: Use the American cot vowel in 'wash' and a rounded 'aw' in 'off', and stress 'off' as the main word. Link the words so it sounds like 'wah-shAWF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes ordinary cleaning, often with a practical or humorous tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'wash off' for dirt, sunscreen, or paint on skin and objects, as in 'Make sure the sunscreen washes off before bed.' It is common in everyday speech and in product instructions. In formal writing, people may say 'be removed by washing'.

distinctions.note: Rinse off means a quick wash with water, while wash off suggests more thorough cleaning that removes stain or dirt.
Wipe off uses a cloth or hand to remove something, while wash off uses water and soap or washing action.

examples.everyday: Don't worry, the grass stain will wash off if you put the shirt in cold water.
examples.professional: Use a removable label that will wash off cleanly during the sanitation process.
examples.analytical: The metaphor suggests that moral guilt cannot simply wash off through ritual alone.

nuance.analogy: Washing off dirt is like erasing pencil marks from a whiteboard with water: the surface comes clean if the mark is not too deep.
nuance.etymology: 'Wash' from Old English 'wascan' plus 'off', from Old English 'of', meaning away from.
common_mistakes: Using 'wash off' for removing things by wiping; Americans often say 'wipe off' for a cloth.
Forgetting 'off' and saying 'wash the mud' when you mean removing it.

conversation.text: There's a hose by the gate where you can wash off your feet.
Wash off the sunscreen before you go to bed.
I need to wash off all this mud from the hike.

senses.definition: Good-looking or pleasing to the eye; handsome.

core.definition: Good-looking or pleasing to the eye; attractive, especially said of a person's appearance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on fav, and the final ed is a reduced schwa-like syllable, so it sounds like 'furd.' Do not pronounce the ed as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive, but dated. It sounds old-fashioned and literary in modern English.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use well-favored in daily speech; they would say 'good-looking' or 'attractive.' You will mostly see it in older translations of the Bible or in literary writing. Use it only if you are reading or quoting older texts.

distinctions.note: Good-looking is everyday American English; well-favored is archaic and literary.
Beautiful is broader and often refers to deeper or aesthetic qualities; well-favored is limited to outward appearance.

examples.everyday: My grandmother used to say that the boy next door was well-favored, which is her old-fashioned way of saying handsome.
examples.professional: The old candidate profile described him as well-favored, which is not a useful criterion for our hiring decisions.
examples.analytical: The translators render the Hebrew phrase as well-favored, but the Hebrew emphasizes outward appearance as a sign of divine blessing in the narrative.

nuance.analogy: Well-favored is like a faded photograph in an old album: charming and clear, but from another era.
nuance.etymology: Well (Old English wel) plus favored, from the Old French favor, meaning goodwill or appearance.
common_mistakes: Using it in modern conversation, where good-looking is expected.
Confusing it with 'favorable,' which means positive or helpful.
nuance.biblical_note: In older English Bibles, well-favored translates Hebrew phrases such as tov mar'eh, meaning good in appearance, used for attractive people. In Genesis 29:17 the narrative describes Rachel as attractive in form and appearance in contrast with her sister Leah. In 1 Samuel 16:12 David is described as ruddy with fine eyes and good in appearance, which the RSV renders with plain modern English rather than this older term. The point is that outward appearance is noted but does not determine God's choice.

senses.definition: Said when you discover a surprising connection with someone.

core.definition: An exclamation said when you find a surprising connection between yourself and another person or place.

pronunciation.tip: Reduce 'what a' to 'wut uh'. Stress 'WORLD' most strongly, and keep 'small' with a lighter secondary stress. The American 'r' in 'world' is strong and clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It expresses friendly surprise at a coincidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when they find that they share a friend, workplace, hometown or past experience with someone new. It is warm and casual. A natural reply is 'It really is!' or 'No way, what are the odds?' It is often said in small talk at parties, church, or in line at a store.

distinctions.note: Coincidence focuses on the chance event. Small world focuses on how connected people are.
What are the odds asks about the probability and often sounds more playful. Small world focuses on the connection itself.

collocations: it really is a small world
what a small world it is

examples.everyday: You grew up in Ohio too? What a small world!
examples.professional: You used to work with my manager at the bank? What a small world, we should set up a quick call.
examples.analytical: The author notes that the phrase what a small world conceals a deeper structure of social networks in which everyone is linked to everyone else through a few steps.

nuance.analogy: A small world is like a village where every road eventually leads back to a familiar face.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'small' more than 'world', which makes it sound less natural.
Forgetting that the phrase is an exclamation and using it as a flat statement.
Using it for things that are not actually surprising connections.

conversation.text: You know my sister? What a small world!
"I grew up in that town too!" "No way, what a small world!"
What a small world! We sat next to each other on the flight last year.

senses.definition: A casual greeting with a meaning similar to hi or nice to meet you.
senses.example: Hey, what's up? – Hey! Good to see you.

senses.definition: What’s the matter? What is the problem? What is wrong?
senses.example: You're looking a bit miserable. What's up?

senses.definition: What's happening? What are you doing?
senses.example: Hey, what's up? – Not much, just working.

core.definition: A casual greeting similar to hi, or a question asking what is happening or what is wrong.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on UP, and the 't' in 'what's' and 'up' is often soft or flapped in fast speech. Say it as one smooth phrase, with 'wuts' rhyming with 'cuts'.

nuance.connotation: Friendly and casual. It is warm among friends but can sound too relaxed in formal settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'What's up?' as a casual hello with friends, coworkers, or neighbors, and the usual reply is 'Not much' or 'Hey, how's it going?'. It can also ask what is wrong when someone looks upset, usually in a tone that shows concern. Avoid it in formal emails, interviews, or with people you have just met in business settings.

distinctions.note: 'What's up?' is a quicker greeting that can mean hello, while 'What's new?' invites news about the past period of someone's life.
'What's wrong?' directly asks about a problem, while 'What's up?' can also mean hi, so context decides the meaning.

examples.everyday: Hey, what's up? Want to grab a burger after work?
examples.professional: Hey Sam, what's up with the deployment? Is it still on for tonight?
examples.analytical: In American English, 'What's up?' works as a greeting and as a probe for trouble, and listeners rely on tone to tell which one is meant.

nuance.analogy: It is like a light tap on a door: it announces you are there and invites a short reply.
common_mistakes: Using 'What's up?' with a stranger in a formal interview; a formal greeting like 'Good morning' is better.
Answering with a long explanation when the speaker only meant hello; a short 'Not much, you?' is normal.

what's-up.etymology: Popularized by the cartoon character Bugs Bunny as part of his catchphrase “Eh.

conversation.text: Hey, what's up? Haven't seen you around lately.
"What's up?" "Not much, just getting ready for the weekend."
You look kind of stressed. What's up?
What's up with the traffic today? It's a total mess.

senses.definition: To cajole or attempt to persuade by flattery.
senses.example: I’d like one of those, too, if you can wheedle him into telling you where he got it.

senses.definition: To obtain by flattery, guile, or trickery.

core.definition: To coax someone into doing something through flattery, sweet talk, or persistent pleading.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final 'le' is a reduced syllable like 'dul'. The dictionary's /ʍ/ is a 'wh' sound used by few Americans, so say a plain 'w'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests the speaker is using charm or pressure to get what they want, sometimes dishonestly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wheedle' for kids who beg a parent for candy, or a salesperson who flatters a customer into buying. It is more casual than 'persuade' and has a slightly critical tone. You can say 'She wheedled a discount out of the manager' in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: 'Coax' is gentle and patient, while 'wheedle' suggests flattery or pressure, sometimes with a slightly unpleasant intent.
'Cajole' also means to persuade by flattery, but it often involves more coaxing and charm, while 'wheedle' sounds more persistent and a bit sly.

examples.everyday: My daughter wheedled me into buying her a second ice cream cone.
examples.professional: He wheedled an extension on the deadline out of the client by praising her design work.
examples.analytical: To wheedle is to exploit affection or vanity as a lever, which makes the act a subtle form of moral pressure rather than open argument.

nuance.analogy: It is like a cat that rubs against your leg until you give it a treat: soft pressure that gets results.
common_mistakes: Using 'wheedle' for a formal request to a boss; it sounds manipulative, so use 'ask' or 'request' instead.
Spelling it 'wheadle' or 'weedle'; the correct spelling is 'wheedle'.

senses.definition: Thinking about unpleasant things that have happened or that might happen; feeling afraid and unhappy.
senses.example: She was worried about her son who had been sent off to fight in the war.

core.definition: Anxious and troubled, thinking about things that have gone wrong or might go wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and use the 'ur' vowel of 'fur,' not the long o of 'worn.' Say it as two syllables, 'WUR-id'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it expresses unease or distress, though it is sympathetic when used about someone you care about.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'worried' for everyday concern about people and situations, such as 'I'm worried about her.' Use 'about' or 'that' after it ('I'm worried that we're late'). It is less intense than 'terrified' and more personal than 'concerned,' which sounds more formal or professional.

distinctions.note: Concerned is more formal and polite; worried suggests more personal anxiety.
Nervous is about tension before an event; worried is about outcomes or someone's welfare.

examples.everyday: I'm worried about Dad; he hasn't answered his phone all day.
examples.professional: I'm worried that the deadline is too tight for the QA team to finish testing.
examples.analytical: The author is worried less about failure than about the quiet erosion of meaning in ordinary life.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio left on in the background, always making a little noise in your mind.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wyrgan, meaning to strangle, later 'to harass,' through Middle English wirien.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long o, as 'WOR-reed'
Saying 'worried of' instead of 'worried about'

conversation.text: I'm worried about my dad; he hasn't been feeling well.
Don't be worried. They're probably just stuck in traffic.
We were so worried when you didn't answer your phone.

senses.definition: Initialism of explainable artificial intelligence.

core.definition: Explainable AI: methods that make an artificial intelligence system's decisions understandable to people.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters one by one: 'eks,' 'ay,' 'eye,' with the main stress on the last letter. Do not say it as one word like 'zack-sigh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; positive when describing transparency goals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the letters separately in technical meetings, papers, and product discussions. You will hear it in data science teams, AI product talks, and regulatory discussions. Usually you should say 'explainable AI' first, then use 'XAI' after that.

distinctions.note: Interpretability usually means how well a model's internal workings can be understood; XAI often includes post-hoc explanations of outputs.
Transparency is a broader idea about openness of a system; XAI is a more specific technical field.

examples.everyday: My cousin works on something called XAI, which as far as I can tell makes computers explain themselves.
examples.professional: In the review, we agreed to add XAI reports so the business team can see why the model flagged each claim.
examples.analytical: Advocates of XAI assume that explanation builds trust, but explanations can themselves mislead if they are unfaithful to the model.

nuance.analogy: XAI is like asking a chess engine to narrate its moves, so you can judge whether its reasoning makes sense.
nuance.etymology: An initialism from 'explainable artificial intelligence,' formed from the initial letters of the phrase.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing XAI as one word, 'zack-sigh.'
Using it before explaining the term to people outside the field.

conversation.text: XAI, short for explainable AI, covers methods like SHAP values and saliency maps.
Some XAI explanations are unstable: small input changes produce very different attributions.
The XAI dashboard shows which features drove each individual prediction.

core.definition: A servant of King Saul's household who told David about Saul's grandson Mephibosheth and later received Mephibosheth's property.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, ZY, with a long i as in 'eye'. The final syllable is a light schwa sound, so do not say ZEE-bah.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name in Bible study and sermons, usually when discussing David's kindness to Saul's family. There is no everyday use. If someone mentions him, a natural reply is to ask what happened in that story.

distinctions.note: Ziba is a servant who received property, while Mephibosheth is Saul's grandson who was shown kindness by David.

examples.everyday: Do you remember Ziba from the David story? He was Saul's servant who told David about Mephibosheth.
examples.professional: When I teach 2 Samuel 9, I point out that Ziba is the link that allows David to fulfill his promise to Jonathan.
examples.analytical: The narrative of Ziba's accusation and David's division of the land in 2 Samuel 16 and 19 raises questions about trust, rumor and royal justice.

nuance.analogy: Like a trusted messenger who brings news to the king that changes the fortunes of a whole family.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as zi-BAH.
Confusing Ziba with Zibeon, who is a different biblical figure.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a short i.
nuance.biblical_note: Ziba appears as a servant of Saul in 2 Samuel 9:2, where David asks about surviving members of Saul's house and Ziba is brought to him. In 2 Samuel 9:9-10 David gives Ziba the land of Saul and his sons to farm for Mephibosheth. In 2 Samuel 16:1-4 Ziba brings David supplies and accuses Mephibosheth of disloyalty, and David gives him Mephibosheth's property.
